“Trump’s federal government has moved from partnership with election officials to suspicion and hostility,” he wrote in an email. “We will continue to ensure voters have their voices heard and stand up against any federal interference.”
The document was contained in a trove of records released by the left-leaning nonprofit Democracy Forward. It detailed scrutiny into nonprofit organizations involved in voter registration — none of which are in Colorado — and it described the potential for undercover operations to find organizations “suspected of illegal alien registration and voter encouragement.” It then lists the 15 states that the Cross-Border Financial Crime Center within Homeland Security Investigations planned to analyze ahead of the primary elections.
The records spotlight the Trump administration’s focus on finding noncitizen voters as the midterm election approaches. Studies and government audits have consistently shown that voter fraud by noncitizens is extremely rare.
“If an organization is found to be actively recruiting illegal aliens for voter registration, (undercover) assets may be used to gather evidence, disrupt activities, and trace financial backing and support structures,” the document reads. “These efforts will support broader investigative and enforcement actions, leveraging UC findings to initiate prosecutions and dismantle illicit facilitation networks.”
The report also claims that Heather Honey, a 2020 election denier and DHS official, obtained 48.4 million records through “independent sources of information.” The agency also drew upon 50.6 million records from the Department of Justice, but it’s not clear what any of those records are.
The records release also includes a letter from Todd Lyons, the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, to Secretary of State Jena Griswold stating that there is “no reason” for ICE officers to be at polling locations. It was a response to a March inquiry from Griswold.
“However, ICE Homeland Security Investigations plays an important role in investigating voter fraud, and will continue to perform this vital mission,” the letter reads.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Humor: Grits, bugs and all the dirt on SC for newcomers
description: Dear Newcomer, Thank you for making South Carolina the fastest-growing state in the nation. And welcome to the land of kudzu, diabetes and data centers. No doubt y’all have a lot of questions. Here are some basics about South Carolina you need to know. South Carolina has four seasons: summer, almost summer, still summer, and […]
text:
The moon rises behind the flags atop the South Carolina Statehouse dome in Columbia, S.C. on Tuesday, March 11, 2025. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Dear Newcomer,
Thank you for making South Carolina the fastest-growing state in the nation.
And welcome to the land of kudzu, diabetes and data centers.
No doubt y’all have a lot of questions.
Here are some basics about South Carolina you need to know.
South Carolina has four seasons: summer, almost summer, still summer, and Christmas.
We don’t have global warming in South Carolina. We have global scorching.
Our state food is grits. This is not a side dish. Grits are a way of life.
Our state hospitality drink truly is sweet tea. We do not know how to make unsweet tea.
Our state vegetable is meat.
Our water quality is so good, it’s almost drinkable.
Our state bird is the mosquito.
Our state insect is the flying palmetto bug reading over your shoulder.
Our state reptile is that thing that just crawled under your porch.
Our state dog is all of them.
Our state flower is kudzu. (It isn’t but give it time.)
Our favorite style of home is mobile.
Our state highway is under construction.
Our individual retirement plan is winning the South Carolina lottery.
Contrary to what you’ve heard, South Carolinians are not a little crazy. We’re a whole lotta crazy.
We’re like the weather here: often unpredictable. We don’t have climate change. We have climate deranged.
South Carolinians will warmly welcome a newcomer — unless you brought your opinions with you.
When we disagree with you, we’ll disagree politely. Then we’ll talk about you after you leave.
We’re a state that loves to share generously — whether it’s food, stories or measles.
South Carolina has all three major religions: fundamentalism, evangelicalism, and football.
We argue about politics. We argue violently about barbecue.
In South Carolina, we don’t ask whether something can be fried. We ask why it hasn’t been fried already.
We always complain about our politicians, and we gleefully re-elect the same politicians so we’ll have something to complain about.
Speaking of which, state lawmakers were six weeks late in approving a state budget this year and punished themselves by doubling their own pay.
If a member of South Carolina’s congressional delegation holds a town hall meeting … just kidding, the congressional delegation doesn’t hold town hall meetings.
South Carolinians, in short, are friendly folk, even when we dislike you. If we say “bless your heart,” you should probably watch your back.
Please stop telling us how much better things were where you came from.
Life is slower here, and we do tend to mosey along. If you need something done right away, bless your heart.
South Carolinians on the road
South Carolina motorists drive either 15 miles an hour or 90 miles an hour. There’s nothing in between.
Many South Carolina motorists drive with their bright lights on, not to see better but to annoy you.
South Carolina drivers have heard of turn signals, but we haven’t found them yet.
If somebody tells you something is “just down the road,” bring a lunch.
We don’t have speed bumps on the road. There’s no need. The potholes control speed just fine.
If you see a deer cross the road, slow down. Mama Deer and Baby Deer are likely right behind.
Our utility poles often look brand new, thanks to the regular replacement program known as hurricanes.
SC’s new choral anthem puts Revolutionary motto to music

South Carolinians identify themselves not by region of the state but by their high school.
Friday night is for high school football. Attendance is mandatory.
Just so you know, a newcomer is someone who has been here less than 50 years. A “native” requires three generations and a family cemetery.
Modernity has not passed us by. It has never come anywhere near us.
Just kidding. We have smartphones, high-speed internet and several counties where nobody can get a cell signal.
Don’t be surprised to see a Confederate battle flag around rural South Carolina. In South Carolina, the past is not dead. It’s not even past.
In fact, the past is often the future.
One of our state mottos is “Prepared in mind and resources.”
Please note: We are not prepared.
But welcome, anyway.

title: NC counties prepare for Thursday start of in-person early voting
description: Elections officials across North Carolina are preparing for the 17-day early voting period that starts Thursday, Oct, 15.  Citizens are able to vote in-person at locations in their counties. Those who missed the regular voter registration deadline are able to register or update their registration and vote at the same time at early voting sites. […]
text:
A crew unloads early voting equipment and tables at the John M. Brown Community Center in Apex on Oct. 12, 2026  This location has had among the highest early-voting turnout numbers in the state, Wake Elections Director Olivia McCall said. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)Elections officials across North Carolina are preparing for the 17-day early voting period that starts Thursday, Oct, 15. 
Citizens are able to vote in-person at locations in their counties. Those who missed the regular voter registration deadline are able to register or update their registration and vote at the same time at early voting sites. Voters who use mail-in ballots may return them at early voting sites. 
Early voting has consistently been the most popular way to cast ballots in North Carolina general elections since 2016, Catawba College political scientist Michael Bitzer has found. 
Wake County will have 18 early voting sites, the most the county has ever had for a midterm election, said Wake Elections Director Olivia McCall. 
Delivery and set up of tables and voting booths at early voting locations started last week, she said. 
McCall suggested voters check their sample ballots, which are available online at the NC Board of Elections voter lookup site, to familiarize themselves with contests and ballot questions. Voters may print out and bring in their sample ballots to the polls to use as a reference as they mark the real thing. 
Early voting turnout ebbs and peaks during the 17 days. The busiest days in Wake tend to be toward the end of the early voting period, McCall said, with the last day producing the longest lines. Early voting ends this year on Oct. 31. Hours around lunch time also tend to be busy, she said. 
Wake County voters can find early voting locations and wait times at readytovote.com. The site also has bus routes to early voting sites, sample ballots, and other information for Wake voters. 
On Election Day, voters must go to their assigned polling place. Same-day registration is not allowed on Election Day, and mail-in voters cannot hand-deliver their ballots to polling precincts on Election Day, 
Setting early voting schedules came with some political turbulence this year, with Democrats and Republicans at both the state and county levels differing on locations and Sunday voting hours.
NC Board of Elections votes along party lines to reject most Sunday early voting hours

In Wake, Democratic and Republican elections board members were initially divided over an early voting site at the Talley Student Union at the center of the main campus. Republican members pushed through their preferred alternative, a building at the edge of the main campus, the NC State University Western Boulevard Business Services building at 1220 Varsity Drive.  
Wake has Sunday early voting hours. 
Tables and voting booths were set up at the business services building last week, McCall said. The building has a good layout for voting equipment and ample parking, she said. 
The business services building is about a mile from the Talley Center. Students who opposed moving the early voting site were worried about not having the time to fit in walking to the business services building with their class and study schedules. 
Pack the Polls, the NC State voter education and engagement project, is sponsoring a free shuttle service from Talley and Centennial Campus to the business services building from Oct. 21 to Oct. 31.

title: Handmade treasures, Delaware artisans take center stage at Hagley Craft Fair this weekend
description: From handcrafted jewelry and award-winning wildlife photography to homemade preserves, the Oct. 17-18 fair offers something beyond ordinary shopping. WILMINGTON — A jar of homemade Delaware preserves, a piece of copper jewelry colored by fire or an award-winning photograph of wildlife could become someone’s favorite holiday gift this year. Those are just a f[...]
text:
From handcrafted jewelry and award-winning wildlife photography to homemade preserves, the Oct. 17-18 fair offers something beyond ordinary shopping.
WILMINGTON — A jar of homemade Delaware preserves, a piece of copper jewelry colored by fire or an award-winning photograph of wildlife could become someone’s favorite holiday gift this year.
Those are just a few of the discoveries awaiting visitors to the annual Hagley Craft Fair, returning Saturday, Oct. 17, and Sunday, Oct. 18, to Hagley Museum and Library along the Brandywine.
The two-day event brings together artisans from across the Mid-Atlantic, transforming Hagley’s historic upper property and Soda House into a marketplace of handmade jewelry, fine art, pottery, woodworking, textiles and gourmet foods.
For Delaware residents, the event is more than an opportunity to begin holiday shopping. It’s a chance to meet the artists and small-business owners behind the products, discover regional talent and enjoy one of the state’s most picturesque historic properties during the fall season.
Among this year’s exhibitors are several makers whose work and personal stories offer a glimpse into the creativity behind the fair.
From a Delaware backyard to a thriving food business
One of the fair’s distinctly Delaware exhibitors is Backyard Jams and Jellies, a Milton-based company offering more than 90 varieties of jams, jellies, mustards, chutneys and other preserves.
The business traces its beginnings to founder Krista Scudlark, who started making preserves from fruit grown in her backyard more than 25 years ago.
What began as a way to use an abundant harvest grew into a specialty food business recognized at farmers markets and shops throughout Delaware.
In 2023, Andrew and Janece Pipon purchased the business, continuing its small-batch production methods and original recipes while introducing additional varieties.
The company remains connected to Delaware agriculture through its use of ingredients from regional farmers.
Its selection ranges from traditional fruit preserves to pepper jellies and savory products, offering shoppers an opportunity to discover gifts made close to home.
Turning fire into wearable art
Visitors looking for something less traditional may be drawn to 222 Creations, which specializes in torch-fired copper enamel jewelry and flame-painted copper designs.
Unlike jewelry produced using standardized manufacturing techniques, flame painting uses heat to produce changing colors and patterns on copper.
The result is jewelry that can be difficult to reproduce exactly, making individual pieces distinctive.
The artist behind 222 Creations explains that while the flame patterns can be guided, the resulting colors are influenced by the heating process.
The work demonstrates one of the attractions of an artisan show: discovering how an artist transforms an ordinary material into something unexpected.
Jewelry designed to become an heirloom
Another featured exhibitor, Anna Biggs Designs, approaches jewelry as a form of sculpture.
Biggs creates hand-carved designs in silver and gold, producing pieces that combine fine-art craftsmanship with jewelry intended to be worn.
Her collections include rings, earrings and necklaces featuring distinctive shapes and detailed metalwork.
For shoppers interested in a special gift or a piece of jewelry that can be treasured for years, her work offers an alternative to mass-produced accessories.
Delaware photographer earns recognition beyond the state
The fair also features the work of Heather Orkis, a wildlife photographer from Townsend whose photographs have earned recognition in national and international competitions.
Orkis specializes in wildlife, particularly ducks and other waterfowl.
Her accomplishments include a 2023 honorable mention in the National Wildlife Federation’s photography competition, recognition from the Ward Museum of Wildfowl Art and a winning entry in a Ducks Unlimited waterfowl photography competition.
Her photographs also have appeared in a national Ducks Unlimited calendar.
Orkis, who works as a paramedic, describes wildlife photography as an opportunity to find solitude and relaxation away from the demands of emergency medical work.
Her photography demonstrates that Delaware’s creative community includes artists whose work reaches well beyond the state’s borders.
More than jewelry and fine art
The fair’s variety extends far beyond these featured exhibitors.
Visitors can browse handmade pottery, wood carvings, furniture, hand-dyed textiles, leather goods, decorative metalwork, glass art and specialty foods.
Other exhibitors on Hagley’s 2026 vendor list include the Delaware Woodworkers Guild, Blue Fox Studio, Avant Garden Pottery, Blazing Bella and Waggies by Maggie & Friends, a nonprofit dog-treat business whose mission includes employing people with intellectual disabilities.
The mix of established artisans, small businesses and specialty producers makes the show attractive to visitors with different interests and budgets.
For those shopping ahead of the holidays, the fair offers opportunities to buy gifts directly from their makers while supporting independent businesses.
A fall outing with a little history
The setting is part of the appeal.
Exhibitors will occupy Hagley’s upper grounds and historic Soda House building, allowing visitors to browse inside and outside while enjoying the surrounding landscape.
The Hagley Museum Store and Hagley Handwork Group also will be located in the Library Copeland Room.
Food trucks will provide refreshments, and shuttle transportation will be available throughout the event.
Admission includes access to the historic du Pont family home and gardens, giving visitors an opportunity to combine shopping with an exploration of Delaware history.
Tickets are valid for both days, and the fair will take place rain or shine.
For anyone who enjoys handmade craftsmanship, local entrepreneurship and the colors of a Brandywine Valley autumn, the Hagley Craft Fair offers an opportunity to experience all three in one weekend.

title: US senators from both parties blast Trump order to import Russian diesel as illegal
text:
The Trump administration’s order to allow import of Russian diesel violates a 2022 law banning Russian energy imports while the country’s war with Ukraine is ongoing, according to a bipartisan group of U.S. senators.Following an Oct. 9 call between President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control lifted sanctions against the “import sale, delivery, offloading, or importation” of Russian diesel. Prices of diesel have skyrocketed in recent months during Trump’s war in Iran.The administration did not consult with Congress before lifting the sanctions, which is required by the 2022 law, six senators said Sunday in a statement.Senate Foreign Relations Committee ranking Democrat Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Democrat Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Republicans Susan Collins of Maine, John Curtis of Utah, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina called on Trump to “immediately reverse course.”“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine,” they wrote. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law,” the group added.U.S. Rep. Lloyd Doggett, a Texas Democrat who sponsored the 2022 law blocking imports of Russian energy products, also said in a Monday statement the administration’s move was illegal.“Trump is directly violating that law, lifting sanctions to permit the first Russian diesel imports into the United States since the law took effect, without satisfying the specific legal conditions it requires,” he wrote. “He illegally rewards his pal Putin while once again blaming Zelensky for not capitulating to Putin. Meanwhile, every day Putin murders more Ukrainian civilians.”Broad support for law The law passed the Senate unanimously and the House 413-9 before President Joe Biden signed it in April 2022, shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine.It allows for the president to lift sanctions on Russian energy imports, after consultation with Congress, if Russia has withdrawn from Ukraine, recognized Ukraine’s right to independence and poses no immediate threat to any NATO members. Throughout his second term, Trump has attempted to use trade policy, including an aggressive tariffs schedule, to extract concessions from foreign governments.

 






Gas and diesel prices in Forest Glen, Maryland, on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)

But reopening Russian energy imports appears to break with that record. Trump did not announce any accommodation Russia provided to reenter the U.S. market, instead framing the move explicitly in domestic economic terms.“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST,” he wrote on social media Friday. “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority. This is a very big and important announcement.”The agreement is in effect until April 7, 2027.The nationwide average price for a gallon of diesel last week was $6.20, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. That marks a $2.49 increase, or 67%, from a year ago. The price of fuel, including diesel, and other consumer goods is among the top campaign issues for the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Diesel prices are particularly important in farm states like Iowa, Kansas and Texas. Democrats in U.S. Senate races in those generally red states are polling unusually well this year.Spokespeople for the White House and Treasury Department did not respond to messages seeking comment Monday.

name: National
title: Researchers point to community violence programs, pandemic recovery in historic homicide decline
description: As candidates debate public safety ahead of the midterm elections, a new assessment of the nation’s historic homicide decline suggests there is no single explanation for the drop — and that some widely discussed enforcement strategies may have played little role. A survey of nearly 50 crime scholars convened by the nonpartisan Council on Criminal […]
text:
Police investigate a crime scene where three people were shot at a housing complex in Chicago. A new survey of nearly 50 crime scholars points to community violence intervention programs, pandemic recovery and focused deterrence as potential contributors to the historic decline in homicides in the United States. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)As candidates debate public safety ahead of the midterm elections, a new assessment of the nation’s historic homicide decline suggests there is no single explanation for the drop — and that some widely discussed enforcement strategies may have played little role.
A survey of nearly 50 crime scholars convened by the nonpartisan Council on Criminal Justice found the strongest support that the top contributing factors to the drop in homicide rates have been community violence intervention programs, the easing of pandemic-related disruptions, and focused deterrence strategies that pair law enforcement with social services.
The findings come amid a historic national decline in homicide. In 2025, the estimated U.S. murder and nonnegligent manslaughter rate fell 18.1% compared with 2024, which equates to about 4 killings per 100,000 people. It tied the lowest rate recorded since national estimates began. The FBI recorded the same rate in 1955 and 1956. 
Violent crime in US fell at record pace in 2025

But a national decline does not mean every community has experienced the same drop.
The decline has unfolded in cities with different public safety strategies, economic conditions and political leadership, complicating efforts to credit any one approach, according to the council’s report.
The researchers rated 48 potential explanations for the decline between 2022 and 2026. Six factors received support from more than two-thirds of respondents as contributing either substantially or to a limited degree:

Expanded community violence intervention programs, which work directly with people at highest risk of violence, were rated as either a major or a limited contributor contributing by 91% of researchers. 
The pandemic recovery was rated as a major or a limited contributor by 83% of respondents. It was the only factor that a majority of respondents, 57%, rated as a major contributor.
Eighty-three percent of the crime scholars gave credit to the increased use of focused deterrence, an approach that targets high-risk individuals and groups directly with a carrot-and-stick approach through social support and law enforcement.
Researchers also pointed to increased local government capacity to provide social services, with 75% rating it either a major or limited contributor.
Greater public safety and support resources relative to demand earned a rating of 68%.
And more proactive policing was likewise named as a major or limited factor by 68% of the scholars.

Researchers largely dismissed more than half of the potential explanations, including National Guard deployments, increased immigration enforcement and increased pretrial detention. 
Other factors thought to have contributed little included homeless encampment removals, improved housing stability, electronic monitoring, GLP-1 medications, declining cash use, presidential public safety signals, DNA databases, neighborhood crime alerts, increased incarceration and increased pretrial detention.
The findings do not establish that any one strategy caused homicide to fall. The ratings reflect researchers’ professional judgments, not definitive findings, and multiple factors may have overlapped or reinforced one another, according to the council’s report. 
The council also cautioned that a factor judged to have contributed little to the recent decline could still help reduce violence in the future.
But understanding what drove the decline could help policymakers determine how to sustain the progress, according to the council’s report. 
“Theories and claims abound, and sorting among them is essential if we’re going to sustain the progress. This diverse array of researchers took the challenge seriously, testing competing explanations, debating the evidence, and making tough judgments,” Adam Gelb, the president and CEO of the council, said in a news release. “Their effort leaves the country with a much clearer picture of what likely contributed, what probably did not, and what we still need to learn.”

text:
Dear Editor,
I am looking forward to Wednesday, Oct. 21, when the two candidates for governor will debate. Affordability is bound to be the general topic. And that discussion will likely fan out in different directions, such as healthcare affordability and the cost of education. 
I am especially interested in energy affordability. I want to know what the candidates can tell us about addressing the needs of Vermonters locked into a dependency on gas and diesel for transport and fuel oil and propane for heating. The Energy Action Network’s 2026 Annual Progress Report says that in 2024 Vermonters spent $3.2 billion on energy — about $1 billion on electricity — and the other two-thirds on fossil fuels for transportation and heating. What is each candidate going to do to help Vermonters better afford heating their homes and businesses, and driving their trucks and cars?
I wonder if the candidates will acknowledge that the $2.2 billion a year fossil fuel number from 2024 has risen by many millions due to fuel cost increases driven by the ongoing U.S. war with Iran. Will the candidates acknowledge that Vermonters continue to be subjected to those cost increases? I’m interested in whether the candidates think that those billions of dollars a year that we send to fossil fuel producers can be better spent here in Vermont. 

READ MORE

The report reminds us that average Vermont annual household energy expenditures in 2024 were more than 30% higher than the U.S. average. Can these candidates convince voters they have a plan to reduce that difference? And that is average energy affordability. Will the candidates have a plan to support not just the average Vermonter but our most economically vulnerable citizens who are continually exposed to these increased energy costs?
It is my hope that those hosting the debate will raise these and related questions, and encourage substantive engagement on energy affordability that Vermonters deserve.
Dave Farnsworth,South Royalton, Vt.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Tuesday is last day to register to vote in West Virginia for the general election
description: West Virginians have through Tuesday, Oct. 13 to register to vote in November’s general election.
text:
A sign telling people to register to vote sits outside of West Virginia Secretary of State Kris Warner's office on Feb. 10, 2026, in the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)West Virginians have through Tuesday, Oct. 13 to register to vote in November’s general election.
A person can register by mailing an application to their county clerk. The application is accessible online at the Secretary of State’s Office. 
Applications must be postmarked by the end of the day on Tuesday, a spokesperson for Secretary of State Kris Warner said. For a complete list of county clerks’ offices and addresses, visit the county clerk directory at the West Virginia Secretary of State’s website. 
People can also register online or check their registration status on the Secretary of State’s website, sos.wv.gov/govotewv. 
Voters will decide on a constitutional amendment. If voters approve Amendment 1, the state’s constitution would be amended to include that “Only citizens of the United States who are citizens of this state shall be entitled to vote at all elections.” 
West Virginia law already prohibits people who are not citizens from voting in elections, but proponents of Amendment 1 say it’s not enough. The constitution requires voters to be citizens of the state, but does not specify that they be U.S. citizens. Adding the amendment would prohibit future Legislatures from allowing noncitizens to vote with the passage of a bill, proponents say. 
Opponents of the measure argue it’s unnecessary. The proposed amendment needs a simple majority of more than 50% of voters to pass.
West Virginia voters will also choose representatives for two seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and one in the U.S. Senate, as well as a host of seats in the West Virginia Senate and House of Delegates.
Early voting in the 2026 general election begins Wednesday, Oct. 21 and ends Saturday, Oct. 31. During early voting, people can vote at their county courthouse or other designated places in their community from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. during the week and on the last two Saturdays before the election. A complete list of early voting locations is available online at the Secretary of State’s website. 
The general election is Nov. 3, 2026.

text:
The exterior of the Clinton presidential library in Little Rock on Thursday, April 2, 2026 (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones and his family announced Monday they are donating $10 million toward the renovation and modernization of former President Bill Clinton’s library and museum in Little Rock.
Jones announced the gift to the Clinton Foundation as he appeared with the 42nd president at the Little Rock Touchdown Club.
“Being able to now grow and combine my long-standing love and support for the University of Arkansas and Razorback athletics, while supporting the important growth, evolution and opportunities the Clinton Presidential Center creates is something I personally cherish and our family is exceedingly grateful for,” Jones said in a news release.
Bill Clinton says namesake public service school is fulfilling ‘urgent need’

The Clinton Presidential Center, which houses a museum and the former president’s archives, opened on the outskirts of downtown Little Rock in 2004. Library officials in 2024 announced an expansion of the center, which will include Hillary Clinton’s personal archives. The expansion will include a renovation of the Clinton-Gore administration gallery, and a new archive dedicated to Hillary Clinton’s lifetime of service.
Plans also call for redesigning the 50-acre park where the library is located to create more gathering space.
More than 5.5 million people have visited the Clinton library since it opened, and the facility remains a major draw for the city. A 2025 study credited the library for having a $4.9 billion impact on the Little Rock and North Little Rock areas. The campus includes the University of Arkansas Clinton School of Public Service. 
Clinton praised Jones as an “American sports icon.” 
“I am deeply grateful for his dedication to our beloved home state of Arkansas, and proud to stand alongside him in accepting this gift,” Clinton said. “The Jones Family’s generosity will support the Clinton Presidential Center’s work as a hub for education, service, and bipartisan dialogue for many years to come.”

39th annual gathering brings business, civic and faith leaders together Thursday at the Chase Center
WILMINGTON — For nearly four decades, the Delaware Leadership Prayer Breakfast has brought together an unusual cross-section of the First State: business executives, elected officials, nonprofit leaders, educators, clergy and other community leaders.
On Thursday, Oct. 15, the tradition continues at the Chase Center on the Riverfront with the 39th annual Delaware Leadership Prayer Breakfast, an event that has grown from a Wilmington-area gathering into a statewide institution connecting faith, leadership and Delaware’s business community.
The breakfast begins at 7:20 a.m. and this year features Bob Doll, CEO and chief investment officer of Crossmark Global Investments, as its keynote speaker. Doll previously held senior investment positions at Nuveen, BlackRock and Merrill Lynch Investment Managers.
A Delaware business tradition
The roots of the breakfast go back to 1985, when Wilmington-area businessmen Bob Nickle, David Ripsom and Bob Townsend attended the White House Prayer Breakfast in Washington and returned to Delaware interested in creating a similar gathering.
The first New Castle County Leadership Prayer Breakfast was held in 1986, attracting about 500 people. Its first speaker was Dr. Richard Halverson, then chaplain of the U.S. Senate.
The founders envisioned more than a religious event. The original purpose specifically spoke about leadership in Delaware’s business, professional and community life — a focus that has remained central to the breakfast.
As attendance expanded beyond New Castle County, organizers renamed it the Delaware Leadership Prayer Breakfast in 2002. Federal, state and local political leaders have regularly participated, but the event also has maintained strong ties to Delaware’s business community.
The volunteer steering committee itself is made up largely of Christian business men and women, according to organizers.
A Wall Street voice for Delaware leaders
Doll brings a particularly strong business connection to this year’s gathering.
He has spent more than 40 years in investment management and has served as president and chief investment officer of Merrill Lynch Investment Managers, chief equity strategist at BlackRock and senior portfolio manager and chief equity strategist at Nuveen.
He joined Crossmark in 2021 as chief investment officer and became CEO in 2024. He regularly provides investment commentary and market predictions and has appeared on Bloomberg TV, CNBC and Fox Business.
For a Delaware audience — in a state where banking, financial services and corporate business play an outsized role in the economy — Doll’s combination of financial experience and faith-based leadership gives the keynote a natural connection to the people who have helped make the breakfast a fixture on the business calendar.
Doll also serves a number of Christian, educational and ministry organizations and is choir director at his local church. His background reflects the intersection of professional leadership, faith, stewardship and service that has defined the Delaware breakfast since its beginning.
A long list of prominent speakers
The staying power of the breakfast can also be seen in its speakers.
Recent guests have included John Templeton Foundation President and CEO Timothy Dalrymple in 2025; Pro Football Hall of Famer and former Philadelphia Eagle Brian Dawkins in 2024; JPMorgan Chase executive Dr. Betty Uribe in 2023; and former National Institutes of Health Director Dr. Francis Collins in 2022.
Earlier speakers have included business leaders, athletes, authors, government officials and nationally known figures such as Interstate Batteries Chairman Norman Miller, Auntie Anne’s founder Anne Beiler, former NFL coach Joe Gibbs, Conoco CEO Archie Dunham and former U.S. Senate Chaplain Barry Black.
That mix has helped the breakfast endure as something broader than either a business meeting or a church event. It provides a place where leaders from different sectors of Delaware life can gather around common themes of character, responsibility, service and faith.
Delaware history takes the stage
This year’s program will also have a distinctly Delaware component.
The cast of the new musical “Big Quarterly” will provide special music. The gospel and hip-hop production tells the story of the Rt. Rev. Peter Spencer and his religious legacy in Delaware.
The musical was written and produced by Bishop S. Todd Townsend, Luke McLemore and Dr. Kim Kilby. Pastor James Burrows Jr. of The Resurrection Center also will lead “God Bless America.”
Nearly four decades after a small group of Delaware businessmen returned from Washington with an idea, the Delaware Leadership Prayer Breakfast has become part of the rhythm of the state’s civic and business community.
Its longevity may be its most significant accomplishment: generations of Delaware leaders have changed, companies have grown and disappeared, political administrations have come and gone, but the breakfast has continued bringing people together each fall to consider the responsibilities that accompany leadership.

When: Thursday, Oct. 15, 7:20-9 a.m.
Where: Chase Center on the Riverfront, 815 Justison St., Wilmington
Keynote speaker: Bob Doll, CEO and chief investment officer of Crossmark Global Investments
Special music: Cast of “Big Quarterly,” a gospel and hip-hop musical about Delaware’s Rt. Rev. Peter Spencer

title: US House Dem leaders condemn Homeland Security raid on home of Rep. Ilhan Omar
text: WASHINGTON — Democratic leaders in the U.S. House condemned a “deeply disturbing” raid early Monday at the District of Columbia home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat who has long been a target of verbal attacks by President Donald Trump and Republicans.House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Democratic Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., called the morning raid by Department of Homeland Security officials “egregious.”The House minority leaders said the search of Omar’s home “raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries.”“For years Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar said in a statement posted on social media Monday. “Now, less than 30 days before the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”Omar, a Somali-born American and one of four Muslims in Congress, represents a deep-blue district.Fox News first published a report on the raid just after 7:30 a.m. Eastern, and cited two sources who told the network the operation was related to an investigation of Omar’s immigration paperwork. Omar was resettled as a refugee in the United States with her family at the age of 12 in 1995 and was later naturalized as a U.S. citizen.A Department of Justice official, asked for comment on the raid, told States Newsroom: “Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.”Omar said in a post on social media Monday that she “will not be silenced.” “I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she wrote on X.Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., wrote in a statement on X that the president is “grossly abusing his power.”“He has repeatedly attacked her, Somali Americans, and Minnesotans. @Ilhan has done nothing to justify a pre-dawn raid ahead of the election. I stand with my sister always,” Tlaib wrote.Trump, without evidence, has accused Omar of being connected to a $242 million fraud scheme involving pandemic-era funds meant for hunger programs, as well as other fraud investigations in the state, and has called for her to be deported.“There is 19 Billion Dollars in Minnesota Somalia Fraud. Fake ‘Congresswoman’ Illhan Omar, a constant complainer who hates the USA, knows everything there is to know. She should be in jail, or even a worse punishment, sent back to Somalia, considered one of the absolutely worst countries in the World. She could help to MAKE SOMALIA GREAT AGAIN!,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Jan 18.

name: VTDigger
title: A new tree pest could be catching a ride on your car
description:
Humans inadvertently brought spotted lanternflies to the U.S. from Asia, and Vermonters play a big role in limiting their spread in the state.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A new tree pest could be catching a ride on your car.
text:
A spotted lanternfly in Brooklyn in an undated photograph. Photo by Rhododendrites (CC BY-SA 4.0)

If you’re not keeping an eye on smears of dried mud on your car, forest pest educators like Ginger Nickerson say now’s a good time to pick up the habit. Nickerson and other experts warn that spotted lanternflies could be hitching a ride into Vermont, where they pose a threat to trees and other plants.
“They could lay their eggs on anything that you have outdoors, like your car, or if you’ve got bikes on the back of your car,” she said. “And then, when you come back to Vermont — or if you’re moving your child to Vermont to go to college — and you park your vehicle here, then (they) could hatch in the springtime.”
What might look like a patch of dry mud could actually be the egg mass of a spotted lanternfly, she warned.
Experts say species like spotted lanternfly and others can disrupt local ecosystems. And, spotted lanternflies are laying eggs around this time, leading up to hard frosts.
When the insect feeds on a plant or tree, they excrete a sticky substance called honeydew. It can disrupt photosynthesis when it falls on leaves, and the insects can impact yields of grapevines, berries and roses. It might not kill most plants, but it is most likely to kill grapevines and black walnut trees.
They’re most likely spread through human means: they can hitch a ride on out-of-state campfire wood or on cars. Spotted lanternflies were first spotted in Pennsylvania in 2014, and they’ve spread along the east coast and into some parts of the Midwest, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Nickerson said people can manage the spread and help prevent avoidable damage. She said the state is relying on people reporting sightings of the insect at any life stage to monitor the potential spread.
Some of the best ways to stop spotted lanternflies from establishing a local community is to carefully inspect any vehicles that are traveling from a spotted lanternfly state to Vermont for the insects at any life stage, she said, and to avoid bringing firewood from a different state.
She also said any sightings should be reported to VTInvasives.org, along with squishing the sighted bug or scraping off an egg mass.
“I don’t think that it’s something that people should be afraid of or overly worried about, but we would really appreciate people being thoughtful when they travel to places where there are infestations, so that they’re making an effort to not bring it home,” Nickerson said.
Spotted lanternflies aren’t the only pest to watch out for, just the latest.
USDA research shows that in the last decade, the leading cause of tree death in the northeastern U.S. has shifted from harvesting, like logging, to natural causes, including damage from insects. Lead author and University of Vermont researcher Lucas Harris said there’s been a fivefold increase in tree mortality by insects over a 15 year period, and insect outbreaks increased by 13 times over 15 years. He said, in a lot of ways, there isn’t really an analog to this increase.
“We know that tree mortality is not typically caused by just one thing; it’s the interaction of multiple factors,” he said. “Maybe a tree experienced a drought a few years back, and it’s experiencing intense competition based on neighboring trees, and then there’s an insect outbreak, and that’s what finally kills the tree.”
He said it reflects what experts are seeing with the spread of insects like the emerald ash borer and hemlock woolly adelgid, which have established populations in Vermont.
“There are a lot of individual insects capable of causing tree death, but I think the surprise is how much it adds up,” he said.

READ MORE

He also said what happens in the future can be hard to predict. And attributing tree death is a tricky practice. In northern New England, he said, we’re pretty lucky in that mortality hasn’t ramped up at quite the same rate as our southern New England neighbors.
“We’re at this time in northern New England where there might be a window of opportunity to think critically,” he said. “We haven’t experienced a lot of tree death yet. There might be opportunities to make our forests more resilient or perhaps stop the spread of particular insects into particular areas.”
While sightings of spotted lanternflies have occurred in the state, officials say they haven’t found an established community. There are three non-native insects which already have a presence in Vermont, and they threaten the health of 14 species of trees.
Emerald ash borers are causing widespread death of ash trees, particularly the culturally significant black ash, and experts say it’s likely almost all black ash trees will succumb to the insect. They were introduced to Vermont in 2018, and were just found in Essex County, the last ‘holdout’ area, this fall, according to Joanne Garton, community forester with Vermont Forests, Parks and Recreation.
And hemlock woolly adelgids, which look like tiny cotton balls on hemlock needles, have been in Vermont since 2007, and have established communities in the southern part of the state, according to Vermont Parks and Rec. They feed on hemlock species throughout North America. They’re most likely to spread from April through August, and officials are unclear as to exactly how much damage they’ll do in the state, particularly farther north.
Garton said it’s important to understand that humans introduced these pests, and our role in the resulting threat to local ecosystems.
“Really taking ownership of our role as humans in moving these pests around is something that, I think, is hard to stomach,” she said. “None of us want to be that person that was responsible, but collectively, we are the people that are responsible for moving insects and diseases and pests way faster than nature can keep up with.” 
There are multiple efforts underway in the state and in the northeast to address pests. Community forester Garton and her team are trained to apply an insecticide to the base of ash trees, and she said a group in Hardwick collects ash seeds to preserve the species into the future. Plus, experts say ordinary people in the community reporting sightings of any introduced pest is one of the best ways to monitor the potential spread.
Garton said there’s a silver lining to protecting the forest from further damage from introduced pests: she’s connected with many people who care deeply about stewarding our shared landscape.
She encouraged people to go outside, look carefully and notice things around them. She said it’s a big step towards more positive change.
“What’s here? What didn’t used to be here, what could I protect that’s here, and how might I do that? It’s a lot, and there’s a lot of places to go look,” Garton said. “But I think together, we can do it. We can keep working on it.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana’s congressional candidates float ideas for affordable gas, groceries
description: Voters are focusing on the high price of gas, groceries and other affordability issues ahead of the Nov. 3 election, according to political experts and national polling. Democrats and Republicans running for Congress in Louisiana have different approaches to bringing down the cost of living.
text:
Democrats and Republicans running for Congress in Louisiana have different approaches to bringing down prices for gas, groceries and other consumer goods. The Illuminator interviewed candidates for the U.S. Senate race and in the competitive 5th District and 6th District races about rising living expenses. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Voters are focusing on the high price of gas, groceries and other affordability issues ahead of the Nov. 3 election, according to political experts and national polling. 
“With $4/gallon gas and $6/gallon diesel, cost of living and affordability are first and foremost on voters’ minds in every poll I do,” John Couvillon, who runs one of the most prominent Louisiana political polling firms, JMC Analytics and Polling, wrote in an email. 
Democrats and Republicans running for Congress in Louisiana have different approaches to bringing down the cost of living. 

The Illuminator interviewed candidates for the U.S. Senate race and in the competitive 5th District and 6th District races about rising living expenses. President Donald Trump has suggested the issue of affordability is “a hoax started by Democrats.”   
Democrats in Louisiana’s congressional race say ending the Iran war Trump started and removing tariffs he has imposed will reduce prices. Republican candidates suggest resolving the war Russian President Vladimir Putin started in Ukraine would control costs. 

Couvillon said Republicans are more likely to be blamed for the high cost of living in this election cycle, just as the Democrats were in 2024. 

“When you have unified control of government like the Republicans do, it makes it easy for voters to punish them,” he said. 
End the war, but which war? 
U.S. Senate candidate Jamie Davis, 6th District candidates Chauna Banks and Pat Forbes, and 5th District candidates Pat Moore and Antonio Wilson — all Democrats — said the best way to immediately bring down the price of gas and other goods is to end the war with Iran. 
“It’s very simple. We started a war that accomplished nothing but raising gas and diesel prices,” said Forbes, who oversaw disaster recovery programs for Louisiana before retiring from state government in the Office of Community Development. 
The Iran war, which Trump launched in February, has disrupted the transportation of petroleum through the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East, driving up American fuel prices.
U.S. Senate candidate Congresswoman Julia Letlow, 6th District candidate state Sen. Rick Edmonds and 5th District candidate state Sen. Michael Echols, all Republicans, support the Iran war, saying it will help improve national security. 

Letlow, who currently represents the 5th District, blames the Biden administration for inflation. Most economists attribute the broad increase in costs in goods and services to global factors, such as the COVID-19 pandemic and energy supply, but also say Biden policy has contributed to the issue.    
“Republicans inherited an affordability crisis, and we’ve been working with President Trump to turn that around,” Letlow said in a written statement from her campaign staff. 
Echols and fellow 5th district Republican candidate state Sen. Stewart Cathey said the Iran war shouldn’t necessarily be the focus. Both said Trump and Congress should be prioritizing an end the war in Ukraine, which started in February 2022, to help bring gas prices down.

Their comments about the Ukraine war mirror those Trump has made as he tries to deflect blame for high gasoline prices away from his decision to go to war with Iran. 
The U.S., Canada, Europe and Australia have embargoes on most Russian oil and refined petroleum imports, though Trump announced a deal Friday with Putin that pauses sanctions for six months on Russian diesel fuel. 

Edmonds and fellow 6th District candidate Lindsay “Rubia” Garcia, a Democrat and former teacher, suggested Congress suspend federal fuel taxes to bring down the cost of consumer goods. The U.S. government collects 18.4 cents per gallon of gas and 24.4 cents for diesel.

“Letlow, Cathey, Echols and state Rep. Gabe Firment, a Republican 5th District candidate, said Congress needs to reduce government regulations to enable an expansion of U.S. oil refining capacity so the country is less dependent on foreign countries for energy production.”

Democrats, Republicans split on Trump tariffs 
Four Democrats — Davis, Banks, Forbes and Wilson — said Congress must also end tariffs Trump has put in place to bring down prices for housing and consumer goods. 
“It’s basically just a tax. We all have to pay it,” Davis, a former Tensas Parish Police Juror, said of the tariffs. 
Letlow, Echols and Firment  support Trump’s tariffs, which they said will protect American workers and business owners in the long run. 
“Our ag producers are getting ripped off because China and others are dumping products,” Echols said. 
Garcia split from the other Democrats in saying that she would back some tariffs, but only in cases where the goal of the tariff was defined.

“I support targeted tariffs when there is a clear purpose, such as addressing unfair trade practices or protecting critical domestic industries and national security,” she wrote in an email. 
Board of Regents chair Misti Cordell, a 5th District candidate, and state Sen. Blake Miguez, running in the 6th District, did not return phone calls for this report.

title: Trump heads West in latest swing to bolster GOP in rocky lead-up to midterms
text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump this week will journey out West in an effort to galvanize support for  Republican candidates three weeks before the midterm elections and convince voters to support his party amid low presidential approval ratings.As the deeply unpopular war in Iran enters month eight, resulting in spiking prices at the gas pump and skyrocketing fertilizer prices for the agriculture industry, Trump is scheduled to rally in Alaska on Tuesday and Arizona and Montana on Wednesday, following stops earlier this month in GOP-friendly states that kicked off the last weeks before the election. On Friday, Trump is expected to campaign in Georgia.Presidents typically sustain electoral losses in midterm election years and in addition, Trump’s approval rating is currently hovering around 37% percent, according to an analysis by The New York Times.

 






(Photo by Getty images)

Those low approval rates, and polls, have shifted several Senate races to toss-ups. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas as toss-up Senate races. Republicans are not only trying to maintain the House, but their 53-seat majority in the Senate as well. The president’s travel also follows a federal judge’s ruling over the weekend that ordered the Trump administration to stop airing ads funded by taxpayer dollars that portrayed Trump in a favorable manner. Trump used about $20 million in Department of Homeland Security funds to pay for the ads. Trump’s comes after a campaign rally in Tennessee over the weekend. During his remarks in Clarksville, he focused on accusing Democrats of being communists and socialists. On Monday, Trump is heading to Youngstown, Ohio to deliver remarks. GOP Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill out the term of Vice President JD Vance, is in a tight race against former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. Trump is not only in Ohio to support Husted, but also to throw his support behind  gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who is up against Democrat Amy Acton.Vance is also hitting the campaign trail this week. On Wednesday, he’ll visit Georgia and on Thursday will make another stop in Michigan. Trump is also likely to bring up in his campaign rallies Monday’s joint Department of Justice and Homeland Security Investigations raid of Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s house in Washington, D.C. It’s a rare move from the Justice Department only several weeks out from the election, given the department generally doesn’t conduct such raids unless in extreme circumstances. She, along with the broader Somali community in Minnesota, are regularly targeted by the president and disproportionately accused of widespread fraud. Recently, the president used violent rhetoric in a social media post that called on Minnesotans to “fight back” against Somali immigrants.The president directed DHS to Minneapolis, where there is a large Latino and Somali refugee population. A months-long aggressive deportation drive there resulted in then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem stepping down from her position after federal immigration officials shot and killed two U.S. citizens, Alex Pretti and Renee Good.

As part of her executive order, Whitmer is temporarily suspending restrictions preventing vehicles with farm[...]
text:
Tractors circle the Michigan Capitol in Lansing, Mich., on March 18, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)As the average diesel price in Michigan sits at nearly $6.50, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer on Monday signed an executive order declaring a state of energy emergency intended to loosen the strain farmers and loggers face when fueling their vehicles.
As part of her executive order, Whitmer is temporarily suspending restrictions preventing vehicles with farm or wood harvester plates from using public roads and highways if they are running on dyed diesel. Only vehicles with those plates are impacted by the order.
Whitmer’s declaration follows similar moves taken by other states, and an Oct. 5 federal executive order, in which President Donald Trump temporarily suspended penalties for using dyed diesel on highways. Both Whitmer and Trump’s order lift those restrictions through Dec. 31.
Dyed diesel is functionally the same as regular diesel fuel, but is designated for off-road uses, like operating agricultural machinery. It is not taxed, and is dyed to differentiate it from the diesel fuel vehicles use on the road.
In a statement, Whitmer slammed Republicans in Washington D.C. over their support for the war in Iran, noting its impact on everyday costs across the board.
According to AAA, the average price of diesel in Michigan on Monday was $6.49 per gallon. One year prior, the average cost for diesel in the state was $3.66 per gallon.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“While I can’t control what’s happening at the federal level, I can try to protect Michigan’s economy,” Whitmer, a Democrat, said. “This order will allow farm and logging vehicles to use dyed diesel on our highways without risk of penalty. We need to keep work moving and reduce pressure on the people who keep our state’s ag economy running.”
In her executive order Whitmer said the state’s farmers and loggers are facing “unprecedented financial strain from record-high diesel prices, tight margins, and significant market volatility,” noting that these increased costs are sometimes passed along to consumers. 
“These industries already purchase and maintain substantial supplies of dyed diesel for off-road equipment,” the executive order reads. “Therefore, granting eligible highway-licensed vehicles temporary access to this fuel would provide immediate relief.”
On Sept. 30, multiple organizations representing Michigan’s timber industry and its various agricultural sectors sent letters to the governor calling for 90-days of temporary relief from the restrictions and penalties on using dyed diesel on Michigan roadways.
While state officials have floated suspending the state’s gas tax, Justin Knepper, the executive director of the Michigan Association of Timbermen acknowledged that a gas tax holiday could be politically challenging due to its cost. 
Alongside the Michigan Farm Bureau and several other agriculture and forestry associations, the Association of Timbermen pushed hard for the suspension of the dyed diesel penalties, Knepper told Michigan Advance, noting that they viewed their ask as a smaller financial hurdle.
While Knepper said they were incredibly grateful to the governor’s office, he noted that the executive order does not help the farmers and loggers who do not have trucks on the road.
“We’re still working hard to figure out how to support those folks,” Knepper said.
Using untaxed dyed diesel will save farmers and loggers upwards of 50 cents per gallon over the next three months, Knepper said, but noted that prices would need to come down further for businesses to survive. 
“It’s relief, but it’s not the long-lasting relief that we need in terms of prices getting back down,” Knepper said.
Michigan Farm Bureau President Ben LaCross told Michigan Farm News “Every bit of savings helps as Michigan farmers work to bring in the harvest and keep food moving from the farm to our communities.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Hillary Clinton tells Nebraska Democrats election offers opportunity to reverse Trump’s policies
description: Hillary Clinton talked to a full room of Nebraska Democrats, emphasizing the importance of seizing the current political environment.
text:
Former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and Omaha Mayor John Ewing  hold  the  key to the city Oct. 10, 2026, at the downtown Hilton. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — Former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton talked to a full room of Nebraska Democrats on Saturday, emphasizing the importance of Democrats’ seizing the current political environment.
Clinton’s event was a Q&A, and the crowd’s inquiries ranged  from her advice for moms and women running for office to questions about her political career. 
Omaha Mayor John Ewing gave Clinton the key to the city of Omaha before she spoke at the downtown Hilton. 
“Everything that we could hope for in the lead-up to the next election is really happening. … We just have to stay focused and on task and turn out the vote and celebrate when we take back the House and the Senate,” Clinton said to cheers. 
Clinton said there is “an opportunity” in this midterm election to “reverse the damage” and begin repairing what “has been deliberately broken,” referring to President Donald Trump. She said the current Congress has done “much damage” by voting for Trump’s tax-and-spending bill.  
Republicans are facing tough headwinds this November. The party in the White House typically doesn’t do well in midterm elections. Democrats are fully bullish on their chances of taking both the U.S. House and Senate. Nebraska currently has a few races that are viewed as competitive, including the Senate and 2nd Congressional District races. Trump recently came to Grand Island as part of a midterm campaign blitz to shore up red states. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Janet Goodman Banks, a 70-year-old Lincoln resident, said after the event that she strongly believes Democrats will take back the House and Senate. Banks said Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District has a “great chance of flipping.” 
“I’ve always believed that CD1 could also earn a blue dot. …This is a chance to do so, and so I’m really hopeful that Chris can pull it out,” Banks told the Examiner. 
Former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton talks Oct. 10, 2026 at Omaha’s downtown Hilton. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Eaminer)
That House race includes Incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Flood and his Democratic challenger Chris Backemeyer, as well as candidates for the America First and Libertarian parties. While the political environment has improved for Democrats, election analysts still rate the race as safely Republican — though national Democrats see it as competitive.
Clinton, when asked how to reach people who view their votes as meaningless, said Democrats must repeatedly show they’ll do everything they can to help people have the life they deserve. She added that Democrats must deliver results if they win the majorities that polling suggests are possible in November. 
The 2016 Democratic presidential nominee said she thinks Trump’s original appeal is wearing off among Americans. 
“I think what originally seemed like, ‘Oh, he’s a different kind of leader. He says what he thinks,’all of that, I think that it’s beginning to finally sink through to people, like, ‘Wait a minute, am I better off? Has my life improved?’” Clinton said. “I look at other people, especially those who are doing really, really well. And they seem to be enjoying a lot of access to the president, and even the president has made a lot of money.” 
Karen Follon and Peg O’Dea Lippert, both Omaha residents, said they’re hopeful about Democrats’ chances this upcoming election. 
O’Dea Lippert and Follon said they already voted for the Democratic nominee for the 2nd Congressional District, Denise Powell, and registered nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn for Senate. 
“We need to get people back in office to take care of our members of society because if anybody in our society is hurting, we’re all hurting,” Follon said. 
Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts released a press release ahead of the event, trying to link Osborn to Clinton. The Ricketts campaign cited Plains Sentinel reporting saying that Osborn voted for Clinton in 2016.
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already started.

text:
VTDigger earned Distinguished News Site honors and two top investigative journalism awards at the 2026 New England Newspaper & Press Association Leadership Summit. Photos by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
VTDigger was recognized as a Distinguished News Site for online publications in the region by the New England Newspaper & Press Association at its 2026 Leadership Summit held in Sturbridge, Mass., on Friday. 
In addition, VTDigger reporters received two of the three top A-Mark prizes, “recognizing and celebrating outstanding investigative journalism that uncovers hidden truths, holds power to account, and drives meaningful public awareness or reform,” according to NENPA.
“These most recent awards build upon a long track record of excellence and impact at VTDigger,” said Brendan Kinney, the organization’s CEO. “There are many people responsible for our continued success, in particular our more than 9,100 members, local businesses and foundations who provide us with the financial resources necessary to do this work.”
For the Distinguished News Site honor, NENPA recognized the in-depth reporting of Kevin O’Connor for his look back at devastating flooding in Vermont on July 10, 2023 and 2024, which incorporated photos by VTDigger photographer Glenn Russell, as well as audio and video from the floods. 
The second piece honored by the award was a profile by Shaun Robinson of Ugandan minister Steven Tendo, who moved to Vermont after facing brutal torture abroad and continues to face the threat of deportation. Russell was the photographer on that piece, as well.
VTDigger’s Greta Solsaa, Government Accountability and Southern Vermont reporter, won the top A-Mark prize for her months-long examination, using public records, of a pattern of care problems at some of Vermont’s most troubled nursing homes under new ownership. Her reporting traced the issues in part to a temporary state approval process that lacked transparency and failed to prevent problems. 

READ MORE

Ethan Weinstein, now a senior editor at VTDigger, placed third in the A-Mark category for his in-depth reporting, using internal communications from state prison officials, to illuminate how ICE uses the state’s prisons and why that arrangement has created challenges for Vermont. 
Glenn Russell was the photographer on both stories. 
“VTDigger continues the in-depth reporting, quality writing and singular photography recognized by NENPA,” said Interim Editor-in-Chief Susan Allen. “Our committed readers expect to find that level of scrutiny and story-telling when they turn to our website and newsletters each day.”
Former CEO Sky Barsch and Editor-in-Chief Geeta Anand led the organization during the reporting period.
Founded in 2009, VTDigger is a nonprofit, nonpartisan digital news organization covering issues of statewide importance in Vermont. It is a project of the Vermont Journalism Trust, a 501(c)3 nonprofit organization. 
Visit vtdigger.org for the latest news, special projects, opinion pieces and more.
