name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida’s 17th execution of this year is scheduled for Tuesday
description: The state of Florida is set to execute 62-year-old James Robertson by lethal injection at noon Tuesday at Florida State Prison in Bradford County. It would be the 17th carried out in Florida this year. The 16 executions to date in Florida are more than all the other states in the country this year combined […]
text:
The execution chamber at Florida State Prison. (Via Florida Department of Corrections)
The state of Florida is set to execute 62-year-old James Robertson by lethal injection at noon Tuesday at Florida State Prison in Bradford County. It would be the 17th carried out in Florida this year.
The 16 executions to date in Florida are more than all the other states in the country this year combined (14), according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Unlike most death row inmates, Robertson has never challenged his death sentence. That’s prompted an anti-death penalty advocacy group to argue his behavior challenges the “misconception” that the death penalty deters crime.
Robertson was imprisoned at Charlotte Correctional Institution in 2008 when he strangled his cellmate with a garrote he made by tying several socks together, according to prosecutors.
At the time, Robertson was 45 years old and had been in prison for 28 years, having first been convicted of a felony before his 18th birthday. Subsequent convictions for offenses committed within the prison system resulted in additional sentences.
The state initially charged him with second-degree murder and offered a life sentence in exchange for a guilty plea. He rejected that offer and said he should be charged with first-degree murder because he admitted that the killing was premeditated.
Robertson has waived all appeals, including on Oct. 1 in the Circuit Court for the 20th Judicial Circuit in Charlotte County.
In that hearing, Robertson acknowledged he had written a letter to then-Attorney General Ashley Moody in 2023 asking why his execution was taking so long. According to court documents, Robertson was asked by the court why he wanted to dismiss postconviction proceedings.
“Because I was found guilty,” he said. “You know, I chose the death penalty over the life sentence, and I just, you know, want the sentence to be carried out.”
In a written statement, the group Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty argue the phenomenon of an individual committing a crime with the goal of being executed is not rare, citing a 1999 article in the Journal of Criminal Justice that identified at least 22 suspected cases of “homicide as suicide.”
They insist his case challenges the “misconception” the death penalty deters crime.
“Frank Hart [the victim] deserved to be safe in state custody, and his loved ones deserve our compassion,” said Maria DeLiberato, legal and policy director of Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty.
“When someone commits murder to try to secure his own execution, we have to confront the conditions that contributed to that decision and the reality that the existence of the death penalty may have caused the very violence it purportedly prevents. Florida has a responsibility to protect the people in its prisons and address the despair that can put their lives, and the lives of others, at risk.”
Robertson’s execution was originally scheduled to be the first of two scheduled this year, along with William Thompson. However, Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew the death warrant for Thompson last week. He did not provide an explanation, but his decision came a week after more than 100 medical professionals sent a letter calling on him to do so, noting that Thompson suffers from dementia and additional medical ailments.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Cindy Holscher, Ty Masterson gain gubernatorial endorsements from labor, ag interests
description: With the clock winding down to the Nov. 3 election, Kansas gubernatorial candidates Ty Masterson and Cindy Holscher continue to tally endorsements.
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Cindy Holscher, an Overland Park state senator, is recipient of an endorsement by the Missouri-Kansas-Nebraska Conference of Teamsters. Her rival in the Nov. 3 election, Republican Sen. Ty Masterson, wins backing from the Kansas Farm Bureau PAC. In this image from April 9, 2026, Holscher offers remarks on the floor of the Kansas Senate. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas gubernatorial campaigns of Republican Ty Masterson and Democrat Cindy Holscher landed endorsements that echo the political alliances they developed while serving in the Kansas Legislature.
Masterson pocketed support from the Kansas Farm Bureau PAC, while Holscher bolstered her resume with backing from the Missouri-Kansas-Nebraska Conference of Teamsters.
Glenn Brunkow, president of Kansas Farm Bureau, said the PAC’s preference was tied to Masterson’s relationship with agriculture interests during his 20-year career in the Kansas Legislature. Currently, the Andover Republican is president of the Kansas Senate.
“I know Ty has developed a strong relationship with his county Farm Bureau during his time in the state Legislature,” Brunkow said. “I look forward to working together to advance our member-developed policies to strengthen agriculture and help rural Kansas thrive.”
The decision was made by a 10-member Farm Bureau board based on input from members of the organization. In 2022, the KFB PAC endorsed GOP governor candidate Derek Schmidt, who lost that campaign to incumbent Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly.
The KFB’s recommendation emerged as the Kansas agriculture economy grappled with federal trade tariffs, low grain prices compared to 2022, escalating fuel and fertilizer costs, regional drought and workforce issues related to immigration enforcement.
“Kansas agriculture feeds the world and Kansas producers deserve a governor who has their backs,” Masterson said.
Masterson promised to protect water and land resources, reduce government bureaucracy and “make sure rural Kansas has the hospitals, schools and opportunity it needs to thrive.”
In addition to an endorsement from President Donald Trump, Masterson’s campaign was previously endorsed by the Kansas Grain and Feed Association and Kansas Agribusiness Retailers Association.
Holscher, an Overland Park member of the Kansas Senate, said she was eager to accept support from the Missouri-Kansas-Nebraska Conference of Teamsters. The organization represents more than 6,000 men and women in Kansas working in freight distribution, highway construction, food distribution, package deliver, railroad maintenance, bus drivers and brewery and soda manufacturing.
Mike Scribner, president of the Conference of Teamsters, said Holscher understood working people were the backbone of Kansas.
“In the Legislature, she has always sided with workers and our families,” he said. “As governor, she will work to create good-paying jobs and to bring down the cost of living.”
Holscher, who grew up on a farm in Missouri and whose father was a union member, said she would make certain Kansas workers had a seat at the table when considering policies related to cost-of-living and workforce issues.
She said she would defend the right of workers to collectively organize and support labor standards and apprenticeship programs. Government should investment in infrastructure projects that weren’t “corporate giveaways that leave ordinary Kansans holding the bag,” she said.
“Teamsters drive our economy, deliver the goods our families depend on and keep Kansas moving every day,” Holscher said. “I know firsthand how a good union job can give a family stability and a path to a better future.”
Holscher, elected to the Legislature nearly a decade ago, has been endorsed by Kelly and former Democratic Govs. Kathleen Sebelius and John Carlin.
Her campaign has been backed by the Kansas AFL-CIO, Kansas National Education Association’s PAC, the American Federation of Teachers, the American Federation of Government Employees, United Auto Workers Local 31, the SEIU Kansas Local 513 and UFCW Local 2.
In terms of labor, Masterson was endorsed by the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers and the IBEW Local 124.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Federal hemp restrictions poised to upend NC’s $3.2 billion industry
description: Chris Karazin started Carolindica with his brother and a friend in 2019, making homemade CBD products in a kitchen while working other jobs to pay the bills.  “I didn’t even get a paycheck until three years ago,” Karazin said.  Seven years later, the Raleigh-based company has grown into a multi-store hemp business with manufacturing operations […]
text:
Chris Karazin founded Carolindica in 2019 after working in the solar industry. He's concerned about the upcoming December deadline and its impact on N.C.'s hemp industry. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)Chris Karazin started Carolindica with his brother and a friend in 2019, making homemade CBD products in a kitchen while working other jobs to pay the bills. 
“I didn’t even get a paycheck until three years ago,” Karazin said. 
Seven years later, the Raleigh-based company has grown into a multi-store hemp business with manufacturing operations and dozens of employees. New customers still walk through Carolindica’s doors every day. 
Now, a looming change in federal law is forcing Karazin to reconsider the company’s future. 
Beginning Dec.11, federal restrictions will sharply narrow which hemp-derived cannabinoid products qualify as legal. Congress approved the new federal regulations in 2025 as part of the tax cut and spending measure known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.  
Under the new law, the only hemp products that will be legal are those with no more than 0.4 milligrams of THC compounds per consumer container, a threshold that could outlaw many products currently sold in stores. 
The restrictions were originally scheduled to take effect in Nov. 2026, but Congress extended the deadline by a month. 
One part of the law is still scheduled to take effect on Nov. 12. It excludes products that cannabis plants can’t naturally produce, including synthetic cannabinoids, from the federal definition of hemp, classifying them as marijuana. 
For Karazin, the impending bans on synthetic cannabinoids and THC mean he’s rethinking the products the company can continue selling, how much inventory to carry and where to invest its money. 
The federal restrictions follow years of rapid growth in the hemp industry, which proliferated after Congress legalized hemp production in 2018. North Carolina’s market has grown into a roughly $3 billion industry that employs about 16,000 people statewide. 
But North Carolina hemp businesses are now preparing for the possibility that much of that market could soon disappear.
A business built around hemp
The federal changes could affect more than intoxicating products such as THC gummies and drinks. CBD products, which contain small amounts of THC and other natural compounds found in hemp, could also exceed the new limit. 
The potential impact extends across the Triangle’s hemp retail market. 
A report by Raleigh Dispensaries, which maintains a database of hemp retailers in the region, found that 79 of 82 shops it tracked across seven counties listed at least one product category that would be affected by the restrictions. 
Jake St. Peter, the founder, said his report suggested more than 90% of the shops could be affected by the changes, and he’s been actively tracking how local businesses are preparing for the deadline. 
“I think this is really going to be a serious blow to these businesses,” he said. 
Some North Carolina hemp businesses are already closing as a result. Bloom Collective in Raleigh announced its closure on social media by the end of the month, saying new hemp regulations are putting “pressure on small businesses.” 
Other retailers and farmers began preparing for the federal restrictions last year. Owners of Durham’s Redhead Hemp said the limit could affect all of their inventory, while a Buncombe County farmer said his farm lacked the equipment to shift to THC-free products.
For businesses that depend on those products, switching to a different line of merchandise isn’t straightforward.  
Hemp-derived products and consumables line the shelves of a Carolindica store in Raleigh. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)
Karazin said Carolindica is exploring supplements, functional mushrooms and other products that could offer alternatives if the restrictions go through as planned.
But he said many smaller hemp retailers won’t have the same options. 
“Most companies are retail, distribution and e-commerce,” he said. “Those types of companies have no way of adapting at all.”
The restrictions would reach beyond the products sold on store shelves. 
Farmers growing hemp for cannabinoid products could lose buyers if manufacturers reduce production. At the same time, merchandisers could have to find new markets for products or ingredients that comply with the federal law. 
 State lawmakers weigh additional restrictions on hemp 
The federal deadline is not the only regulatory challenge facing North Carolina’s hemp industry. 
State lawmakers have also debated legislation that would impose the same THC limit on hemp products as under the federal law, and would also ban the sale of even low-level hemp consumables, including CBD products, to people under 21.
The state Senate passed the measure last summer, saying it would be a backstop in case Congress decides to revise or delay the new federal law.  
However, the House declined to take up the proposal during its August session under conflicting pressure from hemp businesses and law enforcement. House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, said lawmakers needed more time to consider the issue and could reconsider it after the November elections. 
NC House delays vote on hemp ban until November as advocates pack hallways

Meanwhile, the state’s Advisory Council on Cannabis is moving in a very different direction.
The Council was created by Gov. Josh Stein, who is in favor of allowing a regulated cannabis market for adults only in North Carolina. The Council is developing recommendations for setting up such a market should legislators decide to allow it.  Its final report is due to Stein by the end of the year. 
A recent poll from researchers at Elon University of over 1,000 North Carolina adults found that 75% of respondents were in favor of legalizing cannabis for medical use, while 55% were in favor of legalizing it for recreational use. 
Karazin said he supports regulations including age restrictions, child-resistant packaging and standardized laboratory testing. 
He’s worried lawmakers will eliminate the entire legal hemp market instead of creating a strong regulatory framework that could allow his business to stay open. 
“Regulation is what we need,” he said. “Prohibition is just hilarious regression.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: US Interior cancels maintenance, programming at national parks, including several New Mexico sites
description: The U.S. Department of the Interior has canceled contracts to conduct routine maintenance and programming at numerous national parks and downgraded nearly 1,500 more projects across the country to “low priority” status, including several in New Mexico, according to the nonpartisan conservation group Center for Western Priorities. The conservation group pulle[...]
text:
The U.S. Department of the Interior has canceled or downgraded routine maintenance and programming at national parks across the country, including at White Sands National Park, according to a new interactive map published by the nonpartisan conservation group Center for Western Priorities. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)The U.S. Department of the Interior has canceled contracts to conduct routine maintenance and programming at numerous national parks and downgraded nearly 1,500 more projects across the country to “low priority” status, including several in New Mexico, according to the nonpartisan conservation group Center for Western Priorities.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The conservation group pulled records from an internal National Park Service database and published them in an interactive map that contains details for each of the canceled or downgraded projects. Many of the entries contain notes that park officials wrote about the projects’ importance.
New Mexico’s cuts so far include $8,000 to continue operating eight weather stations in Valles Caldera National Preserve; $169,127 to submit documentation on Petroglyph National Monument’s significance to 29 tribes and pueblos to the National Register; $100,607 to finish taking stock of old museum records at Aztec Ruins National Monument and identify items that could be returned to Indigenous communities; and $30,984 for the National Trails Office to manage national park programs along Route 66 and other culturally significant roads.
A spokesperson for the Interior Department previously told the Washington Post that the department specifically focused on nixing deals that are “actively working against the best interests of the American people and the priorities of this administration.”
In addition to cutting projects, the federal agency also has downgraded nearly 1,500 — including 29 in New Mexico — as lower priority.
Advocates like Center for Western Priorities Creative Content and Policy Manager Lilly Bock-Brownstein contend that the federal agency is unfairly targeting “everyday projects that keep parks open and running,” particularly those that the Interior Department recently classified as “low priority.”
“Roof repairs, replacing outdated computers, even buying toilet paper and garbage bags — none of that is low priority. It’s the basic work national parks need to function,” she said in a statement.
Downgraded projects in New Mexico include replacing failing septic tanks at Chaco Culture National Historical Park, which park officials wrote are “past the normal lifecycle of a concrete septic tank.” Not replacing them could lead to sewage leaking into the surrounding area’s groundwater.
At Petroglyph National Monument, park staff labeled a project to replace failing HVAC systems at the visitor’s center an “emergency,” but it is also among the newly designated “low priority projects.” 
In Pecos National Historical Park, the Interior Department downgraded funding for a certified medical director who works with on-site law enforcement officers and rangers.
And at White Sands National Park, the Interior Department downgraded several repairs, including fixing visitor center exhibits that have fallen into disrepair; replacing fencing around sewage lagoons; installing new signage and preserving historic signs; and adding a fence to “protect critical infrastructure” at the park’s water tanks.
“It is illuminating to see which repairs and purchases were pushed aside so Secretary (Doug) Burgum could pay for President Trump’s vanity projects in Washington,” Bock-Brownstein said in a statement. “The National Park Service is supposed to protect every park. Instead, parks across the country are being neglected while money flows to the president’s pet projects.”
Neither the Department of the Interior nor the National Park Service immediately responded to Source NM’s requests for comment.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska AG’s Office seeks $19,000 in attorneys’ fees from City of Lincoln after charter fight
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska Attorney General’s Office is asking the Nebraska Supreme Court to require the city of Lincoln to reimburse about $19,000 in state attorneys’ fees after the state prevailed in its position on three citizen-led Lincoln City Charter amendments. Attorney General Mike Hilgers sued city officials in late August just before officials confirme[...]
text:
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers hosts a news conference in his office in the Nebraska State Capitol in Lincoln on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Attorney General’s Office is asking the Nebraska Supreme Court to require the city of Lincoln to reimburse about $19,000 in state attorneys’ fees after the state prevailed in its position on three citizen-led Lincoln City Charter amendments.
Attorney General Mike Hilgers sued city officials in late August just before officials confirmed they did not intend to place three petitioned charter amendments from the Good Government Lincoln campaign on the Nov. 3 ballot. City officials argued that the measures qualified for voter review but that they would instead appear on city ballots in May.
The high court, in a 5-2 opinion on Sept. 9, agreed with Hilgers’ office.
‘Ignoring the Constitution’s requirements’
Solicitor General Cody Barnett, Principal Deputy Solicitor General Zachary Pohlman and Deputy Solicitor General Lincoln Korell said in a Sept. 18 filing that they spent a combined 61 hours on the case — 42 hours for Korell, 10 hours for Pohlman and nine hours for Barnett.
Justices of the Nebraska Supreme Court (and when they were seated), front row from left: William Cassel (2012), Jeffrey Funke (2016, 2024 as chief justice) and Stephanie Stacy (2015). Back row, from left: Jason Bergevin (2025), Jonathan Papik (2018), John Freudenberg (2018) and Derek Vaughn (2026). (Courtesy of the Nebraska Judicial Branch)
Hilgers’ office estimated pay rates per hour at $300 for Korell and Pohlman, $375 for Barnett. In total, that’s just shy of $19,000 in attorneys’ fees. 
The state is also seeking $132, the cost to file the original lawsuit. The total request is $19,107.
“The costs and attorney time spent prosecuting this action are resources the Attorney General’s Office was required to spend to protect the constitutional rights of Nebraskans to participate in their municipal government at the ballot box this fall,” Hilgers’ office wrote. “These resources would have been devoted to other important state matters had respondents obeyed their constitutional duty before relator had to file this lawsuit.”
Hilgers said on social media Monday that without his office’s work, “the city would have been able to get away with ignoring the Constitution’s requirements.”
City attorney: Officials acted in ‘good faith’
Lincoln City Attorney Yohance Christie and his team, in a Sept. 25 filing, said he agrees that attorneys’ fees can legally be awarded, but that doing so is discretionary. He told justices they should not greenlight costs and fees in this case.
Lincoln City Attorney Yohance Christie during a hearing where the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office is challenging a Lincoln city ordinance enacted in response to a new state minimum wage law at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Thursday, July 2, 2026, in Lincoln. (Pool photo by Kenneth Ferriera/Lincoln Journal Star)
Christie said the matter was a “case of first impression,” a novel matter where state and local officials were dealing with proper constitutional construction and interplay of the state Election Act with conflicting requirements in the Nebraska Constitution and Lincoln City Charter.
Part of the concern, Christie said, was that city officials couldn’t presume signature verification would be met so close to a state-imposed Sept. 1 deadline to certify issues for the Nov. 3 ballot.
“While respondents’ construction of Neb. Const. Art. XI, § 4 was ultimately unpersuasive to a majority of the court, the arguments presented were made in good faith based on a colorable theory,” Christie’s office wrote.
“To award attorney fees would discourage similarly situated public bodies acting in good faith based on a reasonable interpretation of the law on a case of first impression to seek review of their own constitutionally granted rights.”
The three measures seek to limit Lincoln City Council members to two consecutive four-year terms, move the dates of city elections from odd to even years and let certain residents within a 3-mile buffer around Lincoln city limits vote in municipal elections, excluding bond votes.
Proposed alternatives?
City officials argued it was too late for them to review the amendments and suggest any potential alternatives, an option also under the Nebraska Constitution. 
The seven-member Lincoln City Council. Top row, from left, Sändra Washington, Justin P. Carlson, Tom Beckius and James Michael Bowers. Bottom row, from left, Tom Duden (vice chair), Brodey Weber (chair) and Bennie Shobe. (Photo courtesy of City of Lincoln)
After the Supreme Court required the Good Government Lincoln measures to go on the Nov. 3 ballot, the city offered two alternatives, related to term limits and the timing of city elections. The same night, the Lincoln City Council voted unanimously to place all five on the November ballot.
The term-limit alternative would allow three consecutive four-year terms, similar to the mayor. 
The alternative dealing with the timing of elections would not move city elections until 2030 and would limit newly elected officials to 3½-year terms. Under Good Government Lincoln’s version, city officials elected in 2025 would instead serve through 2030. But officials elected in 2027, such as the next mayor, would instead serve only through 2028. Those terms would also count for purposes of term limits.
The Supreme Court has not yet ruled on the request for attorney fees and costs.
Campaign finance, ads
Through Sept. 29, according to the latest campaign disclosure reports, Good Government Lincoln raised $431,5000 toward its effort. All of that is from the conservative nonprofit Restore the Good Life Inc. The group’s full list of donors has not been disclosed. In 2022, the group funded opposition to Republican competitors of future Gov. Jim Pillen.
The campaign has spent more than $431,000, most of it to Vanguard Field Strategies and its subcontractor, On The Ballot, for signature gathering. Vanguard was paid $390,000 in total.
Lancaster County Commissioner Matt Schulte, a Republican seeking reelection, has since helped boost Good Government Lincoln by paying for a comedic, musical ad propping up Good Government Lincoln’s versions of the charter amendments. 
Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird’s campaign last week also sent a text to city residents encouraging support for the Lincoln alternatives, urging residents to “vote ODD, not EVEN.”
No ads paid for by Good Government Lincoln yet appear on Google’s Ad Transparency Center.
Political ads can often be purchased at cheaper rates by political candidates than by ballot question committees. This gained prominence in 2024 around competing abortion ballot measures. A legislative effort this spring to stop future intermingling failed 8-24.
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Five-year-olds can be chronically absent or truant, too
description: Schools are rightly working to fix chronic absenteeism, but much of the focus is on higher grades and ignores kindergarten, the grade with the most absences before high school. Getting those kids in school deserves at least as much focus, writes Kalman Hettleman.
text:
A student raises his hand in a kindergarten classroom at Thelma R. Parks Elementary in Oklahoma City on Aug. 13, 2025. Making sure kindergartners are not absent is just as important as focusing on the higher grades, writes Kalman Hettleman. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)Chronic absenteeism has become a much-publicized national crisis since the pandemic. The face of it is teenagers who are rebellious, bored by school (often for good reason), and beyond parent control.
But we overlook at great cost the chronic absenteeism of much younger students. It begins with absent kindergartners, and there an alarming number of them: about 35% nationally. Happily, Maryland’s rate is much lower, as discussed later, but still not nearly low enough.
The grade with the worst attendance record before high school is kindergarten. And no surprise; children in poverty suffer the most.
In Maryland, chronic absenteeism is when a student is absent for 10% or more school days, including excused absences.
This absenteeism puts them on the perilous path to school failure in later grades. Research shows that starting in pre-K and kindergarten, “chronic absence is associated with lower levels of proficiency in reading and math as well as social-emotional development.”
Why are so many of our youngest students chronically absent? There are multiple causes. Younger children are more susceptible to illnesses like colds, flu, ear infections and strep throats. Some parents think of kindergarten as playtime; they don’t recognize its academic importance. Some don’t want to let “my baby” go. And some neglect their responsibility, often because of problems associated with poverty and addictive behaviors.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Chronic absence and habitual truancy are different. Habitual truancy means absences of more than 8 days in any single quarter, 15 days in any single semester, and 20 days in a school year. It can force parents to appear in Juvenile Court and face possible fines or jail. But punitive practices should be avoided, and in Maryland only about one-tenth to one-fifth of chronically absent students are considered habitual truants.
Of paramount importance, the burden to reduce chronic absenteeism shouldn’t be all on parents. Schools in Maryland and elsewhere are going all out to combat it.
It’s paid off in Maryland: The overall chronic absenteeism rate is 22.8 percent, down from 30.9 percent in 2021-22. But for children in kindergarten, it’s 26.9%, significantly higher than the overall K-12 rate.
In 2025, the General Assembly authorized a Task Force to Improve Attendance and Reduce Chronic Absenteeism in Schools. The state is committed to the goal of reducing chronic absenteeism by 50% and reaching a chronic absenteeism rate of no higher than 15%.
To that end, the Maryland State Department of Education established an early warning system to trigger early action and offers local school districts various toolkits. Many local school districts have developed impressive attendance initiatives.
There are no secrets about the tools. They include friendly outreach to parents and interventions as soon as possible. Health providers in schools, as well as teachers, should be specially trained on when a child should stay home or show up because of health-related conditions.
Maryland has two strong legs up in the battle against absenteeism. The first is a remarkable resource under the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future known as “wraparound” services. Wraparound services provide or connect parents to social work case management, health, mental, dental, food and shelter services.
Annual funding for them has skyrocketed from nearly nothing to well over $400 million (no other state comes close). So why not prioritize wraparound services for 5-year-olds who show signs of chronic absenteeism?
To do otherwise is a mistake. The earlier the intervention services and other tools the better. Kindergarten should come first, followed closely by grades 1-3.
A second advantage is that Maryland is one of only 17 states and the District of Columbia that mandate attendance in kindergarten; 16 of them, including Maryland, require full day.
As the saying goes, children can’t learn if they’re not in school. That’s as true for our teeniest students as for teens.
So, as school systems struggle to combat chronic absenteeism, they should double down on efforts in kindergarten and other early grades — before it’s too late and too difficult to remediate the learning loss students have suffered.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Federal appeals court dismisses Maine lobstermen’s defamation case against Monterey Bay Aquarium
description: The First Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled against a group of Maine lobstermen, who sued the Monterey Bay Aquarium for defamation after the aquarium added American lobster to its list of unsustainable seafood.  In a ruling Friday, the court sent the case back to U.S. District Court to be dismissed, concluding that the lobstermen […]
text:
A lobster waits to be thrown back into the waters of Little Bay after researchers evaluate it on Monday, Aug. 10. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)The First Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled against a group of Maine lobstermen, who sued the Monterey Bay Aquarium for defamation after the aquarium added American lobster to its list of unsustainable seafood. 
In a ruling Friday, the court sent the case back to U.S. District Court to be dismissed, concluding that the lobstermen failed to state a claim because there was not sufficient evidence that the aquarium’s statements made “particular reference” to the lobstermen. 
In a statement Friday, the Monterey Bay Aquarium welcomed the ruling. 
“​​People’s choices have the power to shape the future of the ocean,” the aquarium stated. “Programs like Seafood Watch guide consumers and businesses toward environmentally sustainable choices that support a healthy, thriving ocean, benefiting food security, fisheries and coastal communities whose livelihoods depend on the ocean.”
In 2022, the California-based aquarium’s popular seafood guide downgraded American lobster to a red listing, urging consumers and businesses to avoid buying the crustacean because of risks the fishery poses to endangered North Atlantic right whales.
The Maine Lobstermen’s Association, the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association and three lobster producers and sellers filed suit, arguing that the lobster industry’s gear has not been tied to right whale entanglements and the listing has harmed business.
In a statement Saturday, Maine Lobstermen’s Association Executive Director Patrice McCarron called the ruling deeply disappointing. 
“MLA stands firm in its position that the Aquarium’s red-listing harms the Maine lobster fishery by telling consumers to avoid Maine lobster while ignoring decades of meaningful conservation by the very people who depend on a healthy ocean,” McCarron said. “Maine lobstermen have a strong record of protecting right whales, and those measures are working. The North Atlantic right whale population is increasing, and documented interactions with Maine lobster gear are rare.”
Found along the East Coast, right whales’ migratory paths overlap with highly productive lobster fishing areas in Maine and Massachusetts, making entanglements in fishing gear one of the major threats for the animals. With a population of less than 400 and even fewer reproductively active females, right whales are approaching extinction with more than half a dozen threats to their existence, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: In-home program helps 2,800 new SC moms and babies. Advocates want it to continue.
description: SC advocates are promoting childhood Home Visiting programs, especially in a state that consistently ranks near the bottom for both infant and maternal mortality.
text:
The federal Maternal Infant and Early Childhood Home Visiting program is up for reauthorization in 2027. South Carolina advocates are pushing early to keep the program going. (File photo/Getty Images)When Sanquinita Martin visits the home of new parents in the Upstate, she acts as an extra set of eyes, encouraging parents and answering their questions as they learn to care for their newborn or toddler, “like an outside person looking in, and it’s not your mother-in-law.”
She’s part personal coach, part cheerleader — whatever that parent needs — as part of the federal Maternal Infant and Early Childhood Home Visiting program.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Martin, who works at the Parenting Place in Easley, and other advocates see the benefit the program brings to these parents and want to see it continue as it comes before Congress next fall for reapproval and funding. And while the renewal deadline is a year away, they’re championing it now in an effort to keep funds flowing uninterrupted to the growing effort.
That’s especially important in South Carolina, a state that consistently ranks near the bottom for both infant and maternal mortality — 43rd for infant death rates and 40th for maternal death rates, according to the March of Dimes 2025 report.
Home visits can start ahead of the actual due date for mothers-to-be. The visitors help pregnant women get to doctor’s appointments, to include arranging transportation. They also connect them with available benefits to ensure they’re getting prenatal vitamins, nutritional food and other health needs, such as help to quit smoking that could harm their pregnancy.
It’s all in an effort to help the women carry their unborn baby to term.
In 2024, the most recent year for data, 6,844 babies were born a month or more early in South Carolina. That’s a rate of 11.6%, compared to 10.4% nationally.
And more than 31 in every 100,000 pregnant women died due to complications during pregnancy or childbirth. The national number was more than 23.
As maternal mortality rises, SC report suggests ways of increasing health care access

The rates were even higher for Black mothers and those on Medicaid, the federal health insurance program for low-income families.
After the baby is born, a home visitor keeps coming for as long as the new parents wish — up until the child turns 3 years old.
The visitor again makes sure the mother and baby are making it to all doctor’s appointments. They support mothers suffering from postpartum depression. They help with breast feeding and sleep schedules and anything else a parent says they’re struggling with.
“It’s an intensive service — one that evolves as the child grows and develops, and you encounter different challenges along the way,” said Cathy Ramage, the state’s home visiting director.
In South Carolina, seven in every 1,000 infants dies before their first birthday, compared to a national rate of 5.6. Most often the cause in unexpected or unknown or involves suffocation from bedding in the crib.
Home visitors aim to prevent these deaths by making sure infants have a safe place to sleep and parents are coping with the stresses of raising a newborn.
And as the child grows, they guide the parents as they interact and play with their children in ways to help the child learn. They also screen for any delays in the child’s development and refer them to treatment if necessary. This ensures children won’t fall behind when they reach school age.
“I highlight the parents’ strength during this time,” Martin said. “I can say, ‘Hey, I noticed that she reached out to you and you picked her up right away. She knows that you’re there for her.’ “

“Because sometimes parents don’t think of the small things,” Martin added. “So I’m intentionally supporting the cue, the responsiveness, the attachment, the development. It’s an accumulation of all the small moments, the listening, the encouraging, the educating, the observing, connecting and helping parents believe in themselves.”
And when Hurricane Helene swept through the Palmetto State two years ago, hitting the Upstate where Martin lives especially hard, she messaged the families in her care ahead of time to make sure they were prepared with fresh water, shelf-stable foods, flashlights and batteries, but also stocked up on diapers and formula.
Martin has between 16 and 20 families she’s visiting at any given time.
“If home visiting didn’t exist, I think we’d be missing the opportunity to reach families before they have a crisis,” she said. “We’d be missing those early conversations, those moments where the parents say, ‘I’m struggling. I’m not sure what I want to do or what to do.’”
Fortunately, Ramage said the home visiting program has enjoyed strong, bipartisan support in Congress since its inception in 2010, as well as the backing of administrators within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
When Congress last reauthorized the program nearly five years ago, it also increased funding to the program for the first time in a decade. It also required states to chip in funding for the first time — $1 for every $3 of federal money.
Today, the program reaches 2,800 families in South Carolina, Ramage said. It will add about 200 more over the next year.
That’s triple the number of families compared to 13 years ago, when Ramage first started with the program.
But it’s also only about 10% of the families that qualify for aid.
“We could be serving just so many more families that need this type of support,” Ramage said.
Especially those living in rural areas with no birthing hospital nearby.
SC rural hospitals, doctors’ offices receive share of $200M in federal funding amid Medicaid cuts

Qualifying for the program involves multiple risk factors.
Calculations start by identifying counties with higher-than-average rates of infant mortality, low-birth-weight infants, poverty, crime, domestic violence or high school dropouts. Priority then goes to families living below the federal poverty level, pregnant women under the age of 21, families with a history of child neglect or enrollment in child welfare programs and those with past drug abuse.
Ramage said it’s important to begin conversations about reauthorization now, before expiration on Sept. 30, 2027, because a funding interruption disrupts the program and can throw off state budgets.
In the past, when Congress has had to keep the program running with bridge funds rather than a full, multi-year reauthorization, it’s led to staffing shortages as home visitors, unsure of their next paycheck, left to find other work.
Thomas Engels, administrator of the federal Health Resources and Services Administration which operates the program within the larger Department of Health and Human Services, spoke to these staffing challenges in a Dear Colleague letter last week.
“The effectiveness of home visiting programs depends on a skilled, stable, and well-supported workforce. Replacing a single home visitor costs a local program an average of $60,000, more than the average home visitor’s annual salary, and these losses are increasing,” he wrote. “More than half of home visiting programs experience at least one staff departure each year, and an estimated 20% to 29% of home visitors leave the field annually.”
Engels went on to express the Trump Administration’s support for the program as it heads back before Congress in the coming year.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: 125 Hoosier National Guard members deploying to Texas for immigration enforcement support
description: They'll deploy to southern Texas for a nearly yearlong immigration enforcement boost, relieving another mobilization from Monticello.
text:
Indiana Gov. Mike Braun and First Lady Maureen Braun visit Indiana National Guard members stationed in Washington, D.C. on Feb. 18, 2026. (Photo courtesy of official Flickr)About 125 Indiana National Guard members from Plymouth will deploy to southern Texas for a nearly yearlong immigration enforcement boost, relieving another mobilization from Monticello.
The members said goodbye to their family, friends and other loved ones during a departure ceremony Saturday.
They’re going as part of the ongoing Operation Arden Vanguard, launched in early 2025 to secure the U.S. border with Mexico.
“Our mission there is to support Customs and Border Protection. Essentially, we’re an extra set of eyes and ears on the southern border,” said Capt. Jakob Young, commander of the 381st Military Police Company. “If a soldier sees something, they will communicate that via radio to (U.S. Customs and Border Patrol), stand by, and wait for them to arrive.”
They will assist CBP and its parent agency, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, “within narrowly defined authorities,” according to a news release.
The mobilization also includes members from other guard units, like medics, supply specialists and mechanics.
They spent nearly a month training at Camp Atterbury in Edinburgh to prepare for the mission, and will receive additional training in Texas at Fort Bliss and the mission site.
“Our men and women in uniform are trained and ready to support the needs of our state and nation,” said Indiana National Guard Maj. Gen. Justin Mann, commanding general of 81st Troop Command. “Those of us here at home have the responsibility to look after the families as their loved ones are deployed in uniform.”
They’ll replace the 38th Military Police Company from Monticello, which is scheduled to return to Indiana in “a few weeks,” according to the news release.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Many GOP states have imposed new voting rules this year, some mirroring Trump’s midterm proposals
authors: By Gary Fields and Julie Carr Smyth, Associated Press
description: A voter heads into the Grove Park Community Center to cast her ballot in the primary election, Tuesday, March 10, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
President Donald Trump has pushed Congress to pass a proof-of-citizenship law, signed an executive order seeking a national voter ID requirement and tried to limit mail voting through U.S. Postal Service changes.
None of those moves succeeded in time to affect this year’s midterm elections. It’s a different matter in the states.
More than three dozen voting laws passed in Republican-controlled states are taking effect for the first time this year, many of them containing elements of Trump’s stalled proposals. They include changes to what IDs are acceptable to register for the first time and requirements to show proof of citizenship, an issue the Republican president has tried but failed to get through Congress.
“Trump’s attacks on our elections are deeply damaging, but they are not happening in isolation,” said Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s Voting Rights Project. ”Across the country, states are also advancing restrictions that make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot.”
READ MORE: Legislators send bill to governor to require voter citizenship checks and audits of voter rolls
Some new laws seek to make voting easier. Others continue a trend in Republican-controlled states of imposing restrictive rules that began in 2021 after Trump’s false claims of widespread fraud in his 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden. Trump’s continued false claims have resonated with Republican voters, a majority of whom believe Biden was not legitimately elected despite all evidence to the contrary. Trump lost dozens of court challenges, his own attorney general found no evidence of widespread fraud, and reviews, audits and recounts in the battleground states where he contested his loss all affirmed Biden’s victory.
Among the changes confronting voters as early voting gets underway: Students in New Hampshire can no longer use student IDs. Utah voters returning mail ballots must include more information on the envelope and some voters in Mississippi might need birth certificates or passports to verify their identity.
Under a new Mississippi law signed by Republican Gov. Tate Reeves, if someone tries to register and can’t produce a driver’s license number or if the number doesn’t appear in the Statewide Elections Management System, a county registrar would have to verify whether the person appears in a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services database called SAVE.
Government agencies use the federal database to verify an applicant’s immigration status or citizenship. If a person is flagged in the SAVE database, the registrar would notify them and offer a chance to provide documents showing U.S. citizenship before their registration application is denied or canceled.
Changes to voter ID requirements are challenged
Republican lawmakers who support the tighter voting laws, especially around voter ID, describe them as common sense changes.
New Hampshire state Rep. Donald McFarlane said he sponsored the bill to eliminate student IDs as acceptable for voting because colleges don’t have the same controls when issuing those cards as government agencies.
“The change removes a special exception and applies the same government-issued ID standard to all voters,” he said, adding that his bill had bipartisan support.
Students, he said, can still get state IDs free of charge.
The new requirements have not gone unchallenged.
In South Dakota, the ACLU has filed a lawsuit seeking to halt a new law that includes requiring voters registering for the first time to present the most common forms of ID — driver’s licenses, Tribal IDs and non-driver state IDs. They must be presented in person at places that accept registration.
“Proof of citizenship in itself is not terrible,” said Kathryn Johnson, president of the League of Women Voters of South Dakota.
Her concern is the requirement to present the IDs in person.
“We’re kind of a remote state, so sometimes it takes a drive, and you have to coordinate, you have to take off work, and all of these kinds of things,” she said.
Ohio seeks to scrub voter rolls
Ohio has a proof of citizenship requirement in effect for the first time this year for those registering to vote or updating their voter registration information at a Bureau of Motor Vehicles location. The state also eliminated its four-day grace period for mail ballots, which now must be received at local election offices by Election Day.
Yet the biggest concern for voting rights groups is an ongoing purge of the state’s voter rolls. The databases used to check citizenship against voter registration lists can be outdated, said Freda Levenson, legal director of the ACLU of Ohio, which has sued to overturn the law.
“Vast numbers of perfectly eligible voters are vulnerable to being disenfranchised,” she said.
Republican state Sen. Theresa Gavarone, one of the primary sponsors of the bill, challenged the ACLU’s legal action and said the problem it addresses is a real one.
“In the past two years, hundreds of noncitizens have been removed from Ohio’s voter rolls,” she said in an email. “Every single vote cast by a noncitizen disenfranchises a lawful Ohio voter.”
Voters have mixed views on the changes
Outside an early voting center in Wayne County, Ohio, retired steel worker Dan Walter, an independent voter, said he opposes requiring documentary proof of citizenship to vote.
“It’s to keep people from voting, it sounds to me like,” he said.
His wife, Jody, a retired aerospace executive and a Democrat, said she felt the same way about Ohio’s new requirement for registering to vote.
“A driver’s license doesn’t prove citizenship, and that’s all they ask for now,” she said. “It’s going to be an obstacle for so many people.”
Genia Fortune had a different view. A nurse, the Millersburg resident described herself as an independent and said she voted for President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and later for Trump. She believes Trump’s false claims that the 2020 election was stolen and sees requiring documentary proof of citizenship as a necessary precaution.
“I just feel like you need to be a citizen and show proof of ID,” she said.
Voting and election laws have become a regular target for legislatures
The Trump administration has pushed multiple strategies to influence this year’s midterm elections, most of them stymied by Congress or the courts.
Chris Diaz, the director of legislative tracking at the Voting Rights Lab, which tracks state legislation, said the group has seen several versions of the Republican president’s proposals passed by his allies in the states.
A recently released report by the group highlighted some of the key areas drawing Republican lawmakers’ attention, including mail balloting, voter ID and the hunt for noncitizens on voter rolls.
Noncitizen voting has been a focus of the Trump administration despite it being a rare problem. The U.S. Department of Justice recently announced it had brought charges in roughly 90 cases for various types of election misconduct, including 50 against people who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. The U.S. had 227 million registered voters for the 2024 presidential election.
The Brennan Center for Justice has identified nearly 40 laws in 21 states taking effect this election season that will make it harder for eligible voters to register, stay on the rolls or cast ballots.
The report from the center, part of the New York University School of Law, found that many of the new laws target subsets of voters.
“What I want voters to take away from this is that elections are still run by the states and there are still people in many states who are trying to make it harder for you to vote,” said Sean Morales-Doyle, senior director of the center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program. “But that’s all the more reason to go make a plan to vote and participate.”
___
Mississippi Today reporter Michael Goldberg contributed to this report. AP’s Gary Fields reported from Washington, and Julie Carr Smyth reported from Wooster and Millersburg, Ohio.
