name: Daily Montanan
title: Measure to protect citizen initiatives on Montana’s ballot
description: A measure to make sure Montanans can keep pitching initiatives to shape their government is on the ballot in 2026. In short, it’s an initiative to protect initiatives. Opponents say Constitutional Initiative 133 is vague and unnecessary, but proponents say voters are ready to make sure there’s no government interference in the right to propose […]
text:
Voters casting ballots (Getty Images)A measure to make sure Montanans can keep pitching initiatives to shape their government is on the ballot in 2026.
In short, it’s an initiative to protect initiatives.
Opponents say Constitutional Initiative 133 is vague and unnecessary, but proponents say voters are ready to make sure there’s no government interference in the right to propose and vote on laws that come directly from the citizens.
CI-133 would amend Article II of the state constitution to add the following language, in part:
“The people have a fundamental right to exercise their powers of initiative and referendum under Article III and Article XIV. The government may not deny or burden this right unless justified by a compelling government interest achieved by the least restrictive means.”
Dani Hess, spokesperson for Montanans Decide, which supports CI-133, said the campaign is finding that Montanans are receptive to the idea that the right needs to be protected.
“Montanans know what is best for Montanans, and CI-133 protects our right to propose and vote on laws that put our interests first,” Hess said in an email.
Supporters present the measure as a “homegrown” one, but it’s also drawing national money. According to the most recent campaign finance reports, Montanans Decide pulled in $2.44 million since December 2025, mostly from national groups.
Hess said those dollars are necessary “because of ongoing government interference in the initiative process,” including ones that result in legal battles.
“Montana is one of several states that has seen attempts to increase burdens on and barriers to citizens’ ability to vote on laws directly through the initiative process,” Hess said. “CI-133 itself had to go to the Montana Supreme Court simply to get to the signature gathering phase.”
In a unanimous decision this month, the state Supreme Court said four 2023 laws restricting the ballot initiative process were unconstitutional, including one imposing a $3,700 filling fee.
However, in a statement, Chase Scheuer, spokesperson for the Attorney General’s Office, said most provisions the legislature passed remain in place, and the state “prevailed on a majority of the measures originally challenged at the district court level.”
Charles Robison, with the Montana Chamber of Commerce, said his organization opposes CI-133 for a couple of reasons.
Robison said the language is “vaguely written,” and it’s hard to decipher how the initiative will be interpreted by the courts.
“We’re throwing a wild card out there. I think it’s reckless and also unnecessary,” Robison said.
He said the system is working already, and this year’s ballot is proof.
“As you can see, there’s multiple initiatives on the ballot right now,” Robison said. “We don’t have dozens, like California, but we’ve got a handful.”
In recent years, initiative supporters have challenged attorney general decisions that stymied attempts to place initiatives on the ballot, including CI-133. In some cases, the Montana Supreme Court agreed with the Attorney General’s rationale.
The interest in CI-133 comes from beyond Montana.
Other political committees have provided the bulk of the funding, including American Opportunity Action, with a mission that includes rebuilding the middle class and holding government accountable to the people; The Fairness Project, which works to protect voter access to ballot measures; and the GI Social Welfare Fund, which includes a focus on voter rights.
Hess said the work means Montanans can keep proposing initiatives.
“Passing CI-133 will protect our right to propose and vote on ballot initiatives and prevent further interference from the government, making this process fair, impartial, and more accessible to Montanans,” Hess said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: These Meriden moms want CT to do better on special education
description: The challenges special ed parents face aren't unique, but the processes to hold schools accountable are opaque, often fail to provoke change.
text:
When her son was in third grade, Jess LaMay decided she’d had enough.
LaMay’s son was diagnosed with autism when he was 1. From age 3 onward, he had been enrolled in special education programs at Meriden Public Schools. Much of that time, LaMay said, had been a battle. A battle for services, communication, time with his nondisabled peers, and, most recently, for someone to explain why he was coming home with soiled clothes and handprints of feces on his back.
That clarification never came, however, and LaMay was fed up. She and her husband sold their business, K LaMay’s Steamed Cheeseburgers, and began looking for somewhere to move.
Then, quite by chance, LaMay met some other Meriden residents who were forming an organizing committee to advocate for issues of importance to the town, such as education. Instead of moving, LaMay became an advocate herself, connecting with other Meriden special education parents, meeting with stakeholders from around the state and urging the General Assembly to approve more funding for her district.
Kyrin Highsmith, 7, of Meriden, who has an autism diagnosis, plays with other visitors under a rainbow parachute during a Strides for Neurodiversity Walk, organized by Meriden parents, at Platt High School in Meriden on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
“I started really kind of realizing that I wasn’t alone in this fight, and that there were people trying to change the narrative and what was going on,” LaMay said.
On Saturday, LaMay and her fellow organizers put on Meriden’s first-ever Strides for Neurodiversity Walk at Platt High School. The event sought to raise money for Meriden special education — the very system that nearly drove LaMay’s family to leave town a couple years earlier — and put pressure on state lawmakers to act.
“I’m hoping that it opens some eyes. Like, look, Meriden’s out here, the parents are out here working because you guys aren’t doing what you’re supposed to do at the state level,” LaMay said.
The challenges LaMay and her son faced are not unique to them, or to Meriden. The Connecticut Mirror has spoken with parents in towns across the state who have similar stories, from unexplained injuries to systematic Individualized Education Program, or IEP, violations to classrooms that don’t even have a teacher. The processes to hold schools accountable are cumbersome, opaque and often fail to provoke the changes parents hope for.
Not that many schools are in a good position to fix things, either. 
Special education is expensive but doesn’t factor into Connecticut’s main school funding formula, leaving towns to shoulder many of those costs themselves. There’s also a statewide shortage of special education staff — certified teachers and paraprofessionals — and positions aren’t easy to fill, especially in financially strapped districts like Meriden or New Haven that can’t offer competitive salaries.
“Their hands are tied because they don’t have the supports. So that’s why they give these, you know, people like me that pushback,” LaMay said.
For parents of kids with disabilities, the stakes often feel enormous. Special education is the system they rely on to ensure their children reach their full potential. It’s where a nonverbal child builds language skills and a child with behavioral challenges learns to self-regulate. In theory, it’s what sets them up to achieve everything they can in the course of their lives.
That’s the idea, at least.
Not enough money, not enough teachers
Meriden is one of Connecticut’s least wealthy school districts, meaning it’s highly dependent on the state’s Education Cost Sharing, or ECS, grant for money.
Just about everyone agrees ECS doesn’t provide enough — its formula hasn’t received an inflation adjustment since 2013, and it doesn’t weigh special education at all, even though those are some of the highest costs for districts. The state has a couple other special education-related grants, but they still leave significant gaps.
Generally speaking, it’s much cheaper to educate children with special needs in-district. That’s one reason Meriden tries to keep as many kids in its district as possible, said Director of School Leadership Daniel Crispino, who oversees its special education services. The other reason, he said, is that it’s generally best for kids to stay in their home district if possible.
If a district can’t meet a child’s needs, it turns to an outplacement program. These are among the highest costs for special education services, Crispino said.
“It could be $200,000 just for the top. Then you have another $50,000-plus for transportation. And then some of our kids are so significantly impacted medically, it could be another $100,000 for one-on-one [nursing],” Crispino said. 
The state’s excess cost grant may reimburse some of that, but only if the cost gets high enough, and often only partially.
But running in-house programming has its own challenges — namely, providing enough staff and services to meet every student’s needs.
“Your [special education] class sizes that were originally hoping to be around eight students, well, now that’s just not possible,” Crispino said. “We don’t have enough to add as many teachers as we would need.”
On top of that, there are the “inclusion” students — special education students who don’t go to a separate classroom but remain with their general education peers, typically with some kind of additional support like a paraprofessional who helps them regulate and manage classwork.
As those numbers increase, too, “your caseloads are higher, it’s more paperwork, more students that you’re having to service, more PPTs [Planning and Placement Teams],” Crispino said.
In Connecticut, PPTs are the teams that meet to develop and update an IEP — the plan outlining the child’s special education needs. Those meetings are where the critical decisions about services such as speech and occupational therapy are made. Every child in special education has a PPT, and every PPT includes administrators, teachers and parents.
Meriden works out how to distribute its resources over the summer, but if more kids transfer into the district over the course of the year, those plans begin to unravel.
When students with outplacements transfer into Meriden, the district also assumes the cost for those $200,000-plus services. “That, you certainly cannot prepare for,” Crispino said.
It all leads to a system under significant financial strain — the same system parents like LaMay rely on to ensure their children get the education they need.
“I think that the state level absolutely needs to do something and provide more,” LaMay said. “But while that’s happening, I feel like the district should be making changes with what they have to make it better and safer.”
How it started
When her son entered Meriden’s pre-K special education program — known as PRIDE, or Preschoolers Receiving Individualized Developmentally-Appropriate Education — LaMay was “taken aback by the minimal amount of services they were offering.” She arrived at PRIDE not only with a diagnosis, but a note from a doctor detailing the support her son should receive — including over an hour a week of speech therapy. 
When the school agreed to give him just 15 minutes a week instead, LaMay was nonplussed.
Co-organizer Jess LaMay shouts to a fellow organizer during a Strides for Neurodiversity Walk, organized by Meriden parents, at Platt High School in Meriden on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Under the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, or IDEA, schools have to provide all students with what’s known as a free appropriate public education, or FAPE. Exactly what that education looks like must be determined based on the individual student’s needs — as laid out in the IEP, which parents negotiate with schools. 
Parents are supposed to be an equal member of the PPT meetings where IEPs are hammered out, but in practice, they sometimes feel ignored, belittled or outright intimidated. Many arrive with no knowledge of IDEA or what services their children actually need and lack a robust support network. 
Not one to back down, LaMay educated herself on her son’s condition and the rules around IEPs. She connected with the Connecticut Parent Advocacy Center, which supports families of children with disabilities and which sent an advocate to participate in the PPT meetings with LaMay.
Legally speaking, it doesn’t matter whether a school actually has the resources to fulfill a student’s IEP. They just have to do it, even if they know they won’t get any extra funding for it.
“We don’t make determinations based upon resources or availability. That’s like, No. 1 IDEA principle,” explained Kathryn Meyer, a New Haven-based attorney with the Center for Children’s Advocacy who represents parents navigating special education.
But those material challenges don’t just go away because of what the law says, creating a systemic pressure to push back on parents trying to add services to an IEP.
Crispino acknowledged the difficulty. “We’re trying to provide free appropriate public education without the funding to do so,” he said.
In spite of the friction, Meriden was ultimately responsive to LaMay’s requests: It agreed to an hour of speech therapy, still less than what her son’s doctor had recommended but significantly more than the original offer. LaMay also managed to secure occupational therapy for her son after bringing in an outside occupational therapist to talk to the school.
Occupational therapy teaches children life skills they may otherwise struggle with: eating, opening things, putting on buttons, and so forth.
A few years after LaMay’s son was diagnosed, fellow Meriden parent Shayna Rodriguez began to notice her daughter wasn’t behaving like a typical toddler. At 3 years old, her daughter wasn’t excited to see her mom when she got home from work.
There were other signs, too. She didn’t react to her own name, and she was what Rodriguez used to call “flappy.”
“She would stim a lot. I now know that. And she did not talk,” Rodriguez said. “Stimming” is a repeated behavior someone engages in to self-soothe; it is not limited to people with autism but is often associated with the condition.
Rodriguez’s daughter was diagnosed with autism not long after. Rodriguez enrolled her in a Birth to 3 program in Meriden, and then in PRIDE, where her daughter received an IEP.
Co-organizer Shayna Rodriguez waves to a visitor during a Strides for Neurodiversity Walk, organized by Meriden parents, at Platt High School in Meriden on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
In the beginning, Rodriguez said, she knew very little about her daughter’s condition, or what to expect from the school, or what she could push for. She didn’t know anyone else navigating special education with an autistic child, and what knowledge she did have often came from Google. 
“All alone” was how Rodriguez described herself those early days. More than anything, she wanted to feel like everyone was on the same team. Instead, she sensed resistance from the school. 
“It just feels like there’s a wall up. There is a disconnect between parents and staff,” she said.
That was especially problematic, Rodriguez said, because her daughter was nonverbal and couldn’t tell Rodriguez about her day herself. Rodriguez said there were signs the teacher may not even have been in class some days.
“Whoever worked with her might not have known her well, because she would come home in somebody else’s pullup or with remnants of food on her face that I didn’t send her to school with,” Rodriguez recalled.
Eventually, Rodriguez began sending her daughter to school with a communication journal. In the morning, she would write in the journal what her daughter ate for breakfast and how her mood was; then she would ask the school to fill out the rest and send it back. 
If the entry came back blank, she said, she interpreted it as a sign “that the staff that’s normally in the room may not have been present.”
Although he couldn’t discuss specific cases, Crispino said he’s put an emphasis on communication since taking charge of Meriden special education a year ago. He said proactively keeping parents in the loop makes a big difference to how they experience the system, even if there are issues.
“If you’re giving specifics and you’re asking the family to be a partner in the work … more often than not, the parents would be willing to participate,” Crispino said.
Conversely, if “all of a sudden, you call a parent and say, ‘Hey, I just wanted to let you know for the last two weeks your son or daughter was doing ‘blank,’ you are going to lose that parent,” he added.
Like LaMay, Rodriguez also had to push for speech therapy. And her request for occupational therapy was denied for reasons she didn’t find convincing.
But then, the second year in PRIDE, everything seemed to shift.
“The teacher that we had and the SLP [speech language pathologist] that we had were amazing,” Rodriguez said. “They answered every question that I had. They wrote in the journal every single day.”
The SLP even advocated for Rodriguez’s daughter to get more speech services in kindergarten, a marked change from the year before. Rodriguez said she also began coming into her own as a mother of a child with special needs. She also got to know other parents, including LaMay.
“I’m not all alone now,” Rodriguez said. “I have built my own community through this.”
Entering a new program, challenges start anew
In kindergarten, students like Rodriguez and LaMay’s children enter Meriden’s elementary STARS, or Students and Teachers Achieving Remarkable Success, program. Like PRIDE, the program is straining under a shortage of funding and teachers.
Crispino said the STARS program has grown 57% in the last three years. The students bring a broad range of needs, and the list is only growing, he said.
A fall communication board is offered by Mr. C’s Voice Inc. during a Strides for Neurodiversity Walk, organized by Meriden parents, at Platt High School in Meriden on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Rodriguez’s daughter started at STARS this year, and Rodriguez said the walls have gone back up. “It feels to me, the more questions that I ask the school, the thicker the wall gets,” Rodriguez said. 
For LaMay, whose son is several years older than Rodriguez’s daughter, the shift to STARS was when the “turmoil” started.
At that point, LaMay had leaned so far into her son’s education that she joined the district herself as a special education paraprofessional. “I wanted to help children and families because I saw firsthand what was going on,” LaMay recalled.
Her son’s problems began in kindergarten. That December, the teacher quit, and the school wasn’t able to fill the position until the following February. At the time, some COVID-19 measures were still in place, and LaMay’s son ended up quarantined three times, ostensibly because he came into contact with someone sick.
LaMay had her doubts and a lack of communication with the school only fed her mistrust. She wondered what was actually happening in her son’s class and worried her speaking out might prompt some kind of retaliation.
At the same time, LaMay was pushing for her son to be given inclusion time in general education. Per the IDEA, schools are required to educate students in their “least restrictive environment” — meaning, among other things, if a kid can handle inclusion time, they should probably get it.
In some respects, LaMay said, her son was quite advanced for his age. She described him as “hyperlexic” and capable of reading at age 3. That suggested to her that he should get time in general education.
“I wanted him to be able to thrive and grow off of the skills [from a typical environment],” LaMay said. “And I also wanted the children to have a chance to get to know kids like him and vice versa.”
She said the school pushed back. “They wanted to be able to pull my son out … if he had any little problem, instead of working through it,” LaMay said.
Her experience improved markedly in first grade — again, thanks to a new teacher. But that teacher left the following year, and things got bad again. 
LaMay learned an employee was slapping her son’s hand to redirect his vocal stims. She called the school to ask what was going on, and she said she was told in a phone call that the hand slapping was “a technique that’s widely used across the STARS program.” There is no written record of this, nor is it referenced directly in any other documents. 
Crispino, who was not in charge of special education at the time, said slapping a child’s hand is “not a practice ever used in STARS.”
Then came third grade, and the repeated unexplained fecal handprints. LaMay also found out the school was leaving her son’s soiled clothes in his locker where he also kept his lunchbox, and that he wasn’t going to the gen ed time LaMay had fought so hard for. 
She said her son began eloping from class, sometimes as often as 26 times in one day. He also came home from time to time with unexplained bruises or bite marks from severe dysregulation.
“At that point, I had enough,” LaMay said.
Taking matters into their own hands
What LaMay and other parents have learned is that the challenges with special education are multifaceted. A good teacher who communicates regularly can make all the difference, but without adequate funding, good teachers are hard to recruit and retain.
Based on the latest data from EdSight, Connecticut is short 205 special education teachers and 918 special education paraprofessionals. Those are budgeted positions that schools are actively trying to fill, but can’t. 
“It just makes it challenging, especially for an urban setting. And then you talk about cost, right? How much can you pay a teacher to stay?” Crispino said.
Books featuring neurodivergent stories avaliable at the Meriden Public Library  are on display during a Strides for Neurodiversity Walk, organized by Meriden parents, at Platt High School in Meriden on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Instead of moving her family out of Meriden after her son’s third grade year, LaMay took her concerns to the state. She told the Department of Children and Families about the feces, and she filed a state complaint to get her son his gen ed time again. Nothing came of the DCF complaint, but the state did find Meriden had violated her son’s IEP due to a lack of staffing and required corrective action.
And fourth grade went just fine. “The elopement stopped. There was no more behaviors. There was no more feces,” LaMay said. She called it “probably one of the best years that we’ve had.”
She had been struggling in her role as a paraprofessional, with an increasing workload and the tension inherent in being both employee and an advocate for her son. So she quit.
But she came away with a direct understanding of why teacher quality can be so varied for students in Meriden’s special education programs. “They have a lot of positions open, but nobody’s taking them,” she said. On top of that, she said, the staff who do the best jobs tend to get more work until they burn out.
These days LaMay acts as a liaison between parents, like Rodriguez, and the school.
And she’s going even bigger — doing what she can to address the district’s financial shortcomings that make funding special education such a challenge. 
LaMay said Saturday’s Strides for Neurodiversity Walk raised about $2,500 for Meriden’s special education programming. She said she knew from the outset the event wouldn’t fix the structural gaps in Connecticut’s special education system. Her goal, she said, was to raise enough money for new classroom supplies — maybe even enough to fund a field trip for STARS students, or an end-of-year celebration for STARS families to come together.
She recalled a conversation she had with a staff member about how hard it was to get the services her son needed.
“That staff member came back to me and said, ‘You know, Jess, just because you know the district’s not handing out services doesn’t mean you should stop fighting for them,’” LaMay said. “And I was like, you’re right. You’re very, very right.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: Deported from CT: How one woman parents from Mexico
description: Laura Tillman discusses her story about a Connecticut woman who was deported to Mexico, and what came next for her family.
text:
Deportations are up significantly since President Donald Trump took office. In many cases, the people being deported leave behind family, friends, and community.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Laura Tillman to discuss her article, “ICE deported her from CT. Now, she parents from Mexico.” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read the story here.
WSHU: Hello, Laura. Tell us about Nancy Martinez. How did you come across her story?
LT: So, Nancy Martinez, I first learned about her story at a rally in New Haven in 2025. After she was detained by ICE one morning when she was taking her kids to school, there was a rally in support of her and other people who had been detained by ICE in an operation in Connecticut, and so that was the first time that I heard her daughter speak about her at the rally. And then, about a year later, I attended a press conference at Yale when they announced that they were supporting her in a lawsuit against the federal government.
WSHU: Now, tell us about her arrest on the ninth of June in 2025. How does she describe what happened?
LT: So, there’s actually video of this incident too, so we can see what happened. But essentially, she was walking up to her car with her kids. They get in the car, ready to leave for school in the morning, and then ICE vehicles surround her car, blocking her in, she is told to exit the car, and she’s handcuffed. And there’s a lot of frantic screaming, weeping, and conversation between her and her kids as they try to figure out what to do. And in the end, she’s taken away in an ICE vehicle, and her kids are left behind. And her mother, who was visiting from Mexico at the time, was able to come out of the house and accompany them on the sidewalk.
WSHU: So, did ICE say why she was picked up?
LT: After the press conference about her lawsuit, we did get a statement from ICE that said that she had a criminal history. And that they claimed also that they did ensure that the kids were looked after, which is one of the questions in the lawsuit: Nancy and Yale are alleging that ICE didn’t act properly and that it left the kids behind without ensuring that they had someone to take care of them.
WSHU: Now, she had an assault charge against her.
LT: So our understanding from Yale’s attorneys is that Nancy was arrested as a result of a dispute between her and her sister-in-law. Police were called. In the end, there were charges against her related to that dispute for you know breach of peace and assault, I believe, and those were dismissed by the judge. Nancy agreed to take anger management classes, and she had started those classes at the time. But this is kind of a part of a pattern that we see in a lot of these detention scenarios, where someone maybe has some minor interaction with the law, and then through that process, they’re sort of brought to the attention of ICE, and as a result, are detained.
WSHU: So, if you have any issues with the legal system, you come up on the database?
LT: Right. So, if you have any legal issues, you may come up, and that might prompt them to come and detain you. In most of these cases, people are being deported pretty quickly after that.
WSHU: Laura, as you got hold of this story, you decided to go to Mexico and talk to Nancy herself. Could you tell us a little bit about how that happened? Your experience talking with Nancy in Mexico.
LT: So actually, when this press conference happened earlier this year, I was already planning to go to Mexico City with my family in July. My family and I lived in Mexico City for 10 years before I moved to Connecticut, and so when I learned that Nancy was there in this neighborhood in the Estado de Mexico, which is a state in Mexico that kind of surrounds Mexico City, I decided that it would be really an unusual opportunity to go and and meet her there. I think a lot of the time when people are deported, the story for us as journalists, in some sense, ends there. We don’t get to see what happens on the other side of that. And so this was sort of a rare chance to get to go and meet her in person and talk to her.
WSHU: So, what is she doing there now?
LT: So she is selling clothes. She has a stand that she sets up in her neighborhood, and she sells both new and used clothes. She talks to her kids a lot. She talks to them many times a day. Sometimes her son, who has autism spectrum disorder, you know, calls her during the day when he’s at school because he just needs to hear her voice to calm down, and she’s trying to plan her daughter’s quinceanera party, which is the 15th birthday party for girls, which is a really special event for girls in a lot of Latin American countries, so she is trying to do those things from afar, and she’s living with her mother and her grandmother and other members of her family there in Mexico.
WSHU: So she’s still got a separated family, although her kids were able to come and spend some time over the summer, right?
LT: Yes, there was some fundraising that was done in New Haven by advocacy groups, and they were able to support the kids to get plane tickets to go and visit her over the summer. So I think that it’s clear that a lot of people in New Haven still feel a lot of solidarity with her and her family.
WSHU: Well, thank you so much, Laura.
LT: Yeah, thank you.

title: State Police Investigating Armed Home Invasion in Smyrna
description:
The Delaware State Police is investigating an armed home invasion that occurred Sunday afternoon in Smyrna. On October 11, 2026, at approximately 2:20 p.m., troopers responded to a residence in […]
The post State Police Investigating Armed Home Invasion in Smyrna appeared first on Delaware State Police - State of Delaware.
text:
Two masked suspects entered a Culbreath Street home Sunday afternoon; police are seeking witnesses and information
SMYRNA — Delaware State Police are investigating an armed home invasion in Smyrna after two masked suspects entered an occupied residence Sunday afternoon, threatened a victim with a handgun and escaped with cash and personal property.
Troopers were called to a residence in the 800 block of Culbreath Street at about 2:20 p.m. Oct. 11 for a reported armed robbery.
Police said two victims were inside the home when the two masked suspects entered. One suspect pointed a handgun at one of the victims and demanded money. The suspects then searched the residence before leaving with cash and personal belongings, according to State Police.
Neither victim was injured.
Police have not released descriptions of the suspects beyond saying they were masked, nor have investigators said how the suspects entered the home, whether the victims knew them or whether investigators believe the residence was specifically targeted.
The Delaware State Police Criminal Investigations Unit is handling the investigation.
What is a home invasion?
The term “home invasion” generally distinguishes this kind of crime from the burglary of an empty house because people are inside when the intruders enter, creating the possibility of a direct confrontation.
Delaware law specifically recognizes “home invasion burglary first degree” under certain circumstances. The statute applies when someone unlawfully enters or remains in an occupied dwelling intending to commit a crime and, during the entry, crime or immediate flight, commits or attempts certain serious felonies, including robbery, assault, murder, manslaughter, rape or kidnapping.
That distinction helps explain why an incident such as Sunday’s can be particularly concerning to residents. A conventional residential burglary may occur when no one is home. In a home invasion, occupants can suddenly find themselves face to face with an intruder.
State Police have described Sunday’s incident as an armed home invasion but have not announced arrests or specific criminal charges.
What nearby residents can do
Residents in the Culbreath Street area may be able to help investigators even if they did not witness the crime itself.
Anyone with a doorbell camera, exterior security camera or vehicle camera that captured activity near Culbreath Street around the time of the 2:20 p.m. incident should consider reviewing the footage before it is automatically deleted. Video showing unfamiliar people, vehicles or activity before or after the robbery could potentially be useful to investigators.
Residents should not confront anyone they believe may be connected to the crime. Suspicious activity that appears to present an immediate danger should be reported by calling 911.
The incident also offers a reminder to review basic home security practices.
Federal security guidance recommends keeping exterior doors and windows secured, maintaining outdoor lighting, using cameras where practical and trimming landscaping that can provide hiding places or block views of doors and windows. Families also can discuss in advance what to do during an emergency and where household members can safely retreat while calling police.
Residents also can take several simple precautions:

Keep doors locked even while at home, including during daylight hours.
Identify visitors before opening the door, particularly when someone is unexpected.
Avoid opening the door simply because someone knocks or claims to be making a delivery or providing a service.
Make sure exterior lighting, doorbell cameras and other security equipment are working.
Save potentially relevant security-camera footage rather than assuming someone else has reported it.
Call police rather than confronting suspicious people outside a residence.
Talk with children, older relatives and other household members about what to do if an unknown person tries to enter the home.

The recommendations are precautions, not an indication that police believe additional home invasions are imminent. State Police have not announced a broader threat to Smyrna residents in connection with Sunday’s case.
Police seek information
Detectives are asking anyone who witnessed the incident or has information that could assist the investigation to contact Detective E. Paneda at 302-698-8444.
Tips also may be submitted through a private message to the Delaware State Police Facebook page or through Delaware Crime Stoppers at 1-800-847-3333.
Victim assistance is available
The Delaware State Police Victim Services Unit and Delaware Victim Center provide assistance to crime victims, witnesses and people who have lost loved ones to sudden deaths.
The 24-hour toll-free hotline is 1-800-VICTIM-1, or 1-800-842-8461. The Victim Services Unit also can be reached by email at DSP_VictimServicesMail@delaware.gov.
To Go

What happened: Two masked suspects entered an occupied home in the 800 block of Culbreath Street in Smyrna about 2:20 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 11. One suspect displayed a handgun. Cash and personal property were taken. No injuries were reported.
Have information or video: Contact Delaware State Police Detective E. Paneda at 302-698-8444.
Anonymous tips: Delaware Crime Stoppers, 1-800-847-3333.
Immediate suspicious activity: Call 911 rather than confronting a suspicious person.
Victim assistance: Delaware Victim Center, 1-800-842-8461, available 24 hours a day.

text:
William Skipworth, a staff reporter for the New Hampshire Bulletin since January 2025, won an A-Mark Prize and Publick Occurrences award for his series "A System of Harm." (Photo by Janine Weisman/Rhode Island Current)Bulletin staff reporter William Skipworth took home a pair of awards at the New England Newspaper and Press Association awards on Oct. 9.
Skipworth won a first-place A-Mark Prize for Investigative Journalism for his series on abuse and neglect in the state’s disability care system, as well as Publick Occurrences award for the same series. The A-Mark Foundation awards honor investigative reporting excellence in each state (as well as Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico), while Publick Occurrences awards celebrate “the best work that New England newspapers produce each year.”
“A System of Harm,” Skipworth’s monthslong, three-part investigation of the state’s disability system, was published by the Bulletin in November 2025. Among his other honors for the series are a Livingston Award for local reporting, a third place in investigative reporting from the National Association of Health Care Journalists, and several awards from the New Hampshire Press Association, including Journalist of the Year.
The Bulletin’s investigation had real-world impact in New Hampshire. In July, Gov. Kelly Ayotte signed Senate Bill 670 into law, which strengthened protections for people with disabilities in state care; the state senator behind the law called the Bulletin’s reporting “the genesis” of the legislation. A federally funded watchdog agency, the Disability Rights Center-New Hampshire launched its own investigation into the system, calling the Bulletin’s reporting “probable cause.” The state also convened a System Review Committee, which held a series of meetings to question officials and educate the public before releasing its recommendations for system reform.
Rhode Island Current, which like the New Hampshire Bulletin is part of the States Newsroom nonprofit news organization, also won a pair of awards. The Current was named as a Distinguished Online News Publication and reporter Nancy Lavin won a third-place A-Mark award for her examination of failures in care for homebound seniors.  
The annual NENPA fall awards were held at The Publick House Historic Inn in Sturbridge, Mass.

text:
Delaware Schools Receive $7.1 Million in Early Literacy Grants
The Delaware Department of Education has awarded more than $7.1 million in grants to 28 districts and charter schools to support teacher training, instructional coaching and early literacy instruction during the 2026-27 school year. (Photo courtesy of Delaware.gov.)
The Delaware Department of Education has awarded more than $7.1 million in grants to 28 school districts and charter schools for the 2026-27 school year to strengthen early literacy instruction and improve reading outcomes for students.
The funding is part of the state’s second round of Bridge to Practice grants, which support teacher training, instructional coaching, curriculum development and school leadership initiatives focused on the science of reading.
Several school districts in Kent and Sussex counties received funding, including Capital School District, which was awarded $763,855.93, Lake Forest School District with $321,093.20 and Milford School District with $248,238.10.
Other local recipients include Cape Henlopen School District, which received $316,384.87; Laurel School District, $207,285.75; Indian River School District, $146,448.42; Woodbridge School District, $132,485.60; Seaford School District, $81,799; and Sussex Academy, $84,057.75.
The grants are intended to help educators apply research-based reading instruction methods in classrooms through ongoing professional development and support.
“We know how to teach children to read, and we believe every Delaware student can become a strong reader,” Secretary of Education Cindy Marten said. “Passing strong policy is important. Providing resources is important. Training educators and providing coaching are important. But none of those things alone is the outcome we are working toward. The work is making sure what we know reaches students through strong instruction every day and then showing our progress in ways we can reliably measure, see and report. That is how we move plans into progress and stay accountable as we go.”
The funding supports Delaware’s Birth through Grade 3 Early Literacy Plan, which focuses on improving reading instruction during the earliest years of education.
Grant recipients can use the funding for science-of-reading training programs such as LETRS and AIM Pathways, curriculum-based professional learning, instructional coaching and leadership development through the Early Literacy Leadership Academy.
The state previously awarded $6.1 million to 25 districts and charter schools in March as part of the first round of Bridge to Practice grants.
During that round, Indian River School District used funding to improve consistency in literacy instruction across its elementary schools through districtwide instructional frameworks, monthly classroom observations and professional learning for prekindergarten through third-grade educators.
Capital School District focused on connecting teacher training to classroom instruction through student work, classroom reflections and participation in the state’s Student-Centered Coaching program.
The latest round of funding will continue those efforts while placing additional emphasis on how training and instructional strategies are implemented in classrooms.
Throughout the school year, the Department of Education will work with participating districts and charter schools to evaluate progress through classroom observations, coaching activities and student literacy data.
The grants are part of Delaware’s broader early literacy strategy and the Department of Education’s 2025-2028 Strategic Plan.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Native small business owner: Main Street needs someone in the room
description: I started Lakota Made in 2018 at my kitchen table with six salves, made from plant medicines I learned from Lakota elders. Today, we have a storefront on Riverfront Drive, a small production team, more than 100,000 online orders and customers in 213 countries and territories around the world. Our social media community has 179,000 […]
text:
Megan Bull Bear poses for a photo in her Mankato store, Lakota Made. (Photo courtesy of Megan Bull Bear)I started Lakota Made in 2018 at my kitchen table with six salves, made from plant medicines I learned from Lakota elders. Today, we have a storefront on Riverfront Drive, a small production team, more than 100,000 online orders and customers in 213 countries and territories around the world. Our social media community has 179,000 followers and reaches an average of 2 to 4 million views a day. Along the way I learned where a small business’s power starts and where it ends.
It starts with community. Our storefront sits blocks from where the Dakota 38 were hanged, and we chose that on purpose. It’s a place where Indigenous artists sell their work, where people come to learn about plant medicine and where history gets told by the people it happened to.
It also brings people to Mankato. Customers have told us they changed their vacation plans just to come see our store. People plan trips around our store hours, and groups come in from out of town. While they’re here they ask us where to eat, where to get their car fixed — and what else Mankato has to offer. I couldn’t begin to measure what that means for this town, especially when we hold our big events.
That work doesn’t stay inside our walls. I’ve taught tea blending classes at Hocokata Ti Cultural Center in Shakopee. This summer, a delegation of the Minnesota Indian Women’s Sexual Assault Coalition traveled to a national conference in California, where I gave the opening keynote and led a plant teaching. I also travel to Omaha for classes and speaking events. 
This November, I’ll be working with science teachers from across the state at the Minnesota Conference on Science Education conference in Mankato, helping schools connect with local Indigenous communities. Through our nonprofit, the Mahkato Revitalization Project, we’re building a free plant medicine curriculum for young people that will never be sold.
None of this shows up on a balance sheet. But it matters, especially now, when so much history is being pushed aside and smaller voices are the first ones lost. Small businesses like ours are often the ones carrying that work.
Where our power ends is with the suppliers we depend on. Over the past two years, we spent more than $105,000 with Uline — a packaging and shipping company — on jars, droppers, tins and boxes. In that time our prices on the same items, the same quantities, went up 10 to 22%. An 8-oz jar went from 96 cents to $1.07. The best prices go to whoever can buy the most at once, so a business our size pays more per jar and ties up cash in inventory we don’t have room to store. Switching isn’t simple either, because our labels and listings are built around those exact containers.
We also wanted to buy local, so our soap boxes are made by Taylor Corp. here in Mankato. We paid the setup costs to get our boxes made there. Our orders have been quoted at two weeks, and we have waited as long as six months. Because we don’t know when the charge will come, we hold that money in our account the whole time. That’s money a business our size needs for materials and payroll.
I’m not accusing anyone. This is just what it looks like when a small business depends on companies many times its size. We don’t have the volume to negotiate better terms, and often there’s no real alternative.
That’s why I want our representatives, including U.S. Rep. Brad Finstad, to keep small businesses in mind when they make decisions about trade, supply chains and small business support. 
Main Street shops need someone in the room, too.
I’m not asking for a bailout. I’m asking for leaders who remember that small businesses are what hold towns like Mankato together.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri voters will decide whether to create a sovereign wealth fund
description: Missourians will vote next month on a proposal to set aside and invest state money that could remain untouched for more than a century, with the eventual goal of generating enough earnings to eliminate state taxes. Amendment 7 will ask voters if they would like to enshrine in the state’s constitution a “permanent public endowment […]
text:
A Missouri ballot measure will ask voters in November to authorize the creation of a sovereign wealth fund with the goal of eliminating state-imposed taxes. (Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)Missourians will vote next month on a proposal to set aside and invest state money that could remain untouched for more than a century, with the eventual goal of generating enough earnings to eliminate state taxes.
Amendment 7 will ask voters if they would like to enshrine in the state’s constitution a “permanent public endowment fund to support state government” with the ultimate goal of eliminating all state taxes. The idea, called a sovereign wealth fund, allows a state to invest public money and allow the returns to compound over generations.
It is like a “financial time capsule,” Republican state Sen. Adam Schnelting, who championed the proposal in the legislature, told The Independent. “We invest into the fund once, and we let it ride. Then future Missourians, they will be the beneficiaries of our foresight.” 
By his legislative staff’s predictions, an initial investment of $250 million would grow enough in 125 years to cover the state’s expenses.
The proposal is not tied to Amendment 5, the measure overwhelmingly rejected by voters in August that would have given lawmakers greater authority to move Missouri away from an income tax.  Amendment 7 measure has a much different timeline, benefiting future generations of Missourians instead of those at the ballot box.
State Sen. Adam Schnelting, a Republican from St. Charles, speaks in March at a Missouri Right to Life rally in the Missouri State Capitol Building in March 2025 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Schnelting said the idea came from his personal investment strategy — setting aside money for his kids and future grandchildren.
“When we do these calculations on the power of compounding, it is enormous,” he said. “So I just thought one day, why don’t we use the power of compound interest to ensure that we provide for future generations as far as our tax revenue is concerned?”
Sovereign wealth funds are not novel, but Missouri’s proposed model would be unusual.
For example, Texas’s Permanent School Fund was created alongside the state’s founding and invests revenues from land sales and oil royalties to support public education. The 50-year-old Alaska Permanent Fund uses oil and mineral revenues to fund government services and distributes some of its earnings to residents with annual dividends.
Amendment 7 would rely on money appropriated from Missouri’s general revenue fund, along with any private donations.
Nathan Mauck, a professor at the University of Missouri-Kansas City’s Henry W. Bloch School of Management with expertise in sovereign wealth funds, told The Independent that Amendment 7’s funding source is “a little bit different than what you would normally see.”
“Normally the source of those funds comes from some type of surplus, so maybe it is oil or some other natural resource, rather than a tax appropriation,” he said.
While other states have created their sovereign wealth funds in times of prosperity, Amendment 7 comes at a time when lawmakers are looking for ways to cut spending.
In June, State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick wrote in a report that the state’s spending is exceeding its revenue.
“The state is on track to completely run out of money in the (general revenue fund) and be forced to implement emergency budget reductions,” he wrote.
Setting aside hundreds of millions of dollars for a fund that could not be tapped for generations would leave that money unavailable for current state services.
Schnelting believes there is enough “waste that can be cut” to allow a strong initial investment. But even if the money is not available, the fund can sit empty for future legislatures to pour into, he said.
“If things are just too tight over the next few years… the fund structure is still there, and we could revisit it in a better time if that was required of us,” he said.
The proposal got support from all but eight Republicans in the state legislature while Democrats voted it down. During debate of the bill, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle seemed open to the idea of a sovereign wealth fund but were skeptical of the bill’s timing amid financial pressures.
“We do not have a lot of general revenue that is going to be left on the bottom line this year — and even less next year,” state Sen. Maggie Nurrenbern, a Democrat from Kansas City, said during the Senate’s debate in March.
State Rep. Kemp Stricker, a Lee’s Summit Democrat, zeroed in on a provision that prevents the state from dipping into the fund before it is large enough to eliminate all state-imposed taxes.
“If (revenues) come in too light, we have locked up money that is sitting in a fund that may never be touched for hundreds of years, potentially,” he said in May.
The prohibition on premature spending is part of a few measures intended to protect the fund from political pressure, Schnelting said.
“You have got to invest money and leave it,” Mauck said. “If they are pulling from this fund, it is going to extend the amount of time needed and even the likelihood that that goal is ever reached.”
While voters should consider the source of the funding and the proposal’s ultimate goal, Amendment 7’s framework is also important, Mauck said.
His research has shown that good governance and independence from political influence is essential to a sovereign wealth fund’s prosperity.
“We have elections all the time,” he said. “So if you have a long-term strategy but that strategy pivots because of evolving politics or who wins a given election, it can reduce confidence that the goals of the fund are going to be pursued.”
The amendment would assign responsibility of the fund’s management to the state treasurer, which is an elected position in Missouri.
Giving the power to the treasurer “does not get the type of independence that normally I would recommend,” Mauck said. “However, by limiting the types of investments that the fund can make, it does reduce let’s say some of the some of the concerns.”
Investments would be limited to “exchange-traded funds tracking the stock performance of the Standard and Poor’s 500, or a comparable successor index to be determined by law.”
This measure “reduces possible political influence, but it certainly doesn’t eliminate it,” Mauck said.
Schnelting chose the S and P 500 to “just invest into the American market,” he said. “It won’t give a future treasurer too much leniency and too much power.”
Missouri has already seen political disputes over how public money should be invested.
In 2023, Treasurer Vivek Malek pushed the Missouri State Employees Retirement Fund’s board to divest from Chinese-owned companies. Malek said his rationale wasn’t political in nature but was focused on the “level of risk that is contrary to the interests of our time.”
Schnelting said the choice to have the state treasurer oversee the fund was simple, since it is the office’s role “to oversee the very various funds that we have.”
He pointed to another provision requiring the state auditor to conduct an audit of the fund at least once every three years as a layer of protection.
For Mauck, Amendment 7 presents a test not only of voters’ patience, but of their confidence that Missouri officials decades from now will manage the fund as its creators intend. 
“It could be hugely beneficial if executed well and things go according to plan,” he said. “So it is an interesting trade off that folks have to make as they’re thinking about the wisdom of this strategy.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Second ‘Big Beautiful’ lease sale in Alaska’s Cook Inlet planned after first sale flops
description: The Trump administration on Friday announced that it will hold an offshore lease sale in federal waters of Cook Inlet next March, about a year after a similar federal lease sale offering the same acreage drew no bids. The auction — to offer 1 million acres of federal offshore territory — is part of a […]
text:
Waves roll in on a Cook Inlet beach north of Anchor Point on Oct. 23, 2025. The Trump administration is planning a March oil and gas lease sale in federal waters beyond the shoreline. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The Trump administration on Friday announced that it will hold an offshore lease sale in federal waters of Cook Inlet next March, about a year after a similar federal lease sale offering the same acreage drew no bids.
The auction — to offer 1 million acres of federal offshore territory — is part of a series mandated under the sweeping tax and budget bill called the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” passed last year. The new law requires at least six Cook Inlet oil and gas lease sales through 2032. The first of those sales, held in March, was called the Big Beautiful Cook Inlet 1, or BBC1; the upcoming sale is called Big Beautiful Cook Inlet 2, or BBC2.
The announcement was made by the Marine Minerals Administration, the newly named agency that combines the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management and the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement.
“Alaska remains central to America’s energy future, and Cook Inlet is an important part of that opportunity,” Mike Olsen, the agency’s acting director, said in a statement. “The BBC2 sale continues MMA’s work to carry out a predictable, congressionally mandated leasing schedule that supports domestic energy production, strengthens national readiness and provides a transparent process for the State of Alaska, local governments and industry.”
The lack of any bidding by oil and gas companies in the first “Big Beautiful” Cook Inlet lease sale is part of a pattern. A state lease sale held at the same time drew only a single bid.
The previous federal lease sale in Cook Inlet, a hotly disputed event that was at first canceled by the Biden administration for lack of industry interest but eventually held at the end of 2022 under a mandate from Congress, drew only a single bid. Federal Cook Inlet lease sales in 2007, 2009 and 2011 were canceled for lack of interest; a sale held in 2004 drew no bids.
Hilcorp, the dominant oil and gas operator in the Cook Inlet basin, was the only company holding federal leases in Cook Inlet. But in September, Hilcorp relinquished all eight of its leases – seven acquired in a 2017 lease sale and the sole lease acquired in the 2022 sale.
That leaves Cook Inlet’s federal waters with no active leases.
Environmentalists, pointing to that record, said the upcoming federal Cook Inlet lease sale is a waste of time.
“The government held an identical sale in March, and it failed completely with zero bids,” Hannah Foster, an attorney with the environmental law firm Earthjustice, said in a statement.
“Since then, the only company with any existing leases in federal Cook Inlet waters relinquished those leases. Nobody wants this sale, and yet this administration is determined to waste resources carrying it out – ignoring our bedrock environmental laws in the process,” she said. “Cook Inlet, which provides critical habitat for endangered beluga whales and serves as a hub for fishing and tourism, is too important for more reckless drilling.”
Cooper Freeman, Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, likened Cook Inlet oil leasing to another highly touted development plan for Alaska that has failed to materialize into tangible development, the proposal to build a gasline and send North Slope liquefied national gas to Asian markets.
“I’m embarrassed for our state and our country that we have to endure these Trump lease sales in Cook Inlet again and again,” Freeman said in a statement. “It’s yet another massive waste of time, just like the Alaska LNG project, that will never pencil out and only diverts us from working toward a viable, renewable energy grid. Cook Inlet is being besieged by oil spills, data centers and gold mining. For the sake of our salmon, beluga whales and future generations of Alaskans, we have to start treating it with far more respect.”
The Trump administration is pushing for expanded offshore oil leasing beyond Cook Inlet. The administration’s proposed five-year leasing plan calls for 21 lease sales in waters around the state, including remote sites like the Bering Strait region.
The creation of the Minerals Management Administration in July is also part of the administration’s push for more offshore development.
It reverses an action taken during the Obama administration in the aftermath of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster. In that event, a well blowout killed 11 people and spewed what became the nation’s biggest marine oil spill in history.
The Obama administration split the Minerals Management Service into two agencies to separate the leasing and revenue-generating functions from the environmental oversight functions and thus reduce conflicts of interest. The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management became the agency in charge of leasing, while the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement had the oversight duties.
A July 10 order issued by U.S. Department of the Interior Secretary Doug Burgum reunited the agencies to “streamline governance of the Nation’s offshore energy and mineral resources.”
Hilcorp and other companies continue to operate in state territory in the Cook Inlet basin, both offshore and onshore. The basin, which also includes a small amount of onshore federal territory, is the oldest oil and gas producing region in Alaska. The basin has produced oil since the 1950s and natural gas since the early 1960s, but volumes have diminished dramatically from what they were during peak production decades ago.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Social Security, data centers and healthcare: Senate candidates exchange jabs while talking policy
description: COLUMBIA — The candidates for U.S. Senate traded political digs as they answered policy questions Sunday in their likely only debate ahead of what’s predicted to be a close finish. The debate featured an all-female stage, a first for a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina, on the three-month anniversary of the shocking death of […]
text:
Democrat Annie Andrews, Republican Sen. Darline Graham and Libertarian Kasie Whitener prepare to debate Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026, at South Carolina ETV's studio in Columbia, S.C. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette) COLUMBIA — The candidates for U.S. Senate traded political digs as they answered policy questions Sunday in their likely only debate ahead of what’s predicted to be a close finish.
The debate featured an all-female stage, a first for a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina, on the three-month anniversary of the shocking death of U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham, which reset the race.
Democrat Annie Andrews, who’s seeking to flip a seat that’s been reliably red for decades, cast herself as “an independent voice” — twice noting she grew up in a Republican home — while saying the three-month incumbent has shown she’s “not up for the job.” Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fulfill her late brother’s fourth term, touted herself as the only conservative in the race, while accusing Andrews of being a “radical liberal” who’s moderated her positions for the contest.
As the main party nominees exchanged barbs, Libertarian Kasie Whitener pointed to her skills as a small business owner and entrepreneurship professor at the University of South Carolina and a willingness to be “honest” about the nation’s fiscal woes.
A fourth candidate on the ballot, Mark Hackett with the Constitution Party, did not meet South Carolina ETV’s eligibility rules for the debate.
Here’s a look at their answers to questions on data centers, healthcare, Social Security and the war with Iran:
Data centers
One of the clearest policy divides during the debate involved data center growth.
Andrews proposes a two-year moratorium. Regulations developed during the pause should ensure data centers pay for themselves so that customers’ rates don’t go up. And she wants a “return to real local control,” she said, then accused “data center Darline” of only wanting to build data centers “faster and faster.”
In response, Graham said she too wants local control of decisions.
She noted co-sponsoring the Ratepayer Protection Act, which directed state regulators to consider standards aimed at protecting communities. The proposal easily cleared the House 417-3 in September but was blocked by Democrats in the Senate, who criticized it as a toothless, pre-election gimmick.
She called Andrews’ plan dangerous to national security.
A two-year hold on development means “China is going to be so far ahead. We are going to be in so much trouble,” Graham said. She also characterized Andrews’ proposal as putting the federal government, rather than communities, in charge of data center decisions.
Seeming to echo that argument, Whitener said communities don’t need the federal government’s permission to figure out what’s best for them.
Social Security
Congress must do something over the next six years to avoid an automatic drop-off in Social Security benefits, according to the latest update on the Old Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, the formal name of the program providing benefits to retirees, people with disabilities, and — like the Graham siblings — children of deceased parents. More than 70 million Americans receive Social Security benefits, according to the Social Security Administration.
The 2032 timeline happens to coincide with the six-year Senate term of whoever wins in November.
Asked what needs to be done to keep the program solvent, Andrews said the obvious answer is to raise the cap on wages “so that the very wealthiest among us pay more into the system.”
Under the law’s calculations, which are adjusted annually, workers contribute a maximum of $11,439 of their paycheck this year in Social Security taxes, an amount matched by their employer. That’s because the maximum taxable income is $184,500.
Last year, Lindsey Graham took heat for saying people should work longer in order to collect full Social Security benefits, which has been 67 since the Reagan administration.
Andrews said she would never support raising the retirement age.
Calling Social Security’s collapse an imminent threat, Whitener said the best way to solve the problem is by creating a bipartisan study committee to make recommendations, similar to the Base Realignment and Closure process that decided which military bases to close after the Cold War ended. Young people should be allowed to opt out entirely and invest their own money for retirement, she said.
She also disagreed with Andrews’ proposal to raise the wage cap to increase federal collections, saying that’s only “giving more money to the people who can’t be trusted to spend it.”
Darline Graham, who was 13 when she lost both parents, noted she and brother relied on Social Security to live, as does a 91-year-old aunt.
But she didn’t give any proposal for keeping the system solvent.
Asked about it after the debate, campaign spokesman T.W. Arrighi said Graham is open to discussions but wouldn’t vote to impact older Americans. “No one who’s nearing retirement age will ever be impacted by what Sen. Graham decides to do,” he said.
Healthcare
On stage, Graham used her allotted time on the Social Security question to again accuse Andrews of wanting “government-funded healthcare for all,” saying that would only drive up the nation’s debt and further jeopardize Social Security.
Throughout the debate, Andrews refuted that she supports “Medicare for all,” a term used by progressive U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont in his unsuccessful bids for president in advocating for healthcare to be fully run by the federal government. On the campaign trail, Andrews has called that single-payer proposal outdated.
The pediatrician, who’s made healthcare central to her campaign, instead proposes allowing people to buy a government-run health insurance plan, in conjunction with expanding Medicaid eligibility and restoring the enhanced federal subsidies that helped people afford private insurance on the federal Obamacare marketplace. Congress allowed those enhancements, created as part of a pandemic relief package, to expire at the end of last year, making private insurance too expensive for many.
Andrews’ plan is a flip to the Obamacare plans, letting people buy a discounted government plan, rather than giving people taxpayer money to buy ever-increasing private policies. She believes the competition would cause private insurers to lower their rates.
“Over time, there will be a domino effect as more and more Americans are happy with their public option,” Andrews told reporters after the debate.
The Democrat also supports reversing the changes to Medicaid under the “One Big Beautiful Bill” passed by Republicans in Congress last year.
Those changes include a phase-out of the so-called state directed payment program authorized by federal regulators in 2016, which allowed states to use federal taxes to boost Medicaid reimbursement rates to hospitals. Hospitals in South Carolina, where the program’s use since 2023 has hiked payments to hospitals by an average of 70%, stand to lose $150 million annually over 15 years, according to the state hospital association.
Andrews contends that further threatens already struggling rural hospitals. Graham, meanwhile, pointed to the $50 billion over five years the law provided nationwide for rural healthcare. South Carolina received $167 million for the first year of the program.
Graham’s ideas for bringing down healthcare costs include “more transparency in pricing to help create competition.” She also noted co-sponsoring a bill allowing small businesses to buy insurance at cheaper rates given to larger companies.
Whitener said healthcare costs keep increasing because of government regulations and scarcity of doctors and providers. Government regulations and billing complexities have created multiple layers of administrators who far outnumber doctors, she said. “They want to address the costs, but we really have to address is the scarcity problem,” she said.
Names
While answering a question on U.S. policy towards Israel, Graham said Andrews would not stand up to the “socialist Democratic party.”
In response, Andrews reminded viewers she predicted in her opening statement that Graham would call her a socialist.
“But the truth is, my name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that because, unlike my opponent, I haven’t changed my name recently,” she said, adding that she would stand up to members of her party.
Graham has sometimes used the last name of her husband, Larry Nordone. Campaign fliers supporting Lindsey Graham ahead of the June primary referred to her as Darline Graham Nordone, prompting accusations from both the right and left that she switched her name to run for office.
But Graham has consistently said her legal name is Darline Graham.
She said she used Nordone on a social media account so the “volleyball moms would recognize me,” but Graham has always been what she signs on all legal documents.
“Just so that you and everyone else knows,” she said. “It has always been Graham, and — you know why it’s Graham? — because I lost my parents when I was a little girl, and I kept the name Graham so that I felt connected to them.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida lawmakers passed a bill expanding the armed guardian program to colleges — but none have yet
description: No Florida college or university has yet to opt in on a new law that allows staff to act as armed guards, a coalition of gun safety groups assert — leading them to question whether state lawmakers are out of touch on the issue. The Legislature passed HB 757 during the 2026 regular legislative session. It […]
text:
Florida State University students marched to the Capitol on April 23, 2025, less than a week after a gunman opened fire on their campus, calling for legislation on guns and school safety. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)No Florida college or university has yet to opt in on a new law that allows staff to act as armed guards, a coalition of gun safety groups assert — leading them to question whether state lawmakers are out of touch on the issue.
The Legislature passed HB 757 during the 2026 regular legislative session. It includes a controversial provision allowing professors and other people appointed by a university president to carry weapons on campus. They would have to complete 144 hours of training and pass drug tests and psychological evaluations.
The proposal represented an expansion of Florida’s School Guardian Program, created for K-12 schools following the Feb. 2018, shooting massacre at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, in which 17 people were killed.
Angela Ferrell-Zabala, executive director of Moms Demand Action, said students, staff, and families made it clear as the bill was being debated in committee meetings that they didn’t want more guns on university campuses.
“That’s why not one school has opted into this program,” she said. “The people have spoken. Now lawmakers need to listen. This November, voters will remember who catered to the gun lobby and who stood up for the safety of our communities.”
The gun safety groups Everytown for Gun Safety and its Florida Moms Demand Action and Students Demand Action chapters have been tracking whether any schools have opted-in to the program allowing college and university staff to act as armed guards on campus. Their tracking shows not a single college institution has publicly done so.
The Phoenix reached out to representatives of a handful of college campuses around the state last week to learn whether they intended to implement the program. Only a representative from the University of South Florida replied.
“USF is currently reviewing the implementation requirements of the Guardian Program in consultation with the Florida Board of Governors and will determine how best to move forward,” said Althea Johnson, senior director for media relations on the Tampa campus.
Rep. Susan Valdés, a Republican from Hillsborough County, co-sponsored the bill. She says lawmakers approved it because of what happened at FSU last year, where a gunman killed two people and wounded five on the Tallahassee-based campus.
“It brings me comfort to a certain degree that the universities have felt that they haven’t had the need to implement it,” she said. “But if by the same token they feel in the future that they have a need, they have an avenue to be able to implement and to do what they need to do to protect our students.”
Central Florida Democratic U.S. Rep. Maxwell Frost said that, in the aftermath of the FSU shooting, students were calling on lawmakers to do more to keep their campuses safe from gun violence.
“That should be a signal that we need to take a step back and listen to what students, faculty, and campus leaders are saying they actually need to feel safe,” he said in a statement. “Our focus should be on commonsense measures that prevent gun violence before it happens, not putting more guns into classrooms.”
“Florida lawmakers claimed this program was unnecessary, but a month into the school year, not a single institution has chosen to adopt it. That non-participation isn’t an accident. It’s a clear sign that campus leaders recognize bringing more guns into lecture halls and libraries doesn’t make us safer,” said Emily Dornan, a volunteer with FSU Students Demand Action. “We applaud our university administrators for listening to their students and keeping this dangerous program right where it belongs: off our campuses.”
Second Amendment groups dispute the allegation that the Legislature “sold out” to the gun lobby.
“We view HB 757 as a fake campus carry bill. We demanded real campus carry and got an expansion of the Guardian program instead, which is a dog-and-pony show by squishy Republicans,” said Luis Valdes, the Florida State director of Gun Owners of America and Fuerza 2A, a pro-Second Amendment group for Hispanics.
“Why should their Second Amendment rights disappear on college campuses?” he adds. “Gun-free zones do not stop criminals. Law-abiding students, faculty, and staff must be able to defend themselves without waiting for a university’s permission.”
Other provisions in the law include:

Makes it a second-degree felony to fire a weapon within 1,000 feet of a school.
Promotes the use of a mobile suspicious activity reporting tool, like FortifyFL, to quickly alert law enforcement to dangerous circumstances.
Requires a student’s threat assessment reports and psychological evaluations to be transferred from a K-12 school to their college or university upon enrollment.
Mandates schools create family reunification plans, active assailant response plans, and threat-management teams.
Requires schools to annually conduct security risk assessments.
Increases training for faculty and staff to identify and respond to mental health problems.
Further connects students with mental health services.
