Hinds County voters will go to the polls Nov. 3 to select their next district attorney in a quick-turn special election to fill out the term of former District Attorney Jody Owens, who pleaded guilty over the summer to a federal bribery charge stemming from an FBI sting operation to uncover corruption in Mississippi’s capital city. 
Mississippi Today invited candidates to answer questions about their qualifications and priorities. Their responses have been lightly edited for clarity and length. 
The winner of the special election will serve through January 2028 and take over the job from acting District Attorney Brad McCullouch, who was appointed by Gov. Tate Reeves. The new DA will have to continue campaigning to keep the post.
Next year’s race will take place within a new electoral landscape: The boundaries of the 7th Circuit Court District – which currently coincides with Hinds County’s borders – will expand to include neighboring Jefferson and Claiborne counties.
The deadline to register to vote for this election has passed. In-person and mail-in absentee voting is underway. Find your polling place here.


Meet the Candidates



Credit: Photo courtesy Gwen Agho


Gwen Agho
Agho, 37, grew up in Clinton and began working as a prosecutor in the Hinds DA’s office in 2016, rising to become the chief deputy. She recently led the prosecution of Timothy Herrington, a University of Mississippi student who pleaded guilty last year to killing fellow student Jimmie “Jay” Lee.




Credit: Photo courtesy Greta Mack Harris


Greta Mack Harris
Mack Harris, 57, was born and raised in Edwards in rural Hinds County. She has worked as an attorney for 30 years, serving as an assistant public defender in Hinds County, a special assistant attorney general for the state of Mississippi and a prosecutor in Hinds, Madison and Rankin counties. 




Credit: Photo courtesy Darla Palmer


Darla Palmer
Palmer, 59, was born and raised in Jackson. She has worked as a prosecutor for the town of Edwards and in Jackson’s civil service commission and handled delinquent child support cases for the state. Since 2002, Palmer has worked as a private defense attorney and as a public defender in Rankin County. She twice unsuccessfully challenged Owens for Hinds DA.




Credit: Photo courtesy Marvin Sanders


Marvin Sanders
Born in the Mississippi Delta, Sanders, 53, is a veteran of the United States Air Force. He worked in the Hinds DA office in the 2000s under Eleanor Faye Peterson and as an assistant district attorney in Leflore County before moving to the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office. He is now in private practice and a public defender in Sunflower County. 




Credit: Photo courtesy Wendy Wilson White


Wendy Wilson White
Wilson White, 57, grew up in west central Jackson. She joined the Hinds County DA’s office in 2020 as a member of the grand jury team, reviewing and presenting cases for indictment. In 2022, Wilson White unsuccessfully ran for circuit court judge. She then worked as a deputy inspector general at the Mississippi Department of Human Services before returning to the DA’s office, where she now conducts probable cause hearings. 





Our Questions, Their Answers

Qualifications
Campaign Finance
Most Pressing Issue for the Criminal Justice System
Involvement of Crime Victims
Working Relationships Across the Criminal Justice System
District Attorney Office Funds



What makes you uniquely qualified to be the district attorney for Hinds County?
Agho: I am qualified to be district attorney because I know this office from the inside and have spent years fixing what I found broken. When I joined in 2016, the office was in disarray. Case files were paper, there was no system for storing files, victims were not consistently contacted and there was little institutional memory. When an assistant district attorney left, case information could leave with them, causing delays.
I built my own system. I gave victims my cell phone number so I could update them. I tracked my casework in a spreadsheet so the history of each case would not be lost.
In 2020, I was tasked with finding a case management system to solve these problems. After researching companies, I found one, trained assistant DAs and law enforcement to use it, and helped transfer our data. We went live in 2023, modernizing the office and solving the institutional memory problem. I serve as the system’s case manager.
I am a prosecutor who has tried 100 jury trials to verdict, including six murder trials, with an over 90% conviction rate. I will never compromise fairness to resolve a case.
I know where we are failing and how to fix it. I am ready on day one to restore integrity, clear the backlog and put victims first.
Mack Harris: Not only have I worked both sides of the courtroom – giving me the vantage point of every type of case that could come across the DA’s desk – but my experience in this community with the judicial system from both being a practitioner of the courts to being a community member impacted by violent crime.
Palmer: I am the only candidate who has not worked in the dysfunctional Hinds County District Attorney’s Office. I am also the attorney with the most legal trial experience. My concern is violent crime and, beginning day one, I will organize the office to have a primary focus on violent crime.
Sanders: What uniquely qualifies me to serve as Hinds County district attorney is the depth and range of my prosecutorial experience. I have prosecuted felony cases longer than any other candidate in this race and have prosecuted in more than half of Mississippi’s circuit court districts.
Through my work with the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office, I handled public integrity and vulnerable persons cases. I stepped in when district attorneys across the state had conflicts. I prosecuted cases ranging from home repair fraud to murder. Working alongside numerous district attorneys’ offices allowed me to see what works when an office functions effectively and what does not work.
I have also served as a criminal defense attorney and public defender; so, I understand both sides of the courtroom.
Several candidates have described the current Hinds County District Attorney’s Office as dysfunctional. One candidate has even gone as far to say that some of her colleagues within that office are “lazy.” Yet she and two of the other candidates worked within that same administration. I did not. It is like repairing a house. Living inside the house may tell you where it leaks, but repairing many different houses teaches you how to fix it.
Hinds County needs more than someone who knows the office as it has been. It needs someone who knows what a district attorney’s office can be.
Wilson White: I have the most balanced and broad range of experience: 

Prosecutorial experience on the city (chief city prosecutor, city of Jackson); county (assistant Hinds County district attorney); and state (Mississippi Department of Human Services, deputy inspector general) levels 
Work experience inside the DA’s office (grand jury, case review, trials, pleas, law enforcement relationships, and familiarity with the inner workings of the office and all aspects of the criminal justice system)
Management and leadership positions, promotions and work experiences 
Trial and legal experience gained from working in small, mid-size and large law firms 
Civil rights/mental health advocacy experience 
Long-standing relationships with law enforcement
Strong ties to this community 
Banking experience 
Teaching experience 



Campaign finance: Who is supporting your campaign and do you commit to filing accurate campaign finance reports during this election?
Agho: Yes. I commit to filing complete, accurate and timely campaign finance reports throughout this election. After what this county has been through, voters deserve to know exactly who is funding every candidate. My campaign is supported by individual donors across Hinds County, Hinds County business owners, members of the legal community, friends and family members. Every contribution will be reported as the law requires.
Mack Harris: This is truly a grassroots campaign with much of my funding being self-financed and community members standing with me. I commit to timely and accurate reports pursuant to all applicable laws.
Palmer: My campaign is supported by personal funds and donations from friends, family and local businesses.
Sanders: My campaign is being supported by the Committee to Elect Marvin Sanders, which accepts contributions (including in-kind) from family, friends, professional colleagues, community members and Hinds County residents.
Wilson White: I am financially supporting my campaign, and I commit to filing accurate campaign finance reports during this election. At least 95% of the funds spent on my campaign thus far have been from my personal funds. 


It is widely agreed that the criminal justice system in Hinds County is dysfunctional, but there is no consensus as to why. In your view, what is the most pressing issue facing the criminal justice system in Hinds County? Describe what you would do as district attorney to fix the root problem you identified.
Agho: The root problem is disorganization and a lack of accountability for how cases move. Too many cases sit without anyone owning them. Files pass from desk to desk, grand jury presentations stall and people wait in the Raymond jail for months while victims hear nothing. When no one is responsible for a case, no one is responsible for the delay.
I would bring accountability back to case management. Prosecutors should own their cases – from grand jury through sentencing – with assignments based on experience and expertise. The most complex cases should receive experienced review before grand jury presentation, and every homicide should be reviewed by me and at least two experienced prosecutors to ensure the evidence is sufficient.
I would also establish regular meetings with law enforcement leaders to address problems before they cause delays. Grand jury procedures should have clear standards for complete files and experienced review before presentation.
The jail population should be reviewed weekly, prioritizing violent cases while identifying nonviolent cases for diversion, pre-indictment resolution or bond release. Prosecutors should have clear productivity standards, with case-resolution numbers reported publicly.
Finally, I would hire a qualified victims advocate to keep victims informed, explain their rights and help them follow their cases.
Accountability starts at the top. I will hold myself and every prosecutor to the same standard.
Mack Harris: Cases are won or lost long before they reach a courtroom, in how evidence is preserved, how search warrants are executed and whether constitutional standards are met. When prosecutors and law enforcement are not working from the same standards, cases fall apart, victims are denied justice and public trust erodes.
As district attorney, I will rebuild that relationship as a balanced partnership. The DA and law enforcement are partners in the pursuit of justice, but my office will not be a rubber stamp for bad cases. I will reinstate countywide training academies with our local law enforcement agencies in Bolton, Byram, Edwards, Jackson, Raymond and Terry, along with the Hinds County Sheriff. This training will standardize evidence preservation, search warrant execution and constitutional standards, so that cases are built right from the start.
Partnership also requires accountability. Prosecutors and officers both take solemn oaths. When an oath is broken, accountability will be applied equally. As a felony prosecutor, I told a sitting DA on principle that I would not prosecute a case because it lacked the legal merit to proceed. The public and officers alike respect prosecutors who are fair, consistent and legally unassailable. That is the standard I will bring, because justice is only served when every part of the system works in concert.
Palmer: The central problem is the movement of cases in the office and how the office is organized regarding those cases. I would change how cases are being assigned to assistant district attorneys and the manner in which they are assigned to each judge’s courtroom. I would have a person monitoring cases being sent over from the lower courts and set deadlines for completion or submission to a grand jury if that’s the desired result. Some cases need to be dismissed.
Sanders: The most pressing issue facing Hinds County’s criminal justice system is the time it takes to move a case from arrest to prosecution. Justice is not served when cases sit for two years or more without indictment or when individuals are indicted but their cases are not promptly placed on the court docket.
Fixing this requires accountability at every stage. First, the District Attorney’s Office must work closely with law enforcement so officers understand what evidence and documentation prosecutors need to build a case that can actually be tried. Second, prosecutors must thoroughly review cases at the preliminary hearing stage to determine whether sufficient evidence exists to move forward. Once a case is bound over, it should be promptly reviewed and, when appropriate, presented to the grand jury. After indictment, defendants should be arraigned and cases placed on the criminal docket without unnecessary delay.
I would assign prosecutors responsibility for their caseloads from review through resolution and regularly identify cases that have stalled.
Moving cases faster does not mean sacrificing quality. It means preparing cases correctly from the beginning and creating accountability so cases do not simply sit. Justice delayed affects defendants, victims, law enforcement and the entire community.
Wilson White: In my opinion, the most pressing issue facing the criminal justice system in Hinds County is the volume of crime, specifically the violent crime we are seeing and experiencing.
While I will devote myself to addressing existing crime, I will also make crime prevention a priority. What we’re seeing is disturbing on so many levels.
I want to bridge the gaps between the community, law enforcement, schools, churches and faith organizations. I want there to be an exchange of information and healthy dialogue. I don’t want more words; I want action and active involvement. I believe it will take a unified effort. Hence, my platform, “Together We Can.”
It appears as though criminals are gaining momentum. While the number of criminals appears to be increasing and the courts have grown by one, there have been no real increases in law enforcement, prosecutors, public defenders or many of the others we all rely on to render justice. The “why”’ has to be addressed and I plan to make that one of my top priorities.
I believe education has a role to play. I want to see more done to educate our children about crime so that they can better identify it and avoid it. Our adults need to hear the crime we are living through, and witnessing is not normal and should not be accepted as such. I need everyone to understand they have a voice and begin how to use their voices more to stand against crime.
Criminals truly thrive and multiply when they are allowed to hide and avoid accountability and I believe that is what we are seeing.
I also want to see swift justice. I will look closely at how long it takes a case to work through the criminal justice system. There are obvious delays that need to be addressed. Swift accountability will impact crime in a positive way. 


How would you foster working relationships across the justice system? Please comment on the current relationship between the district attorney’s office, the Jackson Police Department, the Hinds County Sheriff’s Office, local judges and defense attorneys. How should these relationships look?
Agho: Right now, these relationships are strained. Law enforcement and prosecutors too often blame each other for delays, cases reach the grand jury without complete files and judges are left managing a backlog no one owns. Public trust in the office has been damaged, and that damage affects every partner.
I would start with regular, standing meetings with JPD, the Sheriff’s Office and other agencies to screen cases early, agree on what a complete file looks like, and fix problems before they become delays. I would assign prosecutors as points of contact for each agency so officers know who to call.
With judges, I will bring experienced prosecutors to court and be honest about our caseload. With defense attorneys, I will insist on timely discovery and professional, respectful dealings. A fair process is a faster process.
These relationships should be built on shared goals: safer neighborhoods, cases that move and a system people can trust.
Mack Harris: The current relationship with the interim district attorney and law enforcement seems to indicate more efforts are being made to collaborate. The relationship should look like entities seeking to work in the best interests of and for the common good of the citizens who are being served.
From start to finish, that takes intentional partnership, mutual understanding and respect for processes. We can and will achieve this in a Greta Mack Harris administration through the reinstatement of a case review panel system that sought to bring together the necessary agencies to make sure Hinds County citizens are getting the best service from the judicial system.
Palmer: I have personally spoken with law enforcement throughout Jackson and the rest of the county. The relationship between the DA’s office and the parties aforementioned is clearly fragmented. I would personally reach out to foster better relationships and insist that all persons in the office work to ensure that these relationships are mended.
Sanders: I have prosecuted cases for two decades and have been a criminal defense attorney for almost a decade. I do not currently work in the Hinds County District Attorney’s Office, so I cannot fairly comment on the relationships, whether positive or negative, between the District Attorney’s Office and other players in the criminal justice system. I have worked alongside other district attorney’s offices, so I know what the relationship can be.
As the next Hinds County district attorney, I will conduct training with law enforcement, participate in meetings with leadership within each law enforcement agency to include Capitol Police, Hinds County Sheriff’s Department and each municipal law enforcement agency within Hinds County.
Prosecutors need to be able to work with defense attorneys to make sure cases can be properly moved through the courts. Prosecutors must work with judges to make sure cases are moved efficiently off of each judges’ docket.
Finally, as your next Hinds County district attorney, I will work with leadership within the Hinds County municipalities about the procedures within my office which align with access to law enforcement so that we can have effective training.
Wilson White: I do not know that I can truly speak to the current relationship between the district attorney’s office, the Jackson Police Department, the Hinds County Sheriff’s Office, local judges and defense attorneys.
I can say I have been prosecuting crime here in Jackson and Hinds County for 12 years. During those 12 years, I have served Jackson as its chief city prosecutor, Hinds County as an assistant district attorney and Mississippi as the Department of Human Services’ deputy inspector general.
I have worked hard to form and maintain strong relationships with all of the law enforcement agencies, district attorneys, judges and defense attorneys I have had an opportunity to work with. I build my relationships on mutual respect, trust and honesty.
In order to foster working relationships throughout the justice system, I will listen and encourage everyone else to listen as well. I am sure we all hold good ideas as it relates to issues within the justice system and how to address them. Here again, “Together We Can.”


Crime victims and their families frequently feel excluded from the criminal justice process. What role should crime victims play in prosecution?
Agho: Victims should be informed, heard and respected at every stage. They do not direct a prosecution, but they deserve to understand it and to have their voices count.
When I joined this office, no one was tracking whether prosecutors stayed in contact with victims. I built my own system to make sure I did, and it made a real difference for the families I served. As district attorney, I will make that the standard for every prosecutor.
That means a working victim advocate program, which the office does not have today. It means contacting victims before key decisions such as plea offers, keeping them updated as the case moves and preparing them for court. It means making sure they know their rights under Mississippi law, including the right to be heard at sentencing. Victims should never learn about their own case from the news. Every victim deserves to know where their case stands.
Mack Harris: Crime victims should be actively involved from the inception of a case. As a family member of multiple victims of violent crimes, I know first hand that the system is geared more toward the criminal defendant than victims. If and when elected, we will mobilize the victim assistance coordinator to partner with law enforcement to secure testimony logistics and emergency relocation where necessary, maintaining continuous victim-family communication.
Palmer: Crime victims may be in a position to advance the prosecution against a defendant. They play a crucial role. However, the office must be mindful also that certain developments in the case should remain confidential. Victims should be updated to some degree, however.
Sanders: Crime victims should be consulted prior to any resolution outside of a jury trial, especially violent crimes. They should be properly informed of court dates and proceedings and have access to the prosecutors if they have questions about the status of the criminal case. This is the purpose of and the responsibility of the victim coordinator. As your next Hinds County district attorney, I will make sure that the victim coordinator understands this responsibility and is given the proper training to execute this job.  
Wilson White: I think it is a good practice to regularly communicate with victims and keep them abreast of where their cases are in the court system. Victims should have a voice and be heard. They should also be informed and allowed to express their thoughts, feelings and expectations. Justice varies and I believe it is person specific. What looks like justice to one person, won’t look like justice to another. I want to know what justice looks like to our victims so that the DA’s office, in line with the law, can pursue the justice they need.
I often ask, where do broken people go? How do they survive as victims? Victims deserve to be made whole and a part of that is giving them the justice they need and deserve. I want the DA’s office to be the victims’ safe place – a place where they feel respected, seen, heard and valued. The best way to secure those feelings is to be open and honest.


The district attorney’s office generates enormous sums of money through pre-trial intervention programs, but the public doesn’t know how the DA spends these funds. Describe the characteristics of a transparent DA’s office.
Agho: A transparent DA’s office treats every dollar as the public’s money, because it is.
First, all pretrial intervention fees and other self-generated funds should be deposited in accounts subject to regular independent audits, with the results published. Second, the office should publish regular reports showing how much money comes in, where it goes and who approved the spending. Third, clear written policies should govern how those funds can be used, with no discretionary spending outside those rules. Fourth, the office should cooperate fully with the state auditor and the Board of Supervisors.
Transparency also applies to performance. The public should be able to see how many cases the office handles, how long they take, the size of the backlog and how victims are being served.
This county has seen what happens when no one is watching. Under my leadership, everyone will be able to see how this office works.
Mack Harris: A Greta Mack Harris district attorney’s office will be one that is transparent with how pretrial funds are managed. It’s one that includes checks and balances that would require that the person who collects the money isn’t the same person as the one who determines where it will be spent. Checks and balances on allocation of funds coupled with routine audits will ensure that the DA’s office is not only honest in its reporting, but efficient.  After each fiscal year, I will publish a financial statement breakdown of the money collected and spent.
Palmer: A transparent DA’s office will provide the budgets as required by the Board of Supervisors as well as what state statutes require.
Sanders: As your next Hinds County district attorney, if there is a question, we will make ourselves open to review by the state auditor. As deputy director of the public integrity division for the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office, I prosecuted numerous cases where there was a significant lack of transparency. So, I know what you can and cannot do with public funds.
Wilson White: The DA’s office under my leadership will not hide or shield the amount of funds it receives or how such funds are expended. The DA’s office under my leadership will have a legitimate system of checks and balances to ensure proper receipts, spending and documentation. The DA’s office belongs to the people, not the DA. I am confident my business education and business work experience will be an asset to the DA’s office in this regard.

title: Michigan needs more behavioral health professionals.
description: There is a particular kind of frustration that comes with needing mental health care: finally deciding to ask for help, making the call, and then being told the next available appointment is weeks or months away. text:
Getty ImagesThere is a particular kind of frustration that comes with needing mental health care: finally deciding to ask for help, making the call, and then being told the next available appointment is weeks or months away.
For many Michigan residents, that is already a reality. Our state needs more behavioral health professionals, and the people experiencing that shortage don’t care whether the reason is a workforce statistic, an education policy, or a federal regulation. They simply need someone available to help.
Michigan knows it has a workforce problem. The state is putting real resources toward solving it, including investments in social work education and training. But at the same time, federal policymakers are changing the way graduate programs are financed and evaluated, making it harder to enter the field.
One of the newest changes deserves particular attention because it could affect not only how students pay for graduate education, but whether some programs can continue participating in the federal student loan system at all. The federal government’s new earnings-accountability system is intended to identify programs whose graduates do not earn enough to meet a specified earnings benchmark and prevent them from taking out federal student loans.
The goal is understandable: students should have meaningful information about the financial outcomes associated with their education, and they should not be encouraged to take on debt that is unlikely to be manageable. But good intentions do not eliminate the need to ask whether we are measuring the right thing.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
For graduate programs, the earnings benchmark is based on workers with a bachelor’s degree. That means the earnings of workers whose education stopped at the bachelor’s level are being used as a benchmark when evaluating programs that prepare students at the master’s level.
Consider social work. A bachelor’s degree in social work and a master’s degree in social work are not interchangeable. They represent different levels of education and professional preparation, and they can lead to different roles, licensing opportunities, and wages. A graduate social worker may go into clinical practice, administration, research, teaching, policy, or other specialized work.
So what does it tell us about the value of a master’s degree if we compare its graduates against people who did not pursue that degree?
That question matters because the consequences of the earnings measure are significant. A graduate program that fails the measure in two out of three years can lose access to federal Direct Loans for at least two years. This is not simply a question of whether a student can borrow more or less. It can become a question of whether students can use federal loans to attend the program at all.
And social work is not a profession that exists on the margins of Michigan’s healthcare system. It is a core part of the behavioral health workforce that communities rely on every day. This is also happening alongside another federal change affecting graduate education. Social work is not included among the programs currently classified as professional degrees eligible for higher federal loan limits.
That classification deserves scrutiny. The U.S. Department of Education describes professional degrees as programs that prepare students to enter a profession, require skills beyond those normally expected from a bachelor’s degree, and generally require professional licensure. Social work meets those core characteristics. The Department received extensive comments making that case and ultimately chose not to include MSW and DSW programs in the professional-degree classification.
The result is a policy landscape in which students pursuing the education needed to become social workers face lower federal borrowing limits, while the programs educating them may also face a new federal earnings test that could ultimately affect their access to federal loans. That should matter to Michigan.
At LifeWays, we envision “a fully integrated healthcare network that supports individuals in our community to reach their full potential.” Reaching that vision requires more than expanding services on paper. It requires having qualified professionals available to provide those services.
Michigan is already investing in the behavioral health workforce because we know we need more of those professionals. There are an estimated 530 annual openings for mental health and substance use social workers alone.
We should absolutely continue asking whether students are receiving a good return on the education they finance with federal loans. But we should also ask whether the measures we use to answer that question accurately reflect the value of graduate education—and whether they account for the workforce consequences of getting that answer wrong.
Because when a policy makes it harder for a student to become a social worker, the impact does not necessarily end with that student. It can eventually reach the person sitting in a waiting room, hoping someone will call their name.

text:
Carrie Buck's campaign posted National Republican Congressional Committee photos on social media of herself (right) and House Speaker Mike Johnson at Pinecrest Academy Sloan Canyon charter school in Henderson on Aug. 25, 2026. Congressional candidate and state Sen. Carrie Buck violated federal tax regulations when she campaigned at a Henderson charter school in August with Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, says a parent who alleges the school was used for partisan political activity, a violation of its nonprofit status.
Pinecrest Academy Sloan Canyon, the school Buck and Johnson visited, like all charter schools in the state, is designated a 501(c)(3) nonprofit under the tax code. As such, it is “absolutely prohibited” from engaging in political activity, according to the IRS. The prohibition is also stated in the school’s by-laws. 
“While I question the very legality of this event, I also question Pinecrest’s judgment in having a blatant partisan visit at an elementary/high school, within the very classrooms of our students, without any choice for students or parents to participate,” Adelei Kaplan wrote in a complaint filed with the State Public Charter School Authority. 
Buck, a Republican who is challenging Democrat Rep. Dina Titus in Nevada’s Congressional District 1, previously served as principal and executive director of the school. 
Her campaign did not respond to numerous requests for comment. 
While at the school, Johnson spoke of why he supports low taxes and small government, and hailed President Donald Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill, which he said cut taxes, according to media reports. He exalted Buck and her “extraordinary track record” as a principal and education reformer. 
“That sounds like campaigning to me,” Kaplan wrote in her complaint to the state.  
Pinecrest officials maintain Buck and Johnson, who were accompanied by a camera crew from the National Republican Congressional Committee, were not campaigning. 
“I don’t believe our student’s (sic) are ideal audiences for campaigns seeing the majority are not of voting age,” Coby Sherlock, who serves as Pinecrest’s treasurer, said via email. 
According to news reports, however, Buck and Johnson visited with high school seniors who will soon be old enough to vote, if they are not already. 
“The fact that the photo was taken by the NRCC (the political arm of House Republicans) is evidence that this was a political event,” Kaplan wrote to the Charter School Authority. She noted she had spoken to “fellow Pinecrest parents. Sadly, most of them are too afraid to formally speak up in the current political environment…”  
Kaplan, whose children attend Pinecrest’s adjacent sister campus, asked the agency to investigate. In a response this week, the state asked Kaplan if she had reached out to the school’s board of directors. She subsequently filed another complaint with that board. 
“The parents should have the right to expect that if they’re sending their child to school or church, you shouldn’t have somebody telling you how to vote,:” attorney Bradley Schrager, who specializes in nonprofit law, told the Current. “It’s Trump’s IRS. In this country right now, nobody’s going to do a damn thing about it. They should, but they won’t.” 
Charter schools are publicly funded but are not subject to local school district regulations, which in Clark County, prohibit campaigning, except for organized events in which all candidates are represented. 
Sherlock, Pinecrest’s treasurer, says parents of affected students were notified and given the opportunity to opt out. 
However, a student who posted a video on social media noting “most Sloan Canyon Students aren’t MAGA,” told the Current that parents were not notified until after the event. 
After visiting classrooms, Buck and Johnson “held a media availability focused on Trump’s new Education Freedom Tax Credit and Buck’s three-decade career in Nevada education,” the Nevada Globe reported.
The school “regularly welcomes elected officials from both parties to campus because we want our students to see firsthand how our government works, not just read about it in a textbook,” Sherlock told the Current.
He declined to provide the names of other elected officials who have visited the campus. 
Titus, Buck’s opponent, did not respond to a request for comment.

title: A pair of prosecutors vie for new seat on Henderson Justice Court
description: Henderson assistant city attorney Michael Allmon and Clark County prosecutor John Cory are competing for a newly created seat on Henderson Justice Court. text:
Michael Allmon, John Cory. (Candidate photos)Henderson assistant city attorney Michael Allmon and Clark County prosecutor John Cory are competing for a newly created seat on Henderson Justice Court.
Henderson Justice of the Peace Department 4 was created to meet the court’s growing caseload. Allmon and Cory — both first time candidates — advanced to the Nov. 3 general election after defeating two other candidates in the June primary. 
Henderson Justice Court justices serve six-year terms and handle criminal and civil cases, including preliminary hearings, traffic cases, protective orders, evictions, misdemeanors and small claims within the Henderson Township jurisdiction. 
A career prosecutor, Allmon served as a major in the Marines before earning his law degree at the Sandra Day O’Connor College of Law at Arizona State University.
As a Clark County Deputy District Attorney, Allmon prosecutes cases for the Special Victims Unit. He says he’s running for the bench because “we need judicial officers who are actually focused on public safety.”
Allmon is endorsed by District Attorney Steve Wolfson, the Henderson Police Supervisors Association, the Las Vegas Police Protective Association, Henderson Police Officers Association, SEIU Local 1107, and the Southern Nevada Building Trades Union. 
Allmon, who says he has a 100% conviction rate during his seven-year career, has completed three trials in the last year. 
If elected, Allmon says he won’t be prone to prosecutorial bias
“As a prosecutor, your client is the community, and so you’re always evaluating to see what’s right for the community,” he said during a phone interview. “Part of the job is looking at cases and determining whether or not it’s a meritorious prosecution. You’re always balancing all these competing needs.” 
Henderson Justice Court currently lacks specialty courts such as drug and veterans court, where offenders are channeled into programs designed to address their individual needs and keep them out of the criminal justice system. 
“I don’t know if the answer is necessarily building that in Henderson Justice Court specifically, or if it’s continuing to work with the other jurisdictions and doing that. I think it’s a matter of scale,” he said of efforts to bring specialty courts to Henderson. 
As of July, Allmon reported raising $34,000 and has roughly $10,300 on hand. Allmon took out roughly $9,000 in loans to fund his campaign, according to financial statements. 
“It would be nice if judicial candidates didn’t have to raise money,” he said, adding he favors appointments over elections. 
Judicial contributions from attorneys who appear before the court “can’t be ignored. You can’t pretend it didn’t happen.” At the same time, he says, “there’s no way to make it an issue in court. You can’t stand up and say, ‘Judge, you’re ruling for this person because they gave you a huge campaign contribution.’ I’m a lawyer who has been on the other side from lawyers who have paid heavily into campaigns, and I’ve known it.” 
Allmon says his goal as a judge would be “to make sure that the process is fair and everyone comes out feeling they got a fair shake. Maybe not everyone is happy but they understand how we got to that decision.”  
Cory, who is also a prosecutor, says his combination of civil and criminal experience gives him the qualifications to serve on the Dept. 4 bench.
“Over the course of my career, I’ve worked really hard and succeeded at building good relationships with opposing counsel,” he said during an interview. “I think Henderson voters can feel confident that if I should win, as a judge I will bring the same reasonable, level headed, calm, thoughtful decision making” to the bench. He says he’s completed five trials in the last year. 
Cory was born and raised in Southern Nevada and earned his law degree from Boyd Law School. 
As of July, Cory raised more than $62,000 and had about $3,800 on hand. 
His website lists endorsements from more than 100 local attorneys. He’s also endorsed by the Third Branch PAC, an organization that bills itself as nonpartisan but is funded solely by the Nevada Republican Club.   
Cory says he can “be tough on crime but always protect constitutional rights and make sure everybody gets treated fairly and respectfully.” 
Cory says he’s not a “pushover” and is seen by other attorneys as “reasonable, because I will listen to them. I will show them respect, and when they come to me with issues, when they want me to consider things in a case, I’ll absolutely give them my time and attention.”
The candidate says he finds “high value in the specialty courts, and that’s definitely something I’m interested in bringing about in Henderson Justice Court. I think a mental health court would be very important for the City of Henderson to have better access to some mental health services.” 
“When I used to work in the Las Vegas City Attorney’s Office, we had a specialty court called Women in Need,” he says. “We also had one for youth offenders.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Will the US Supreme Court’s recent ruling affect CT absentee voting?
description: Mail-in ballots, or absentee ballots, began going out Oct. 2 in CT for the general election on Nov. 3. Here's what CT voters should know.
text:
In a ruling last month, the U.S Supreme Court ended President Donald Trump’s attempt to restrict mail-in ballots.
Mail-in ballots, or absentee ballots, began going out Oct. 2 in Connecticut for the general election on Nov. 3. In the past, voters in the state could only vote by absentee for specific reasons — like having an illness or being out of town on Election Day. But beginning this year, absentee ballots are available to anyone who requests one.
So what would Trump’s executive order have meant for elections in Connecticut and what does the court’s decision change, if anything? And how is absentee voting different from “early” voting?
Here’s what Connecticut voters should know.
What would Trump’s executive order have done?
The executive order — issued in March — ordered the creation of a “state citizenship list” using citizenship, naturalization and Social Security records. That list would have been sent to each state’s election officials. 
It would also have given the U.S. Postal Service a larger role in elections. The agency proposed a requirement for states to submit a mail-in and absentee participation list of all people who were intending to vote by mail, which would have given the Postal Service the ability to block mail-in ballots from states that didn’t send the list.
The president said he was trying to crack down on noncitizen voting, which is already prohibited by federal law and rare.
What does the Supreme Court’s ruling mean for Connecticut?
In a concurring opinion, Justice Brett Kavanaugh stated that even if the Postal Service has the authority to implement the change, “applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”
The court’s decision allows states to continue sending out mail-in ballots using the same process they’ve been using.
“We feel a lot more confident the elections will go more normally in Connecticut now,” David McGuire, executive director of ACLU CT, said. “We do think people should take advantage of the early voting window as well.”
What’s the difference between early voting and absentee voting?
While absentee voting allows people to vote early by mail, the term “early voting” in Connecticut actually refers to the process of voting in person ahead of Election Day. 
Early voting opens in Connecticut on Monday, Oct. 19 and will run through Sunday, Nov. 1. Voters can look up their town’s early voting location here. Note that it may be different from Election Day polls. Early voting locations will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., except on Tuesday, Oct. 27 and Thursday, Oct. 29 when they will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.
If a person prefers to vote on Election Day, which is Nov. 3 for this year’s midterm elections, the polls in all towns will be open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. on that day. Voters can look up their poll location on the secretary of the state’s website.
How can someone vote by absentee?
To get a ballot, voters can fill out an application on the Connecticut Online Absentee Ballot Request Portal.
The local town clerk’s office automatically will get the application, check that the person is an eligible voter and enter their information into the Central Voter Registration System, which is used to ensure no one can vote twice. A unique ballot identification number is created for each ballot to ensure only the voter who requested it can vote with that ballot.
The voter will receive the ballot by mail and can return it by mail or in person to the town clerk’s office. They can also put it in a drop box in their town. But for an absentee vote to count, a ballot must arrive before polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day.
The last day to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2. 
McGuire noted that if a voter requests a mail-in ballot and decides not to cast it, that person can still go to the polls in person, noting the state’s cross-checking system. “The earlier people can figure out their plan the better,” McGuire said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Judge: Lawsuit against ABC liquor warehouse operator can proceed
description: Levure Bottle Shop in Jackson has empty shelves due to problems at the state's alcohol distribution warehouse on Tuesday, Feb. 17, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A federal judge has rejected a request from the operator of Mississippi’s Alcoholic Beverage Control warehouse to dismiss a lawsuit brought against it on behalf of Mississippi businesses.
Uno Mas, an Oxford restaurant, filed a class action lawsuit against Iowa-based Ruan Transport Corporation over the debacle at the ABC warehouse earlier this year when a software change led to long delivery delays and liquor shortages at Mississippi restaurants, casinos, bars and stores. The restaurant said the delays resulted in lost revenue and harmed businesses, and that Ruan kept fees for deliveries it failed to make.
The ABC warehouse is the single wholesale distributor of almost all alcoholic beverages in the state. With the exception of beer and light beverages, all alcohol in Mississippi package stores and restaurants goes through the warehouse in Gluckstadt. While ABC is run by the Mississippi Department of Revenue, the state contracts operation of the warehouse with Ruan, which has been operating it since 2023. 
When Ruan asked the judge to dismiss the case it argued that its contract was with the Department of Revenue, not Uno Mas and other businesses that receive products from the warehouse. 
However, Ruan’s contract with DOR requires the company to “guarantee next workday delivery” to businesses buying alcohol. The judge found that even though Uno Mas did not sign the contract, it was intended to benefit from the contract and can sue Ruan over a potential breach. 
The outsourcing of ABC operations resulted from 2022 legislation to address longstanding problems with the state running the warehouse.  The “alcohol crisis” early in 2026 renewed calls by some lawmakers to privatize the operations.
In court documents, the judge noted that “interestingly, it appears the Legislature did anticipate an inefficient company might poorly operate ABC’s warehouse, resulting in a lawsuit.” The state specified in the law that any lawsuits brought over warehouse operations would be brought against the operator, not the state.
The ABC warehouse operations not only impact Mississippi businesses, but also state revenue. The ABC division collected $108 million last year, about 1.5% of the state’s total annual tax revenue.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Healthcare attacks at center of campaign for 7th District House seat
description: Candidates in the race for New Jersey’s 7th District House seat agree healthcare is broken, but disagree on a solution.
text:
Rebecca Bennett (D) and Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) are competing in the closely watched House race in New Jersey’s 7th District. (Photos by Anne-Marie Caruso/Hal Brown)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]The two candidates leading the race to represent New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District agree healthcare must be more affordable and accessible, but they have very different ideas on how to improve the system, especially when it comes to publicly subsidized care.
On the campaign trail, both Rep. Tom Kean Jr (R) and his Democratic challenger, Rebecca Bennett, highlight the ongoing changes to Medicaid, the state- and federal-funded health insurance system that now covers some 1.8 million New Jersey residents and is facing massive cutbacks under President Donald Trump.
Bennett, a first-time candidate and health technology executive, joined a nationwide bus tour calling attention to these cuts Friday in Westfield. The changes could force more than 350,000 people out of NJ Family Care, New Jersey’s Medicaid program, and eventually cost the state more than $3 billion annually in federal hospital funding.
The event was hosted by Sick of It!, a campaign by the nonprofit advocacy group Protect Our Care and focused on the Medicaid cuts and other changes resulting from legislation Trump signed in July 2025 known as the One Big Beautiful Bill.
“Tom Kean Jr. was the deciding vote on the One Big Beautiful Bill, which is why tens of thousands of people in our district are losing access to their health insurance. It’s why all the rest of us are seeing our premiums go up. So No. 1, we’re going to undo those cuts that were in the legislation,” Bennett said Friday.
Healthcare costs remain a concern for a majority of New Jerseyans, according to a recent Rutgers Eagleton Institute of Politics poll. Bennett said it’s one of the biggest worries on voters’ minds and she’s called for creating health insurance options that aren’t tied to people’s jobs.
“I hear these stories day in and day out. I think it’s important that we recognize our healthcare system is not working. It’s broken and we have to fix it,” Bennett said in Westfield.
Kean, who is seeking a third term, has defended his vote to support the changes to Medicaid as necessary to protect the future of public subsidy programs for poor, elderly, and disabled people. He blames insurance companies for denying care to those who deserve treatment.
“Congressman Kean successfully protected Medicare and Medicaid for every single one of its intended beneficiaries in New Jersey. Every New Jersey senior, child, and disabled person can now get every kind of care they need. Under the plan passed last year, Medicare will grow by $1.134 trillion and Medicaid by $273 billion over the next decade,” Kean campaign spokesman Harrison Neely told the New Jersey Monitor.
Neely declined to answer additional questions about the impact of the cuts.
Trump and his allies have noted that Medicaid spending is projected to grow even with the cuts in the bill Trump signed in July 2025. A Congressional Budget Office analysis of the bill’s effects said that projected growth is slower than what was projected before the bill was signed.
The 7th District race has drawn national attention as Republicans worry about their ability to continue to control Congress when its new term begins in January. The seat was in the GOP’s hands for decades until Tom Malinowski won it for Democrats in 2018. Kean flipped it back for Republicans in 2022.
In debates and TV ads, Kean and Republican allies have tried to paint Bennett as a wealthy executive exacerbating healthcare’s problems, alleging she prioritized profits over patients in her work with Midi Health, which connects women with care for menopause-related symptoms using telemedicine. At Midi, Bennett launched a partnership with Lifepoint Health, a hospital system that has been flagged for poor quality control and denial of care.
“Liberal Rebecca Bennett brags about partnering with the same company putting profits over patients,” says one TV ad from Kean’s campaign.
Bennett frames her work with Midi and Oshi Health, which seeks to link patients with gastrointestinal care, as her way of helping people, a focus on service she connects to her 15 years as a Navy helicopter pilot. Women’s health is also a passion for her, Bennett said Friday.
Carly Jones, a spokesperson for the Democrat, said Bennett is the only candidate focused on lowering healthcare costs.
“In Congress, she’ll reverse healthcare cuts and take on pharmaceutical companies that are jacking up the price of lifesaving medicine for New Jerseyans,” Jones said.
Micah Rasmussen, director of Rider University’s Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics, said it’s hard for voters to form an opinion about Bennett’s work with Midi based on the GOP attacks, but “she had a pretty good answer” to those charges in framing it as work to help people navigate a broken system.
While Medicaid cuts have been paramount in the campaign, the biggest changes don’t take effect for several more years.
“We know that some of those impacts were end-loaded not to take effect until after the election, so that people aren’t feeling it as they go to the polls this year,” Rasmussen said.
The biggest issue in the 7th District may not be either Kean or Bennett, but Trump, Rasmussen said.
“In a nationalized midterm environment where voters are really thinking along the lines of either two more years of Trump or checking and balancing Trump, the main motivating factor of most voters is either to give him more runway, or to take the runway away from him,” he said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: In a time of distrust, how do we know Utah’s elections are secure? Clerks show us
description: Editor’s note: This story is part of We Vote Utah, a partnership between KUER, PBS Utah and Utah News Dispatch to cover Utah’s 2026 elections. Ballots will start hitting Utahns’ mailboxes this week ahead of the contentious midterm elections, marking another year when a national spotlight has been cast on voting by mail — largely […]
text:
Davis County Clerk Brian McKenzie poses for a photo in a ballot processing center at the Davis County Administrative Building in Farmington on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Editor’s note: This story is part of We Vote Utah, a partnership between KUER, PBS Utah and Utah News Dispatch to cover Utah’s 2026 elections.
Ballots will start hitting Utahns’ mailboxes this week ahead of the contentious midterm elections, marking another year when a national spotlight has been cast on voting by mail — largely due to President Donald Trump’s ongoing rhetoric of widespread fraud without evidence. 
Utah clerks on both sides of the political aisle, frustrated by national discourse that’s not based in fact but has cast a shadow over voting by mail, are pushing back.
“The general rhetoric, I’m very tired of it because it continues,” Grand County Clerk/Auditor Gabe Woytek, who is unaffiliated, told KUER in an interview for the station’s State Street episode that aired Monday. “There continues to persist a rhetoric that threatens the idea that it’s safe and secure, when I know in practice that it is a very safe and secure system … and we continue to add in those safeguards. Yet the conspiracy and the discontent continues to persist.”

In Utah, voting by mail has a long history. Since 2018, when nearly all of Utah’s counties started running elections primarily by mail while also allowing in-person voting options, the system has been lauded by state leaders, Republicans and Democrats alike. But in recent years, as Trump has continued raising doubts about its security, Utah’s GOP-controlled Legislature has reacted. 
Lawmakers have enacted more ID requirements and slowly pulled back on universal, automatic voting by mail by requiring voters to opt in to continue receiving their ballots in the mail by 2029. 
Meanwhile, the federal debate rages on. 
Although Utah’s own top election official, Republican Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, has been ardently opposed to it, the state’s senior GOP Sen. Mike Lee continues to push the SAVE Act that would demand voters prove their citizenship in order to cast a ballot. And Trump, through an executive order, has tried to change how the U.S. Postal Services processes by-mail ballots. That rule would require states to send voter information to the federal government while also banning the Postal Service from delivering or collecting mail-in ballots from people who haven’t been confirmed as eligible voters. 
Had Trump’s Postal Service executive order not been blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court for this year’s election, Henderson, a Republican, has said it would have been an “unmitigated disaster,” since it would have been logistically impossible for clerks to adhere to it with such a short timeframe before the Nov. 3 election.
To highlight allegations of voter fraud and to make the case for Trump’s Postal Service rule, the Trump administration last month spotlighted federal charges against a former Utah letter carrier accused of throwing 300 primary ballots into a dumpster before they could be delivered to Eagle Mountain voters’ mailboxes. 
Utah’s top election chief says Trump admin’s ‘gamesmanship’ with voting keeps her up at night

In an interview with law enforcement, the ex-letter carrier indicated he did not have a political motive but said he threw away the mail, which also included advertisements, “because he wanted to ‘lighten his workload’ so he could presumably go home earlier,” prosecutors said in charging documents. 
The tossed ballots are unusual. Even so, 300 ballots make up a fraction of Utah’s more than 2 million registered voters, and the charges don’t indicate a concerted fraud effort. And multiple recent state audits, while they’ve found some areas of improvement, have concluded that Utah’s election system contains “no significant fraud.” 
All of this political debate over voting by mail has cast doubt and confusion over a longstanding voting system that Utah clerks of all political stripes — Republican, Democrat and unaffiliated — defend. 
‘When people have doubt, they disengage’
Davis County Clerk Brian McKenzie, a Republican, said in an interview with KUER one of his “biggest concerns” is that the rhetoric doesn’t match reality. 
“Even if our elections are run very well and are very efficient and are very accurate, we do have some criticism out there, recognizing that the system is not perfect; it never will be perfect,” he said. “But sometimes people take those small issues and amplify those and add to them when it’s not justified.”
McKenzie noted change is not a foreign concept to elections — in fact, in his more than two decades working in various election roles, he said the process has evolved “significantly.” But he gets concerned when big changes are proposed under a tight timeframe.
National scrutiny on mail ballots changed Utah’s elections system

“That creates disruption, that creates question, and when you have questions like that, that creates doubt. When people have doubt, they disengage,” McKenzie said. “That is a concern for me as an administrator. It’s a concern for me as a fellow voter as well.” 
From Wasatch County, Woytek shared a similar concern.
“Added rules, added regulations, more confusion for the voters, I can handle it,” he said. “You know, it’s my duty to follow the law, and I will do so, and I won’t complain about it. But what I will complain about is it causing discontent and confusion among voters, which either causes them to not participate at all, or develop their own uncertainty regarding the system that they wouldn’t have had otherwise.”
Henderson, another Republican and Utah’s top election official, has been a fierce defender of Utah’s vote-by-mail system, and she’s called out the Trump administration’s political “gamesmanship” with voting, which she said in a recent interview keeps her up at night. 
“I learned a long time ago that (the Trump administration doesn’t) want to know that we’re doing things OK,” Henderson said. “They don’t want to know that things are going well, because it goes against a narrative that is being pounded relentlessly of mass fraud or ineligible people voting. And the facts just don’t support that narrative.”
Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman, a Democrat, said Henderson’s willingness to speak out is “reassuring” in an interview with States Newsrooms’ CEO Chris Fitzsimon for a “Stories from the States” podcast episode that aired Friday. 


“It’s not just me. It’s not just me waking up in a panic at 3 a.m. The Republicans are too,” Chapman said. “This isn’t a partisan issue. This is (an) access issue. This is ensuring that voters who are eligible to participate in elections understand the methods that they can do so and make a plan ahead of time, as opposed to the chaos and confusion, frankly, that we’ve been inundated with over the last couple months.”
Chapman said since 2020, Utah lawmakers have passed more than 60 laws changing the state’s election administration — and clerks have been doing their best to keep up. She said for the most part, the changes have been good, increasing transparency and creating additional layers of security, but she’s critical of the shift away from automatic voting by mail. 
“It’s going to make it a lot more difficult for people to have that easy access to a ballot earlier on,” she said. “We’re going to notice more people waiting until closer to Election Day to participate in elections, causing maybe a little bit more congestion on Election Day, and a little bit more panic. … That’s not the Utah way.”
Janalyn Christensen feeds paper ballots through an “envelopener” machine at the Salt Lake County Government Center on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)
What happens to your ballot and how do you know it’s safe?
In an effort to combat distrust, Utah clerks welcome Utahns to come to their offices and see for themselves how ballots are processed. 
“I love to encourage people to come in and see how ballots are processed, and I’ve given hundreds of tours,” Chapman said. 
McKenzie did just that for KUER and PBS Utah last month. During a tour of the Davis County election center, he walked through how ballots are processed. As he did, he described layers of existing — and new — security measures. 
‘Not a widespread problem’: Lt. gov. releases early findings from voter citizenship review 

“There’s always going to be a minimum of two election workers that go and pick up those ballots, they have to log the date, the time, the location, and who it was that retrieved those ballots,” McKenzie said. “They’ll bring those ballots directly here to our election facility. The moment that they come into our building, they’re under 24/7 video surveillance.”
The election center, where ballots are stored and processed, is also armed with an alarm system. Only certain staff have access to it. When ballots are being processed, it has three observation areas where election watchers can keep an eye on everything. 
Each ballot envelope has a unique barcode that ensures no voter can vote twice, even if they request a second ballot, maybe because they lost it or if it was delivered to the wrong address.
“What’s important is any time that we issue a new ballot, the previous ballot has been canceled,” McKenzie said. “So that barcode has been canceled. It cannot be utilized again.”
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election

When ballots are returned, election staff must follow chain of custody rules that ensure they’re always handled by two or more election workers. They log “where they came from, when they came in, and who received them,” McKenzie said. 
Ballots are then put through a machine to authenticate whether the envelope and the barcode are valid to ensure the voter hasn’t already voted, maybe through early voting or another method. It will also date stamp the ballot and take a picture that election workers can use to verify the signature. 
Ballots are then organized and stored into batches, while election workers verify votes one by one by looking at the image of the signature on the envelope and comparing that to the signatures the clerk’s office has on file. 
“We can have up to five different images of your signature,” McKenzie said, from voter registration records and driver’s license records. 
Under new state law, voters have the option to put the last four digits of their state ID, driver’s license or Social Security number on their envelope. Starting in 2029, those last four digits will be required. But currently, if voters include those digits, election workers must verify those numbers match as well. 
Utah Legislature approves bill to require voter ID, phase out automatic voting by mail by 2029

If signatures match and the ballot is validated, election workers then determine that it can be counted, and they’ll indicate that in the clerk’s system. If it can’t be validated and counted, they’ll indicate that and give a reason why, McKenzie said. 
“Maybe the signature doesn’t match, maybe the last four don’t match, or maybe the signature is missing, or any number of reasons,” McKenzie said. “Then those envelopes are going to be run through this machine again. It’s going to sort out the valid ones from the invalid ones. All of the invalid ones, we have to notify the voter and let them know that there’s a problem with their ballot and how they can correct it.” 
To count verified ballots, election workers then put them into machines that remove the ballots from their envelopes. An operator will watch to make sure the process goes smoothly, but the machines ensure votes are separated from their envelopes, “maintaining your constitutional right to a secret ballot,” McKenzie said. 
Ballots are then put through a scanner to capture an image and count the votes on each one. After ballots are scanned, their data is stored on machines, and whenever the data is transferred to the clerk’s election management software, it’s through a special encrypted device.
Ballots are scanned and sorted at the Salt Lake County Government Center on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)
“These pieces of equipment really have multiple levels of encryption,” McKenzie said. “So you can’t just get a jump drive from Walmart, say, and plug it in here. … It has to be vendor specific. It has to be equipment specific. So that machine’s memory stick, I can’t take from there and plug it into this one. It won’t communicate.”
McKenzie said when it comes to data transfer, “nothing is wireless, nothing is web based. It’s all a physical manual process to transfer that data from one place to another.” 
“A lot of people ask, ‘How could our election results be manipulated or changed?’ You have to have physical access,” he said. “So nothing remote can connect into our facility here on any of our tabulation equipment.”
The only time that data is shared with a web accessible computer is when it’s shared with the state, he said. 
How to make sure your vote counts: By-mail ballots now have tighter deadlines

“Yes, we do transmit reports to the state, and sometimes people will say, ‘Well, that could be interrupted,’” McKenzie said. “In theory, yes, it could, but the official results will always be maintained here at the county. And so, if somebody was ever curious and (they) say, ‘Well, how do we know?’ Well, quite easy. You can look at the results that we’ve posted on our Davis County website and compare it to the results that are available on the state’s website.”
One of the best ways Utah voters can keep track of whether their ballot has made it safely back to the clerk’s office and been counted is by signing up for Track My Ballot notifications through the state’s website. If election workers run into a problem, they’ll automatically send a notification to voters urging them to contact the clerk’s office to resolve the issue. 
Clerks encourage voters not to wait until too close to the election to mail their ballots back, especially if they’re sending it through the mail. Under a new Utah law, ballots must be in clerks’ possession no later than 8 p.m. on election night, regardless of their postmark. 
Voters can also drop their ballots off at secure drop boxes (they can find locations on the state’s website) up until voting closes on election night. But for those sending them back through the mail, McKenzie recommended signing up for the Postal Service’s Informed Delivery notifications, a free service to track mail. 
“That empowers our citizens to be aware, to be to make sure that the process is transparent,” he said. “and that they can take responsibility on tracking and making sure that their ballots are being handled correctly.”
