title: Pennsylvania’s GOP members of Congress are failing us on measles.
description: Tragically, more than 1,000 people in Pennsylvania have been infected with measles in 2026, now associated with 198 hospitalizations and five deaths. In neighboring New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul just declared a statewide health emergency as cases surge in rural counties.  Yet of Pennsylvania’s 1,078 cases in 41 counties (as of last Thursday), less than […]
text:
A sign at a University of Utah health clinic warns visitors about the spread of measles. Under the Trump administration, federal health officials have cut back the number of recommended vaccines, and more states are offering exemptions for parents who don't want to vaccinate children entering public schools. (Photo by McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)Tragically, more than 1,000 people in Pennsylvania have been infected with measles in 2026, now associated with 198 hospitalizations and five deaths. In neighboring New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul just declared a statewide health emergency as cases surge in rural counties. 
Yet of Pennsylvania’s 1,078 cases in 41 counties (as of last Thursday), less than one percent occurred in fully vaccinated individuals even though measles is largely preventable with the (MMR) vaccine, the single best protection against measles.
Much has been made about how Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has actively dismantled vaccine infrastructure and spread false information about vaccines, contributing to the highest number of measles cases in 35 years. 
However, Congress has also played a significant role in weakening the public health infrastructure needed to prevent and contain outbreaks, threatening an increase in serious, preventable diseases like measles.
Last summer, Pennsylvania U.S. Representatives John Joyce, Mike Kelly, Dan Meuser, Scott Perry, Guy Reschenthaler, Glenn Thompson, Lloyd Smucker, Rob Bresnahan, and Ryan Mackenzie, along with U.S. Senator Dave McCormick — every Pennsylvania Republican in Congress except Brian Fitzpatrick — voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). The OBBBA is causing millions of Americans to lose health care coverage while giving tax breaks to the wealthiest. 
A worker applies an adhesive bandage to a child at a vaccination clinic in Minneapolis’ Corcoran Park in August 2023. Minnesota and other Democratic-led states have sued the federal government over relaxed childhood vaccination standards, and New York has declared a state of emergency as measles cases surge in neighboring Pennsylvania. (Photo courtesy of the City of Minneapolis)
By cutting funding and imposing systemic barriers, this legislation makes healthcare harder to afford and access, including vaccines. 
People with health insurance are much more likely to receive recommended vaccinations than uninsured individuals. In one study, adults with private or public insurance were two to three times more likely to be vaccinated against influenza, pneumococcal, shingles, and HPV compared to those without insurance. 
And we know when parents are uninsured, their children are less likely to visit the doctor, including for well-child visits where vaccinations are routinely provided. 
The Affordable Care Act (ACA) requires all insurance plans — including Medicare, Medicaid, and private health insurers — to cover certain recommended vaccines at no out-of-pocket cost. Additionally, the Vaccines for Children Program provides recommended vaccines free of charge to low-income children. For those who lack health insurance, however, a two-dose series of the MMR vaccine costs between $180 and $250 on average.  
By the end of June, more than 55,000 Pennsylvanians had lost Medicaid or CHIP coverage. By September, more than 200,000 Pennsylvanians had disenrolled from Pennie, the state’s ACA marketplace, following the expiration of premium tax credits. Some reported dropping coverage as costs rose just to be able to keep paying for food, rent, and utilities. People who lost their health insurance are now forced to pay out-of-pocket for vaccines; if they can’t, they risk facing serious illness and massive, uncovered expenses for measles treatment. 
Real leaders prioritize dependable, affordable healthcare for all individuals and families, without forcing them to compromise their family budgets. They invest in hospitals and clinics so that all constituents can access care, regardless of insurance type. And they protect public health by creating conditions where people can stay healthy and thrive. 
For highly contagious and possibly life-threatening diseases like measles, vaccination protects more than just the individual; it shields entire communities. In the case of measles, achieving “herd immunity” requires a 95% vaccination rate, which reduces spread and protects vulnerable people who cannot be vaccinated or have compromised immune systems, like cancer patients. Supporting evidence-based recommendations and reducing barriers to vaccination are vital steps to stopping the transmission of preventable diseases. 
Pennsylvania Republicans’ votes for the OBBBA have contributed to making Pennsylvanians more vulnerable to measles as well as future preventable outbreaks. No one should have to endure the pain of losing a family member to a preventable illness simply because they can’t afford care or because they were fed false information about vaccines by the federal government. 
 
Jill Rosenthal is the director of public health policy at the Center for American Progress Action Fund.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s primary care shortage is costing lives
authors: Howard Selinger M.D., Margaret Gradie, George Reigeluth, Vida Javidi and Wendy Barr M.D.
description: The first step toward solving Connecticut's primary care shortage is understanding its true scope.
text:
Imagine a 58-year-old Hartford resident living with diabetes, high blood pressure, and depression. She has done everything right. She takes her medications, sees her primary care physician regularly, and is well enough to continue working and living independently.
Then her longtime primary care physician retires.
She begins calling practices throughout the region, only to discover that few are accepting new patients. Those that are have wait times of four to six months. As the weeks pass, her prescriptions run out. Her blood pressure climbs. Her diabetes becomes more difficult to control. She develops increasing shortness of breath but delays seeking care because she has no trusted clinician to call.
Six months later she arrives in the emergency department in heart failure. She spends several days in the hospital at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars.
The tragedy is that nothing about her illness was especially complicated. A handful of office visits, medication adjustments, and early intervention might have prevented the hospitalization. What failed was access to a continuous relationship with a primary care clinician.
This is what a primary care workforce shortage looks like. It is not simply an abstract staffing problem or longer appointment wait times. It is preventable suffering, avoidable health care spending, and, in some cases, preventable death.
This is not speculation. The Province of Ontario recently committed to ensuring that every resident has access to a primary care clinician by 2029 because its research shows that people without an ongoing primary care relationship experience significantly worse health outcomes, including a higher risk of death. Losing a primary care clinician has consequences that extend far beyond inconvenience.
Connecticut should take notice.
The state’s primary care workforce has been under increasing strain for years. Physicians are retiring faster than they can be replaced, many practices have closed their panels to new patients, and others have reduced the number of patients they see. Connecticut needs more primary care clinicians, but exactly how many remains uncertain.
Just looking at the numbers is not enough. Workforce needs estimates should account for communities requiring bilingual clinicians, physicians with expertise in caring for people with disabilities, behavioral health integration, rural communities, or other populations with specialized needs. And they must reflect the reality that physician panel sizes continue to shrink as practices attempt to reduce burnout and improve clinician retention.
More troubling, Connecticut does not even know precisely how many primary care physicians are currently practicing in the state. Because it lacks comprehensive, timely physician workforce data, it cannot accurately measure the size of its workforce gap. The federal Health Professional Shortage Area designations commonly used to estimate shortages were designed to determine eligibility for federal resources -—not to measure statewide workforce adequacy—- and they almost certainly underestimate the shortages patients experience.
Connecticut has many of the ingredients needed for success. The state is home to nationally respected medical schools and sponsors hundreds of graduate medical education residency positions each year. Yet too many physicians complete their residency training here only to establish practices elsewhere.
Research consistently shows that physicians are far more likely to practice in the state where they complete residency than where they attended medical school. Residency is where physicians establish careers, families, and professional networks. Every physician Connecticut fails to retain represents a missed opportunity to strengthen its primary care workforce.
Recognizing these challenges, Connecticut’s Physician Recruitment and Retention Working Group has submitted two reports to the General Assembly describing the state’s physician workforce challenges and recommending practical strategies to improve recruitment, retention, and the primary care practice environment.
Yet perhaps the most important recommendation has received relatively little public attention.
The Working Group recommended establishing a permanent Standing Committee on Physician Workforce.
That recommendation deserves immediate action.
A standing committee would provide sustained leadership to collect accurate workforce data, monitor trends, evaluate physician retention, and identify emerging shortages before they become crises. Instead of relying on intermittent reports, Connecticut would have an ongoing mechanism to guide workforce planning using current evidence.
The committee should also be adequately funded and empowered to answer questions Connecticut currently cannot. How many primary care physicians are actively practicing? Where are shortages greatest? How many residency graduates remain in Connecticut? How many residents have access to continuous, relationship-based primary care?
These are not academic questions. They are essential measures of whether Connecticut residents have access to the care that keeps people healthy and prevents unnecessary hospitalizations.
Which brings us back to our Hartford resident.
Her story illustrates more than a shortage of physicians. It illustrates the value of continuity. Primary care is not simply about obtaining an appointment when you are sick. It is about having a clinician who knows your medical history, helps manage chronic illness, recognizes subtle changes in your health, and intervenes before small problems become medical emergencies.
Continuity of care saves lives. It reduces hospitalizations, lowers health care costs, improves patient satisfaction, and increases life expectancy. Yet Connecticut currently has no reliable statewide measure of how many residents enjoy that continuity—or how many have lost it.
We cannot improve what we do not measure.
The first step toward solving Connecticut’s primary care shortage is understanding its true scope. The General Assembly already has a thoughtful roadmap from the Physician Recruitment and Retention Working Group. It should now act on its central recommendation by creating and funding a Standing Committee on Physician Workforce charged with collecting the data, monitoring the workforce, and guiding long-term policy.
Connecticut has the expertise, the institutions, and the recommendations. What it needs now is a commitment to act.
For thousands of residents searching for a primary care clinician, the cost of waiting is measured not simply in dollars, but in lost health, lost opportunities, and, for some, lost lives.
Howard Selinger M.D., Margaret Gradie, George Reigeluth, Vida Javidi and Wendy Barr M.D. write for Primary Care For All Americans.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: California U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna rallies with Iowa Democrats ahead of midterms
description: U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna told Iowa Democrats Sunday he believed Iowa Rep. Josh Turek could help bring a “moral renewal to America” if he is elected to serve in the U.S. Senate. Khanna was the headline speaker for state Rep. Sean Bagniewski’s annual Fish Fry dinner in Des Moines, a fundraiser that has regularly brought […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, a California Democrat, met with Iowans after headlining Iowa state Rep. Sean Bagniewski's annual Fish Fry dinner in Des Moines Oct. 11, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna told Iowa Democrats Sunday he believed Iowa Rep. Josh Turek could help bring a “moral renewal to America” if he is elected to serve in the U.S. Senate.
Khanna was the headline speaker for state Rep. Sean Bagniewski’s annual Fish Fry dinner in Des Moines, a fundraiser that has regularly brought influential national Democrats to the state. Last year, former President Barack Obama’s chief of staff Rahm Emanuel spoke at the event.
Bagniewski referenced the potential implications of a figure like Khanna visiting Iowa even as the state lost its first-in-the-nation status for the Democratic presidential nominating calendar, saying, “I hope he has higher aspirations very soon. We’re not going to talk about those tonight.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Though the California Democrat is considered a potential presidential contender in the 2028 election, he did not discuss any potential future runs. Instead, he focused on the upcoming Nov. 3, 2026 midterms, and his support for Turek and other Iowa Democrats heading into the election.
Though Republicans have seen major victories in recent election cycles, political forecasters and some polls predict Democrats have the potential to win back ground in Iowa in the upcoming 2026 election. Alongside several Iowa U.S. House races, the U.S. Senate race between Turek and Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson is expected to be close — and one of a handful nationwide that could determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.
Khanna held an event with Turek earlier in the day hosted by The Iowa Mercury about a “Conversation on Government Transparency & Accountability.” Khanna said this event was focused on “the moral clarity that we need in our country.”
“I think we need a moral renewal in America, a spiritual renewal in America, and that to me was what the Epstein fight was about,” he said.
The California Democrat was a leading figure alongside Republican U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie in efforts over the past two years to compel the U.S. Department of Justice to publicize files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. After gathering enough signatures on a discharge petition to override leadership and force a vote in the House, the “Epstein Files Transparency Act” passed both chambers in 2025.
Khanna said after this vote, “we showed that you can stand up to power when you have people on your side and you’re standing up for justice, and that the American people will respond.”
“There was one person who didn’t get the memo — and I don’t say this in a partisan way — Ashley Hinson never getting on the original discharge petition,” he said. Hinson voted in favor of the Epstein Files Transparency Act when it successfully made it to the U.S. House floor.
Though Hinson did not sign off on the initial discharge petition, he said there was a second discharge position she could support, on legislation titled the “Epstein Files Transparency Act II.” This measure would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the U.S. attorney general “over alleged unlawful withholdings, redactions or failure to produce records,” according to a news release, in addition to requiring the U.S. attorney general provide certain unredacted documents to victims when requested.
Other Republicans — U.S. Reps. Nancy Mace and Brian Fitzpatrick — have signed onto the petition. Khanna said at the event he wanted Hinson to join the effort.
“Today, I’m calling on Ashley Hinson to text or call Thomas Massie and sign that discharge petition so we can get a vote and hold the Epstein class accountable,” he said. “You can’t talk about bipartisanship and not act in a bipartisan way. I don’t know Iowa that well, but I know here people care more about what you do than what you say. They care more about your action and character than giving a fancy speech. And if you’re really on the side, which should not be political, of the survivors, then please get on this discharge petition so we can pass this bill and see the prosecution of the Epstein class.”
Hinson said in a statement Sunday night that she voted to supported the release of files related to Epstein.
“I’ve voted to release the Epstein files,” Hinson said. :We should release every single bit of information and have full transparency and accountability for any predators. Sexually abusing a woman or a child is the sickest thing you can do — and anyone who did that should be permanently behind bars. Protect the victims. Hold the creeps accountable. That is what I’m for.”
Khanna says he’d support impeaching Trump
Answering questions from the crowd, Khanna also said if Democrats gain control of Congress in the 2026 midterms, he would support impeaching President Donald Trump.
“I don’t understand some of my party — I’m not going to call them out — who say, ‘oh, we got to just move on,'” Khanna said. “You know, if someone is robbing your neighbor’s house, you don’t just say, ‘oh, let’s just move on.’ … This is not a very hard question. Donald Trump has committed impeachable offenses. He should be impeached. It’s not about Trump. It’s about standing up for our constitutional values.”
He also called for impeaching U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — another effort by Massie that Khanna said he supported.
Looking ahead to the November election, Khanna said he had faith in the “resilient spirit” of America — and of Iowa, which he said has played an important role in determining the future of American politics through the Iowa caucuses.
“I believe this country hungers for decency, hungers for people who can argue well, hungers for a sense of reason, and a belief in this nation again, and that’s how I think we have a responsibility to lift up this country to remind what we’re capable of,” Khanna said. “And Iowa, you have been such a part of that.”
Turek, who also spoke at the event, urged Democrats to stay engaged and focused in the final weeks before the election.
“This is the chance,” Turek said. “This is when the pendulum swings back our direction. Opportunities like this do not come around very often. … If we’re able to win this race this year here in Iowa, we will not only make a generational change to the state, we will be able to flip the United States Senate, and we will be able to change this country.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: EPA head Lee Zeldin says agency is updating Iowa’s impaired waterway list
description: ALTOONA — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin said Sunday in Iowa that the federal agency is processing “updates” on Iowa’s list of impaired waterways amid a lawsuit challenging the decision to delist seven waterways that had been added due to nitrate impairment. The EPA administrator toured Summit Products in Altoona, his first Iow[...]
text:
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin, left, spoke with Albert Marasco, CEO of Summit Products on a tour of the Summit Products manufacturing facility in Altoona Oct. 11, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)ALTOONA — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin said Sunday in Iowa that the federal agency is processing “updates” on Iowa’s list of impaired waterways amid a lawsuit challenging the decision to delist seven waterways that had been added due to nitrate impairment.
The EPA administrator toured Summit Products in Altoona, his first Iowa stop of a trip which will also include events Monday in Iowa City and Dyersville. Speaking with reporters, Zeldin said the EPA was taking steps to address Iowans’ concerns about water quality — specifically about nitrate levels and potential environmental factors that may be contributing to the state’s high and rising cancer rates — by partnering with local businesses, farmers and the state government.
“Here in Iowa, there are so many farmers and others who understand that they have an obligation to protect their land, the water,” Zeldin said. “And that concern that Iowa residents have to make sure that rivers, waterways are clean … they want to pursue more answers, they have more questions, and all that is important to communicate to EPA. And then for EPA to do our part with our statutory obligations, with the opportunities that are in front of us in the months and the years ahead, to help find those answers.”
He said “when necessary,” the EPA sets new maximum contaminant levels on the levels of nitrate allowed in water, adding, “respecting the fact that we believe that a state and local community knows their water better than anyone who’s sitting behind a desk in Washington, D.C.” in this consideration.
Concerns about EPA recognition — and potential regulation — on nitrate levels in Iowa waterways has been a point of concern in the state after the EPA attempted in late 2024 to add seven additional segments to Iowa’s Impaired Waterways list due to nitrate impairment. This list determines if a water segment meets designated criteria for uses like fishing, recreation and drinking water using retroactive data — if a segment is listed as impaired, it triggers a restoration process under the federal Clean Water Act.
After the Iowa Department of Natural Resources challenged the EPA’s seven additions to the list, the federal agency removed these waterways from the 2024 list. This decision was challenged in a May lawsuit brought by Food & Water Watch, the Iowa Environmental Council, and the Environmental Law & Policy Center, which called for the court to order the EPA to relist these segments as impaired waterways.
While this lawsuit is ongoing, the EPA finalized its decision to delist the waterways in late September. A Thursday news release from the Environmental Law & Policy Center criticized this move for not taking action to address high nitrate levels in the state.
“Iowans know that we have a water quality crisis. We deserve more than the Trump EPA putting their head in the sand and refusing to act on water quality,” ELPC Senior Attorney Josh Mandelbaum said in the news release. “That’s why we will continue our lawsuit to provide accountability to the Trump EPA and to push for action on water quality for Iowans.”
But Zeldin said the EPA is focused on advancing “cooperative federalism between the federal government and the state government,” and working with the Iowa state government to address water quality concerns.
“We’re going through a process with recent updates in the last couple weeks with regards to impaired waterways, not just with adjudicating Iowa’s list from 2024, but also Iowa’s submission of a new list for 2026, that partnership is key,” Zeldin said. “I do not feel like our agency is or should be in conflict with the state of Iowa and the people of Iowa. It should be a partnership working together to make Iowa residents proud to be able to answer their questions when they have them, and to to set regulations according to law that are appropriate to help strengthen Iowa’s land, air, and water.”
Zeldin touts EPA action to certify aftermarket vehicle products
The first stop of Zeldin’s Iowa trip to a motor vehicle parts and accessories manufacturer comes after the EPA’s move to allow the Specialty Equipment Market Association, known as SEMA, to certify aftermarket vehicle products to show compliance with the EPA Clean Air Act.
Before President Donald Trump signed a July memorandum making this change, Zeldin said the only body able to perform this certification was the California Air Resource Board (CARB) – which he said made the process “backlogged” and “very expensive,” with the certification process taking a year or more to complete.
Albert Marasco, CEO of Summit Products, thanked Zeldin for visiting their facility and said steps recently taken by the EPA to help certify aftermarket products has been “helpful to our business,” especially as the business is expanding.
“We got another 30,000 square feet going up this year, more on the way,” Marasco said. “and I don’t know if we can do it without proper support from the government.”
Summit Products was one of “hundreds of SEMA members, just in the state of Iowa” Zeldin said who will benefit from Trump’s memorandum.
Zeldin said the SEMA certification process shows “Iowa issues are front and center for this agency” – and said the action builds off his agency’s other work in the Office of Air and Radiation. He brought up the work he discussed during his last trip to Iowa in 2025 to the Iowa State Fair, where he announced guidance to engine and equipment manufacturers to prevent sudden shutdowns and power losses that occur in diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) systems.
These are issues related to “right to repair” efforts to prevent manufacturers from banning independent repairs. In February, the EPA issued a clarification letter stating the Clean Air Act does not prohibit repairs to offroad diesel equipment like farm machinery.
In Dyersville, he will be joined by U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican candidate for U.S. Senate in 2026, to tour an energy facility. Because he was visiting Iowa in his official capacity, Zeldin said he would not offer “personal” opinions on the Senate race or other contentious elections in Iowa. However, he said Iowa’s federal delegation has “strong influential leadership in Washington D.C.” and that many of the issues the EPA has taken action on have been driven by one-on-one discussion with Iowa leaders.
“That’s something that serves, in my opinion, Iowa’s best interests when you have a delegation as strong and as influential as Iowa has had,” he said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC’s State Health Plan moves to block Atrium program it calls an ‘unlawful pricing scheme’
description: North Carolina’s State Health Plan announced Friday it had requested a temporary restraining order in Wake County Superior Court to halt Atrium Health’s new “affordability program.” State Treasurer Brad Briner, whose office oversees the State Health Plan, said while Atrium’s new program could lower out-of-pocket costs for some state employees at Atrium facil[...]
text:
(Stock photo by Wichayada Suwanachun/Getty Images) North Carolina’s State Health Plan announced Friday it had requested a temporary restraining order in Wake County Superior Court to halt Atrium Health’s new “affordability program.”
State Treasurer Brad Briner, whose office oversees the State Health Plan, said while Atrium’s new program could lower out-of-pocket costs for some state employees at Atrium facilities, it is intended to destabilize the state’s own Preferred Provider Program and could push the plan into bankruptcy.
The State Health Plan has said that its new tiered provider system is designed to keep the plan that serves 750,000 members financially stable.
UNC Health and Novant have agreed to lower their pricing for state employees to be designated as preferred hospital systems. Atrium has not.
Instead, Charlotte-based Atrium Health announced a new “Affordability Protection Program Tuesday,” saying it addresses the higher copay  costs created for patients seeking care at Atrium Health.
According to Atrium, the program will ensure lower out-of-pocket costs for plan members who use its services. But Atrium did not say it has  committed to lowering what it will charge the state plan for those services.
The State Health Plan says it was “blindsided” by Atrium’s announcement, which it says could confuse members as open enrollment begins.
Premiums rise, but overall costs could fall for NC State Health Plan members under a new system

“We think this proposal is a violation of various state and federal laws,” Briner said during Tuesday’s Council of State meeting. “It will never become reality.”
Atrium said in a statement Friday it does not agree “that offering discounts to NC State Health Plan members is somehow unlawful.”
Atrium is also in the process of merging with WakeMed, the largest medical system in Wake County, where the highest number of state employees work. Briner has said he is “profoundly concerned” about that possible merger.
“Every taxpayer in the state will have to bear the burden of Atrium’s proposal when additional funding is needed for the [State Health Plan] at the expense of other public programs, pay raises and COLA’s,” Briner’s office warned in its statement Friday.
“We share the concerns about the solvency of the NC State Health Plan, so it’s unclear to us why the Plan rejected our offers to save money for taxpayers and members,” Atrium said in Friday’s response.
So that members of the state plan don’t feel rushed in selecting insurance coverage next year, the open enrollment period is being extended through Nov. 6, 2026.

name: Maryland Matters
title: TSA considers next steps for privatized screening after scrapping Gold+ plans
description: The Transportation Security Administration has scrapped the Gold+ concept for privatizing some security operations, but is still exploring how to expand privatized airport screening, agency leaders said recently.
text:
A Transportation Security Administration officer checks a traveler at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport in this 2023 photo. TSA officials are still committed to privatizing some security operations. (Photo by Tia Dufour/Department of Homeland Security)By Justin Doubleday
The Transportation Security Administration has scrapped the Gold+ privatization concept, but TSA leaders are still exploring how to expand privatized airport screening.
Meanwhile, industry is pushing for TSA to consider the ideas that came out of the Gold+ acquisition process as the agency explores an “evolution” of its existing Screening Partnership Program (SPP).
Officials, speaking at a conference hosted by the Airports Council International – North America in Arlington, Va., this week, made clear they are still bullish on expanding private airport screening.
“The concept around Gold+ was confusing to folks in terms of what it was and what the solution was, what the carrot was, and there was just a lot of confusion in the industry, and so I decided to sunset the Gold+ initiative, but not the desire to increase membership in SPP,” TSA Administrator David Cummins said in a wide ranging keynote address Tuesday.
Cummins said he has spoken to “a number of airports that are interested” in joining SPP, which is TSA’s existing program for having a private contractor manage airport screening.
“What we’re setting out to do, and we have a whole team focused on this, is how can we evolve this SPP concept,” he said. “How can we tie it into what I just talked about in terms of the modernization of the checkpoints, not just the PreCheck checkpoints, but the standard lane checkpoints, where we can provide a carrot, an incentive, that the airports would be like, ‘Yeah, we want that.’”
Rockville diner group files lawsuit against airport concessionaire

Steve Lorincz, executive assistant administrator for security operations at TSA, said the agency is discussing establishing a “tiger team” to evaluate the Gold+ process and next steps for the agency. TSA has already established several such teams to make recommendations on various reforms under Cummins’ Horizon 25 strategy.
“We still have all the information from TSA Gold+, so all all that information is going to be kind of incorporated, but the boss wants to really look at it and provide a fresh perspective,” Lorincz said during a Wednesday panel.
“And even when you look at, you know, Horizon 25, right? It’s like, what is TSA going to look like in the next 25 years, and we know that the SPP product has been in place since the beginning, but it’s time to evolve,” he said. “So I think there’s going to be a lot of work in that space.”
The current SPP private screening model is in place at 20 airports across the country. The Trump administration has already proposed cutting some TSA jobs and expanding that model to the smallest commercial airports.
Under Gold+, previous TSA leadership had tried to sell airports on an evolution of the SPP model where contractors would manage both the screening workforce and the technology. The pitch was that contractors could upgrade screening technology and introduce new “innovations,” while seeing less disruption to the workforce during a government shutdown.
The push for the privatized model generated significant concern among TSA’s 55,000 transportation security officers. The American Federation of Government Employees, which represents TSOs under a collective bargaining agreement, also argued the model would prioritize profits over security.
Three airports initially opted into the Gold+ program. But the largest of those, Tampa International Airport, decided not to pursue the initiative after studying the program further and hearing concerns from the TSOs at the facility. Around the same time, TSA decided to cancel the Gold+ program and consider an “evolved” SPP instead.
Before TSA canceled the program, it had released a final Gold+ solicitation and had been evaluating proposals from industry. Raymond Laroche, chief operating officer at Punta Gorda Airport, near Sarasota, Florida, said he hopes the agency will consider those proposals as it moves forward with new plans. Punta Gorda is among the 20 airports that uses a private screening contractor under SPP.
“In a lot of the discussions that I’ve had this week, a lot of the people that were intending to get into the Gold+ program had spent a lot of time and effort and money in coming up with those ideas, and I don’t want to see those ideas go to waste,” Laroche said. “There should be a group getting to present those ideas to the administrator and at least laying it out, what the process was, what worked, what didn’t work, and put those ideas forward so they aren’t lost and it’s not a complete waste.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Clean-up, power restoration mark the second day post-Hurricane Isaias
description: Some 300,000 utility customer remained without power in the western Florida Panhandle two days after Hurricane Isaias hit — the majority of them customers of Florida Power & Light, Gov. Ron DeSantis said Sunday. Meanwhile the scope of damage was becoming clearer. Most of the destruction came not on the coast, which saw less storm […]
text:
Throughout much of Destin, piles of tree parts were huddled on curbs the evening after Hurricane Isaias made landfall. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Some 300,000 utility customer remained without power in the western Florida Panhandle two days after Hurricane Isaias hit — the majority of them customers of Florida Power & Light, Gov. Ron DeSantis said Sunday.
Meanwhile the scope of damage was becoming clearer. Most of the destruction came not on the coast, which saw less storm surge than expected, but rather in north Santa Rosa  and Escambia counties, where powerful winds lifted roofs off structures.
“Normally, you would think right there on the coast would be the worst. Here, you see that go inland,” DeSantis said during a news conference outside a Waffle House in Milton.
“So, as these storms go, those are very strong wind gusts for being this far inland. But I definitely think Santa Rosa, they have the highest percentage of power outages. I’m sure they have a high percentage compared to the other areas of downed power lines and poles, and I know we’re working with the utilities for them to help get those back up as soon as possible,” he continued.
Appearing with DeSantis were U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody, appointed by DeSantis and running for election in her own right against Democrat Angie Nixon. Also there was Commissioner of Agriculture Wilton Simpson, who said employees of his agency were helping with cleanup.
Santa Rosa County Sheriff Bob Johnson said there’d been no looting.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, around 50 miles east of Pensacola, about 8:30 p.m. Central time Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph.
On Saturday, residents marveled to a Phoenix reporter at their good luck, relatively.
“I thought it was going to be worse,” Ted Wolford said, pointing to the three spots in his yard that had previously been occupied trees he’d lost in earlier storms.
A city park was covered with pine needles and tree limbs and sheriff’s deputies were directing traffic at busy intersections, other lights powered by generators. Generators were still running traffic lights on Sunday, and state troopers were directing traffic too, DeSantis said.
A walk through a Destin park was accompanied by a hum of generators from neighbors.
The Publix and Target parking lots were busy. It was a calm, 74 degree evening.
A tree-sized tree branch landed on the street immediately in front of Welcome Mat trailer park in Pensacola, Florida, the result of Hurricane Isaias’ high winds on Friday Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)
Power
As for power restoration, “if you’re without and you’re FPL, you may get it today, a lot of people will get it today. Others will get it tomorrow. And if anything goes beyond that, it’s because there’s some extenuating circumstances in terms of needing to rebuild some of the infrastructure,” DeSantis said.
“Now, as it happens, most of the schools in Northwest Florida were already scheduled to be off for Columbus Day, which is tomorrow. And many of them, Tuesday is a teacher planning day. So, keying in on that Wednesday to get the schools back, I think that’s gonna be possible for the vast, vast, vast majority of schools.”
“Our Florida public power crews were called on to assist other utilities with power restoration efforts in affected areas, including Florida co-op electric utilities and out-of-state municipal electric utilities in Alabama,” said Amy Zubaly, executive director of the Florida Municipal Electric Association.
“Enabled by our mutual aid agreements, eight Florida Municipal Electric Association members are assisting a Florida electric cooperative in Northwest Florida, and another five public power utilities have assisted with power restoration efforts in six Alabama cities.”
The state is trying to learn the scale of the harm to businesses through a survey, available at FloridaDisaster.biz. An emergency program offers zero-interest bridge loans of up to $100,000 for agriculture and aquaculture and $150,000 for citrus and cattle operations. Applications are available at Floridajobs.org/EBL, Floridajobs.org/EBL.
“We’re monitoring rising water levels along the Blackwater and Shoal rivers, particularly near U.S. 90 and I-10, in the Crestview area, that flooding could impact roadways,” the governor said.
“Hopefully, it wouldn’t get to the point where it would be dangerous for folks to even remain in their homes, but that has happened in the past in different storms, and so that’s why we’re keeping all of our search and rescue personnel on standby in case their services are needed.”
Deaths
The death toll Florida remained at two DeSantis said— one a woman killed when a tree fell on her house and another from fumes from a generator operating inside a garage.
“We have not gotten any more reports for any additional fatalities,” DeSantis said. “I would just urge people to be very careful. There’s a lot of debris out there, particularly as you get into the northern part of the Panhandle. A lot of trees knocked down. A lot of hazards. There may be still power lines knocked down.”
Authorities received “not a huge number of 911 calls compared to past storms,” the governor noted.
“We did not have to mobilize air assets for search and rescue, and that’s ultimately a good thing. We had the assets ready, didn’t end up having to deploy them, at least not yet. Hopefully, we don’t have a lot of bad flooding come on the heels of this.”
DeSantis said he’s heard carping about deploying assets that in the end weren’t needed.
“So, somebody, ‘Oh, you shouldn’t have spent money by bringing the guard or doing this. You didn’t need them.’ Well, you don’t know that. You don’t know that before the storm happens. So, our view is kind of bring overwhelming power to these things. Use whatever we need, including everything, if you need to,” he said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: I opened a primary care practice. Now I see why doctors are giving up.
description: When I opened an independent family medicine practice, I believed I was creating the kind of care patients say they want: A physician who knows them, listens and has enough time to think. Instead, I learned why so many primary care doctors are leaving. The problem is not that physicians have stopped caring. It is […]
text:
Traditional health insurance pressures doctors to work at volume, or if they add layers of bureaucracy that independent physicians can't easily handle, writes Dimitri Coupet, who runs a family practice in Laurel. (Photo by Rawpixel.com/Stock.adobe.com)When I opened an independent family medicine practice, I believed I was creating the kind of care patients say they want: A physician who knows them, listens and has enough time to think.
Instead, I learned why so many primary care doctors are leaving.
The problem is not that physicians have stopped caring. It is that the system asks us to accept enormous responsibility while paying mainly for brief, billable encounters.
A patient may spend 20 minutes in my office, but the work rarely ends there. I review laboratory results, answer messages, refill medications, read hospital records, coordinate referrals, appeal denials and complete forms. Much of that work is unpaid or poorly compensated.
Meanwhile, an independent practice must pay rent, employees, malpractice insurance, electronic medical record fees and billing expenses regardless of delayed payments or missed appointments.
The financial prescription is always the same: See more patients, shorten visits and move faster.
But patients are not becoming simpler. Good primary care requires time. Yet taking that time can reduce revenue and put the practice at risk.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Maryland should care about this because our emergency departments are already strained. Maryland’s emergency-room stays have historically been among the longest in the nation. And a substantial share of emergency-department use involves problems that are non-emergent, primary-care treatable or potentially avoidable with timely outpatient care.
When patients cannot get timely primary care, the emergency room becomes the default. That is expensive and frustrating for patients who may wait hours for a problem a family physician could have addressed earlier. Strengthening primary care is not simply about helping doctors. It is part of solving Maryland’s hospital-access problem.
Maryland’s AHEAD model recognizes this connection and seeks to invest more in primary care. But it also illustrates our tendency to respond to complexity with more complexity: quality measures, reporting requirements and multiple program pathways. Large health systems can hire teams to manage those obligations. Small independent practices often cannot.
Maryland should also test something simpler, a marketplace insurance designed to work with direct primary care.
Under direct primary care (DPC), patients pay a physician a transparent monthly membership for routine and ongoing primary care. The practice does not submit an insurance claim for every visit, phone call or message. The physician is paid to care for the patient over time rather than maximize billable encounters.
The accompanying marketplace plan would remain real insurance, covering hospitalization, specialists, emergency care, prescriptions, imaging and other major expenses. Government subsidies could focus on making that insurance affordable, while patients pay their DPC physician directly.
Imagine an eligible Marylander paying about $100 monthly for DPC and no more than $100 for subsidized insurance. The state could then measure whether better access and continuity reduce emergency visits, hospitalizations and total insurance spending. If improved access and continuity reduce avoidable emergency visits and hospitalizations, those savings should eventually be reflected in lower premiums and lower taxpayer subsidies. 
Maryland already has the regulatory tools to test this. The state could pursue this through a Section 1332 waiver, or as a pilot administered through the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange. 
The principle should be simple: Primary care must be accessible to patients, sustainable for physicians and financed in a way that rewards continuity rather than volume.
I opened my office because I still believe in community-based family medicine. I now understand why doctors sell to larger systems, reduce clinical work or leave primary care entirely.
If Maryland wants stronger primary care and fewer patients relying on emergency departments for problems that could have been managed earlier, it should be willing to test financing models that make it easier — not harder — for family physicians to remain in practice.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Nancy Lavin wins A-Mark Prize for watchdog journalism
description: Rhode Island Current Senior Reporter Nancy Lavin was honored Friday with a 2026 A-Mark Prize for Investigative Journalism for her work exposing a gap in state law that prevented homebound seniors from receiving care needed to avoid severe health complications. Lavin was awarded third prize in the annual competition administered by the New England Newspaper [[...]
text:
Left to right, Rhode Island Current Senior Reporter Nancy Lavin, Editor-in-Chief Janine L. Weisman are shown at The Publick House in Sturbridge, Massachusetts, on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. The inn was the site of the New England Newspaper & Press Association's 2026 Leadership Summit and awards luncheon. (Photo by Will Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Rhode Island Current Senior Reporter Nancy Lavin was honored Friday with a 2026 A-Mark Prize for Investigative Journalism for her work exposing a gap in state law that prevented homebound seniors from receiving care needed to avoid severe health complications.
Lavin was awarded third prize in the annual competition administered by the New England Newspaper & Press Association during the regional journalism organization’s annual leadership summit at The Publick House Historic Inn in Sturbridge, Massachusetts. The prize comes with a $2,000 cash award for Lavin and an additional $1,000 for Rhode Island Current.
Rhode Island Current was also named as a Distinguished Online News Publication for the New England region during the summit’s awards luncheon.
A-Mark prizes are funded by the A-Mark Foundation to honor excellence in watchdog reporting. Three prizes are awarded for the best journalism in each New England state. 
Lavin was covering a different hearing at the State House on March 27, 2025, when she saw dozens of caregivers, healthcare workers and podiatrists flowing into a first-floor hearing room. She learned they were there to testify on a bill that would allow certified nurses to provide basic foot care to homebound seniors and diabetics.
Lavin made a mental note to learn more about this compelling bill at a later time. But there were other priorities demanding her attention after the death of then-Senate President Dominick Ruggerio led the upper chamber to cancel a week of its session and sparked behind-the-scenes drama over a leadership transition.
The House of Representatives unanimously approved the foot care bill on June 12, but it failed to advance in the Rhode Island Senate. It ultimately died without even a hearing before the Senate Committee on Health and Human Services. 
Lavin learned that Rhode Island was the only state in the nation that did not let nurses provide home foot care to manage toenail growth, corns, and detect foot ulcers. That left vulnerable patients unable to get the basic care they need to prevent minor issues from escalating into severe infections. They included a homebound veteran who took a jackknife to his neglected toenails and ended up in a “pool of blood,” according to the testimony of a home hospice nurse.
For her story published Aug. 13, 2025, Lavin interviewed the bill’s advocates and opponents, along with a foot care nurse whose practice was shut down by the state health department a year earlier, prompting the legislation in the first place. It captured the attention of lawmakers who previously paid little attention to this problem.
Nearly identical legislation was introduced in both chambers at the start of the 2026 legislative session. It was approved unanimously by both chambers and signed into law by Gov. Dan McKee on April 29 in an uncharacteristically early bill signing for the six-month legislative session. 
The new law immediately allowed the Rhode Island foot care nurse to restart her in-state practice and offered both a solution and dignity to patients and their families in desperate need of care. 
The first place A-Mark prize for New Hampshire went to Will Skipworth, a reporter at the New Hampshire Bulletin, for his three-part series, A System of Harm, which probed systemic rampant abuse and neglect within New Hampshire’s disability care system. Skipworth also received a Publick Occurrences Award for the same series at the awards luncheon.
Rhode Island Current and New Hampshire Bulletin are both part of States Newsroom, the nation’s largest nonprofit state-focused news organization. 
Rhode Island A-Mark Prize prizes also went to the Providence Journal. Antonia Noori Farzan and Jonny Williams took first place for their reporting on hospital dumping, when nursing homes and assisted-living facilities refuse to accept back residents ready for discharge after hospitalization. Alex Kuffner won second place for his reporting on the contamination of well water in Glocester with PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” believed to be linked to a research facility where PFAS-containing firefighting foam was used for years by insurance giant FM.
The New Bedford Light was named Online News Site of the Year for New England. VT Digger was also named distinguished a finalist.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Organizaciones eliminarán 34 millones de dólares en deuda médica para 21,000 habitantes de Kansas
description: Traducido por Claudia Amaro. TOPEKA — Más de 21,000 habitantes de Kansas recibirán este mes una carta en la que se les notifica que su deuda médica ha sido cancelada. Un par de organizaciones sin fines de lucro anunciaron que eliminarán casi 34 millones de dólares en deuda médica para 21,490 habitantes de Kansas que […]
text:
Un par de organizaciones sin fines de lucro anuncian un amplio alivio de la deuda médica para casi 21,500 habitantes de Kansas. (Foto por Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Traducido por Claudia Amaro.
TOPEKA — Más de 21,000 habitantes de Kansas recibirán este mes una carta en la que se les notifica que su deuda médica ha sido cancelada.
Un par de organizaciones sin fines de lucro anunciaron que eliminarán casi 34 millones de dólares en deuda médica para 21,490 habitantes de Kansas que cumplan ciertos criterios, en una iniciativa económica única y a gran escala.
“Esto, en realidad, no se trata de deudas médicas”, dijo Melissa Morales, fundadora de Somos Votantes y originaria de Kansas. “Esto se trata de un sistema de salud roto que la gente no puede costear.”
La mecánica para borrar $33.9 millones en deuda médica en Kansas comenzó con una alianza entre la organización nacional sin fines de lucro Undue Medical Debt, que adquiere deudas médicas al mayoreo de proveedores y agencias de cobranza por centavo por centavo, y Somos Votantes Education Fund, una organización de participación cívica no partidista que dona para abolir la deuda. En promedio, un dólar donado borra $100 de deuda médica, según un anuncio de ambas organizaciones.
Kansas es la primera en la historia de la asociación en recibir alivio estatal de la deuda médica para los habitantes de bajos ingresos de Kansas. Las dos organizaciones abolieron $133 millones en deuda médica para más de 128,000 personas en condados seleccionados de Nevada en 2025 y este año se espera que eliminen $240,000 en deuda de servicios públicos en Michigan. Cada esfuerzo forma parte del  programa Seeds of Relief del fondo educativo.
Las personas elegibles en Kansas incluyen a quienes tienen deudas médicas que representan el 5% o más de su ingreso anual, o a quienes ganan menos de cuatro veces el nivel federal de pobreza, lo que equivale a alrededor de $100,000 para una familia de tres personas.
Recibirán cartas marcadas con la información de Deuda Médica Indebida a partir de la semana del 19 de octubre que indicarán qué deudas han sido perdonadas. No es necesario tomar ninguna acción.
“Nadie elige tener deudas médicas”, dijo Morales. “Nadie elige enfermarse.”
Dijo que espera que el alivio de la deuda les dé “un poco de espacio” a los habitantes de Kansas. Morales, quien es de Liberal, fundó Somos Votantes, una organización dirigida a votantes latinos. Las iniciativas de deuda médica del brazo filantrópico de la organización, Somos Votantes Education Fund, son no partidistas, dijo Morales, y ayudan a las familias sin importar su partido o afiliación.
“En Somos, creemos que una factura médica no debería ser la razón por la que alguien no pueda pagar la renta o poner comida en la mesa, pero esa es la realidad para demasiadas personas en Kansas, trabajadores en este momento”, dijo Morales en un comunicado. “Somos intervendrá por las familias trabajadoras cuando nadie más lo haga.”
Dijo que se planea brindar ayuda adicional en otros estados el próximo año.
Hasta 2024, el 36% de los hogares estadounidenses tenían deuda médica, según una investigación publicada en la University of Oxford Press. Los costos de salud se han mantenido en 2026 cerca de la cima de la lista de preocupaciones financieras de las personas, según encuestas de KFF, una organización de investigación y noticias sobre políticas de salud. Seis de cada diez personas dijeron a la organización que están “muy” o “algo” preocupadas por costear la atención médica para ellas y sus familias, lo que incluye seguros y costos de bolsillo.
En Kansas, la deuda médica se ha convertido en un tema político candente después de que el New York Times reportara en septiembre que el senador estadounidense Roger Marshall, republicano que busca la reelección en noviembre y ex ginecólogo en Great Bend, demandó a cientos de pacientes por deudas médicas y tuvo a decenas arrestados por no responder a sus casos de cobranza en la corte. Kansas Reflector informó en julio sobre acciones de cobranza agresivas de un hospital de Topeka contra personas que calificaban para atención médica gratuita.
Allison Sesso, presidenta y directora general de Undue Medical Debt, dijo que las familias están cada vez más apretadas entre las facturas, el súper y el aumento de los costos.
“La deuda médica, o el miedo a acumularla, no deberían impedir que nadie busque la atención que necesita”, dijo Sesso, “y tengo la esperanza de que eliminar estas cargas en Kansas empodere a las familias para volver a involucrarse con el sistema de salud y poner su salud primero.”

name: VTDigger
title: A Vermont degree should come with a green card
description:
As international enrollment falls, Vermont stands to lose millions in economic activity. A green card for full-tuition graduates would change that.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A Vermont degree should come with a green card.
text:
This commentary is by Justin Neuman, who is a professor of literary studies at Eugene Lang College, The New School and a developer of philosophical software. 
I’m in the export business. I teach literary studies to college students.
That’s not how professors usually describe themselves, but it should be. American colleges and universities sell one of the world’s most desirable goods or services: an American education.
Education is an unusual export because when someone buys it, the product stays here and the customer comes to us, rather than the other way around. When international students enroll in American universities, currency from international sources flows to an American institution. What’s more, much of what international students spend on housing, food and other services lands in American communities too.
No state should be paying closer attention to this than Vermont. In 2024-25, the most recent year for which we have full data, 1,279 international students attended Vermont colleges and universities. They contributed an estimated $57.6 million to the state economy and supported 336 jobs.
For scale, compare the value of international students to that of Vermont’s most famous export, maple syrup. The state’s entire 2025 yield was valued by the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets at $101.7 million. Obviously, we’re not comparing apples to apples here, but the students-to-syrup comparison conveys the size of what’s at stake: The money international college students bring into Vermont is worth more than half of the state’s syrup business.
And that $57.6 million doesn’t count the value of Vermont’s secondary-school export market. Nowhere is this logic more apparent than at Vermont’s private boarding schools and ski academies, where hundreds of international students come from around the world to study and train. Families want their children inside the American educational pipeline as early as possible; those students go on to American colleges, have American careers and become American taxpayers.
Education is an export industry and a potential growth engine hiding in plain sight — and we’re losing customers. New international enrollment at American colleges fell 17% in fall 2025. NAFSA: Association of International Educators estimates that the decline cost the American economy $1.1 billion and nearly 23,000 jobs in a single fall, including an estimated $1.5 million loss in Vermont. During the critical May-to-August visa season in 2025, the United States issued 36% fewer F-1 student visas than during the same period the year before.
The verdict this fall is worse. NAFSA’s August numbers estimate that international enrollment could have declined another 9.5% in 2026, meaning as many as 111,000 fewer students, translating to $3.4 billion less economic activity and nearly 40,000 fewer American jobs. Vermont’s projected share of that loss is $4.6 million.
Vermont also knows, better than any state, what happens when a college dies. Burlington College closed in 2016. Green Mountain College, Southern Vermont College and the College of St. Joseph all shut their doors in 2019. Marlboro College followed in 2020, Goddard in 2024. Sterling College in Craftsbury graduated its final class in spring 2026 after more than 65 years. Green Mountain College was Poultney’s largest employer, with more than 150 faculty and staff; when it closed, people moved and property values fell. 
In 2019, PBS reported that Vermont had more colleges and universities per capita than any other state in the country, with 22. Since then, seven Vermont colleges have closed, merged or reorganized. 

READ MORE

These aren’t elite schools; they’re tuition-driven institutions in small towns whose economies depend on a campus staying open. And Southern Vermont’s campus is moving toward resort redevelopment; the Marlboro campus is operated in the summers by Marlboro Music; Goddard has become an arts and community hub; the Green Mountain campus is proposed as a Christian university.
One of those names is personal for me. In 1994, I was a senior at a rural high school that didn’t offer AP courses, so I took four courses at Marlboro College instead, a few miles from our home, mostly on dirt roads. The professors there treated me like a scholar, and that year set the course of my life. I teach literature today because a tiny Vermont college had an open door and a seat at the table.
Instead of arguing about comprehensive immigration reform for another generation, let’s start with the easy case.
Call it the “full-tuition path.” If an international student is admitted legally to an accredited American college or university, pays full tuition and graduates in good standing, they should receive a green card at graduation. Especially undergraduates, who arrived at places like the University of Vermont or Middlebury College at 18 and spent four years in the dorms, classrooms and towns where assimilation actually happens.
They shouldn’t face a lottery, a bureaucratic obstacle course or a decade in a visa queue. If this sounds like a fast track to citizenship, it is. Naturalization usually requires five years as a permanent resident. I’d go further and count the years they spent studying here toward that requirement. And if this sounds like it favors those who can pay their own way rather than the needy and desperate, it does.
I’m arguing that if we’re going to admit immigrants by some criterion, “graduated from one of our own universities while paying their own way” is a pretty darn good one. I’m emphasizing that this issue is separate from border control. And it’s an intuition that has emerged on both sides of the aisle. Donald Trump himself made a version of this argument in 2024, while Hillary Clinton’s 2016 technology agenda proposed stapling green cards to accredited American master’s and doctoral degrees in science, technology, engineering and math.
Vermont needs these students in two ways. First as customers of institutions and communities already struggling with declining enrollment. Then we need them as young, educated residents in a state whose own fiscal analysts warn that its labor force will continue to shrink without substantial in-migration.
Rarely have Americans agreed on so much while doing so little. Congress should pass legislation opening a full-tuition path to qualified international students, and the president should sign it. Vermont’s colleges will welcome the students and the tuition; businesses across the state will welcome the customers; and eventually, fellow citizens will welcome their new neighbors.

title: Political mailer sparks Vermont disclosure complaint
description:
The attorney general is reviewing allegations that a PAC failed to disclose donors and file a required report.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Political mailer sparks Vermont disclosure complaint.
text:
Attorney General Charity Clark discusses the work of the Vermont Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force in Waterbury in December 2023. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Ryan Pacheco was first published in the Manchester Journal on Oct. 8, 2026.BENNINGTON COUNTY — A second round of politically critical postcards have been mailed to Bennington County residents by “Common Sense PAC”, the Independent Expenditure Political Action Committee (IEPAC) that was responsible for late September’s similar mailer regarding State Sen. Seth Bongartz, D-Bennington. The second mailer, which is part of a planned series by Common Sense PAC, focused on State Sen. Rob Plunkett, D-Bennington, accusing the senator of failing to deliver on crime and public safety, education, property taxes and affordability. The mailer also included a message of support for Republican candidates who are running for the same seats, Spike Whitmire and Josh Williams.Plunkett told the Manchester Journal that the ad was a mischaracterization of his work, and was disappointed to see what he views as ‘attack ads’ becoming commonplace in Vermont’s political landscape.
“It is so transparently incorrect, and clearly sent out by people who have never spoken to me. Even responding to it gives it more credence than it deserves. Apparently, the worst they can come up with is that I’m quiet,” said Plunkett, referring to a picture of a cricket that was included on the mailer.
“If they want someone who is going to be a grandstanding politician, that won’t be me. A lot of the work I do is not exactly the work that makes headlines, but it is building the relationships and trust with your fellow legislators in Montpelier, which I did on both sides of the aisle. Another thing that has bothered me about this is that Vermont is meant to be citizen legislators, people who just go and do their duty. This felt so drastically different than the type of politics in Vermont that I want to be a part of, and I was really saddened by the idea of others seeing this. I think this will be a disincentive for a lot of good people to run,” added Plunkett.
Following the second wave of mailers from Common Sense PAC, former legislator and concerned citizen Bob Stannard issued a complaint to the office of Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark, alleging that the PAC violated campaign finance laws related to properly disclosing donor names on the mailers, and required filing of a ‘mass-media report’ for the second mailer.
Stannard’s first complaint alleges that violations of 17 V.S.A. § 2972(c) occurred when names of individual contributors were not disclosed on the mailers, which only included the words ‘paid for by Common Sense PAC’.
“Section 2972(c)(1) is not complicated. An electioneering communication paid for by an independent expenditure-only political committee ‘shall also contain the name of any contributor who contributed more than 25 percent of all contributions and more than $2,000.00 to that committee … since the beginning of the two-year general election cycle,’ ” said Stannard in his complaint regarding the first statute, before sharing publicly available donor data from the Campaign Finance System of Vermont.
“By the time the PAC paid Spectrum another $10,470.72 on September 24 for the mailer attacking Senator Plunkett, it had taken in $25,000; $10,000 of it, 40 percent, came from a single California limited liability company, Durin Systems LLC. The law says that name belonged on the second postcard. That name was not disclosed. This is not a technicality. The whole point of § 2972(c) is that when a handful of people, or one out-of-state company, bankroll a political attack, the voters on the receiving end get to know who’s behind it. Common Sense PAC told the Secretary of State who its funders are, but it didn’t tell the voters,” added Stannard. 
Stannard’s second complaint, alleging violations of 17 V.S.A. § 2971, regarding the proper filing of a ‘mass media report’, said that Common Sense PAC failed to file the report for the second mailer.
“Section 2971(a) requires anyone who spends $500 or more (adjusted for inflation; the Secretary of State’s current form says $650) on a single mass media activity within 45 days before a general election to file a mass media report with the Secretary of State within 24 hours. Section 2971(d) adds a specific obligation for independent expenditure-only PACs that spend $5,000 or more in that window: a 24-hour report that also discloses every contribution over $100 accepted since the committee’s last report,” Stannard said in his complaint to the Attorney General’s office.
“The 45-day window before the November 3, 2026 general election opened on September 19. The PAC’s own October 1 disclosure reports a $10,470.72 payment to Spectrum Marketing Companies on September 24 for ‘Media – Postcards,’ which is the Plunkett attack mailer that was in our mailboxes within the past week. That expenditure is squarely inside the window and roughly double the §2971(d) threshold. A mass media report was due by September 25. As of today, the Secretary of State’s campaign finance system shows no mass media report from Common Sense PAC for that expenditure. The only mass media report on file is for the September 8 Bongartz mailer. This demonstrates that the PAC knew how to file that one. It chose not to file the second. It should be noted that the $10,000 from Durin Systems LLC arrived on September 16, after the PAC’s last periodic report. Section 2971(d) exists precisely so that a contribution like that gets disclosed in real time, before the election, rather than buried in a monthly report. That is the disclosure Vermonters were denied,” added Stannard.
Durin Systems LLC has drawn public attention following the second mailer, as the mailing address listed on the Campaign Finance System of Vermont’s website is listed as 228 Nevada Street, El Segundo, California. The listed address is associated with Durin Mining Technologies Corp, a California-based mining startup. The Manchester Journal reached out to the mining company to ask why they were donating to a county senate race in Vermont, and Founder and Chief Executive Officer Ted Feldmann explained that his company has nothing to do with the similarly named Durin Systems LLC, and is unsure as to why his company’s address is listed.
“I’m not familiar with Durin Systems LLC and have never heard of the Common Sense PAC. My business is called Durin Mining Technologies Corp. I am frankly very confused as to why the Durin name and El Segundo address were used. I double-checked our bank and credit card statements and can confirm that this donation was not from us. We do not make political donations,” said Feldmann.
Common Sense PAC Treasurer Richard Kaufman declined to comment on Stannard’s allegations, but did confirm that the California mining company was not involved.  
The mailer’s disclosure said that the mailer was “not authorized by any candidate or candidate’s committee.” Spike Whitmire confirmed for The Manchester Journal that his campaign had nothing to do with the mailer. The Manchester Journal was unable to reach Josh Williams via the phone number provided on his campaign website, but previous reporting by The Manchester Journal on the Common Sense PAC mailer regarding Seth Bongartz confirmed that Williams and his campaign had no influence on the PAC’s mailers. 
“To be clear, the Common Sense PAC is an independent political organization that has nothing to do with my campaign. I am not involved with any part of it, including the drafting of the recent flyer. But I would note that everyday Vermonters feel like they can’t afford to live here much longer and have become desperate for change. They feel that Mr. Plunkett and Mr. Bongartz have not delivered any relief.  During the last two years government spending is up over $1 billion, taxes have continued to rise and healthcare and Housing have become unaffordable. After twenty-two years of one party controlling both the House and Senate, everyday Vermonters are looking for a new breed of Senators to represent them that have practical  solutions, are fiscally responsible with their tax dollars and will demand change. Spike Whitmire and Josh Williams will fight for all Vermonters and deliver results,” said Whitmire.
Haley Sommer, senior advisor to the Attorney General said that the office has received the complaint, and outlined the review process going forward.
“The Attorney General’s Office has received the complaint, and it is currently under review. After a complaint is received, the general process is to reach out to the subject(s) named in the complaint and request a response by a specified deadline. It’s important to note that any information gathered by the Attorney General’s Office during the course of this process is confidential under 17 V.S.A. § 2904(a)(4),” said Sommer.

title: Fight trafficking by decriminalizing consensual adult sex work
description:
Vermont's prostitution laws make it harder for people to report exploitation and for survivors to rebuild their lives.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Fight trafficking by decriminalizing consensual adult sex work.
text:
This commentary is by Henri Binx, a co-founder and co-director of the Ishtar Collective and a member of Safe Sex Work Vermont.
Vermont has an opportunity to strengthen its response to human trafficking by reforming our state’s archaic anti-prostitution laws.
Vermont’s prostitution laws criminalize “sexual intercourse for hire” and “indiscriminate sexual intercourse without hire,” any sex outside marriage. They contribute to the stigma around sex work and reinforce the idea that it is inherently exploitative, when it is not. Trafficking involves force, fraud or coercion. Consensual adult sex work does not. When sex work is viewed as inherently exploitative, it is much harder to focus on the exploitation that defines trafficking.
In July, Safe Sex Work Vermont hosted a policy briefing in Burlington with Freedom Network USA, which describes itself as the largest coalition working on human trafficking in the United States. Freedom Network USA works with trafficking survivors, service providers, researchers and advocates on policy, training and support. The briefing was co-hosted by the Vermont Workers’ Center, Vermont Harm Reduction Advocates, People’s Health and Wellness Clinic, American Civil Liberties Union of Vermont, and the Vermont Association for Mental Health and Addiction Recovery. Elected officials, advocates, local anti-trafficking and domestic violence organizations and community members attended.
The briefing focused on what the evidence tells us about trafficking, sex work and criminalization. Trafficking is not necessarily caused by sex work. It occurs in all labor sectors, including agriculture, restaurants, hospitality, domestic work, factories and the sex trade. Poverty, economic instability, discrimination and lack of access to basic resources make people vulnerable to trafficking.
Criminalization compounds that vulnerability. When people fear arrest or prosecution, they are less likely to report violence or trafficking. Criminalization pushes sex work into more hidden conditions and creates barriers to healthcare, housing and other services.

READ MORE

A 2018 Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health meta-analysis reviewed more than 130 studies published since 1990. The review found evidence suggesting that repressive policing is associated with increased risks of physical and sexual violence, HIV and other sexually transmitted infections, and sex without condoms. It also found that decriminalization improves sex workers’ ability to negotiate safer sex and access justice and other services.
People who are afraid of arrest are less likely to report violence or seek help when they are being exploited. Trafficking survivors can also end up with prostitution-related criminal records, making it harder to find housing, employment and other resources they need to rebuild their lives.
Freedom Network USA specifically supports decriminalization as an anti-trafficking policy. The ACLU, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, the World Health Organization and the Global Network of Sex Work Projects also support the decriminalization of consensual adult sex work.
Decriminalization removes criminal penalties for consensual adult sex work while maintaining criminal penalties for trafficking and other conduct involving force, fraud or coercion. Vermont has robust statutes against human trafficking and related crimes. Decriminalization would not weaken those laws. Freedom Network USA argues it would bolster Vermont’s response to trafficking by making it easier for people to seek help and allowing law enforcement to focus on conduct that causes harm.
Decriminalization legislation has been introduced in both chambers of the Vermont Legislature over the past several years and has gained momentum in the past. As economic pressures increase and more Vermonters face financial insecurity, it is time to pay attention to policies that can reduce vulnerability to exploitation. Vermonters should ask their elected representatives to support decriminalization and give this legislation the serious consideration it deserves.
